The WTO adopted the departmental valuer’s report and determined the value of the asset at Rs.72 lakhs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also confirmed the valuation made by the WTO.

On second appeal, the assessee contended that while arriving at the figure the Departmental Valuation Officer did not take into consideration several factors which should have been considered and the estimated net profit per year should have been proportionately reduced:

The assessee carried forward depreciation for a number of years - the earliest of which, was 1998-99. For assessment year 2010-11, the Assessing Officer disallowed the amounts claimed as depreciation on the ground that the amendment in section 32(2), which removed the cap, was prospective and effective only from 1-4-2002.

The Commissioner (Appeals), however, reversed said decision.

The Tribunal upheld, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals).

The question came up for consideration was as to whether interpretation of section 32(2) as amended by Finance Act, 2001, could be given effect to beyond period of eight years, prior to its commencement?

On revenue's appeal:

The assessee, a financial corporation, was involved in long-term finance of infrastructural facilities. For the relevant assessment year, the assessee claimed deduction under section 36(1)(viii). The Assessing Officer disallowed the assessee’s claim.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) upheld the impugned order.

On appeal by the assessee, the revenue contended that the assessee had made representation only on March 28, 2000 seeking approval from the Central Board of Direct Taxes, in fact the assessment year was 1999-2000, such request for approval was not made to the concerned authorities at the earlier stage, and that the amendment to section 36(1)(viii) was with effect from 1-4-2000 and that the same could not have retrospective effect.

The land for the assessee-hotel was provided by a HUF whereas the building was constructed by one D who was an individual. The said HUF and the individual had entered into an agreement to form and promote the assessee-company. By a resolution, the Board of directors of the assessee approved the total expenditure incurred by D and directed that the same be incorporated in the books of the assessee for the year ended 30-6-1976 by crediting to the account of D. In its return for the assessment year 1977-78 the assessee disclosed the amount spent on the construction of the building.

In the assessment proceedings of D for the assessment years 1975-76 to 1977-78, the ITO refused to accept the figure disclosed by the said individual as the amount spent on construction. On the basis of the opinion of the Valuation Officer, the ITO was of the opinion that the total amount spent on construction was Rs. 14,11,485 and not Rs. 10,04,292 as claimed by D. He, accordingly, sought to add the difference to the income of D for the aforesaid years. D challenged the same by way of appeal and the matter was ultimately carried to the Tribunal. The Tribunal held that the said additions could not be made to the income of D and that he could not be asked to explain the source of the said investment. It observed that the assessee was responsible for explaining the source of investment in such construction.

On the basis of the above findings, a notice was given to the assessee proposing to reopen its assessment for the assessment year 1977-78. On writ petition against the notice the assessee contended (i) that the notice did not satisfy the requirements of section 151 of the Act as section 151 requires not only the approval of the Board but also the approval of the Commissioner where a notice under section 147/148 is issued after the expiry of eight years; (ii) that section 147(b) was not attracted in the present case and, therefore, it could not be invoked by the assessing authority against the petitioner; (iii) that the jurisdictional facts necessary to invoke the power under section 147(a) were not present in this case and, hence, the notice was invalid.

The Assessing Officer noted that assessee had earned tax free dividend income and he required the assessee to explain as to why disallowance under rule 8D should not be made. Assessee submitted that in order to pay 'upfront fee' of Rs. 150 crores to AAI, assessee had approached banks for such a payment and since funding by way of borrowing of such payment was taking time it was decided to bring equity and the surplus arising from the operation was kept in mutual funds. When the funding was received, then the same got substituted by the borrowed money of Rs. 150 crores from the banks which was utilised in incurring of cost of airport project. Thus, investment in funds was not made from borrowed funds but from share capital and internal accruals from time to time.

However, the Assessing Officer applied the provision of rule 8D for making the disallowance.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that same could not be disallowed, because assessee had owned interest free funds sufficient to cover the investment made and therefore, no apportionment of any interest expenses could be made for the purpose of disallowance under section 14A. He further held that provision of rule 8D were not applicable in assessment year 2007-08 as the same had been made applicable for the assessment year 2008-09.

On appeal:

The assessee-company was in the business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts. During relevant assessment years, the assessee collected revenue from timeshare members but same was not recognised as revenue for the current year. The explanation of the assessee was that it had considered only 40 per cent of the membership fees collected as income and the balance 60 per cent was treated as deferred income. It was stated that the balance amount was to be spread over the next 33 years during which the assessee was expected to provide timeshare facilities to the members. It was also stated that in order to provide various facilities during the next 33 years, it had to incur many costs. Further explanation of the assessee was that the AMC was exclusively meant to cover the maintenance of various facilities which were an integral part of the timeshare property. These charges were for the maintenance of various electronic gadgets made available in the accommodation, furniture, kitchen equipments, central air-conditioning etc. On the other hand, the consideration for future obligations received in the initial stages was towards transfer facility from one resort to another, split, accumulation and advancing facility, domestic and international exchange, transmission, upgradation etc. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and, hence, income had to be accounted for on accrual basis. He was of the view that the receipt was undisputedly income as the assessee itself had shown it as deferred income. However, the Act does not recognise the concept of deferred income and, hence, the assessee’s explanation could not be accepted. Considering all these aspects, the Assessing Officer added certain amount being 60 per cent of the receipts shown by the assessee as advance subscription. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee had to construct holiday resorts and provide timeshare facilities over a period of time. Further, the annual subscription fee collected met only the maintenance of the resorts. The utility charges collected ‘were as per actual consumption of things like electricity, water etc. It did not cover major renovation and repairs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also took note of the fact that over a period of 24 years, the assessee had to incur about 171 per cent of the original investment for major renovation and replacement of assets. Accordingly, he upheld the contentions of the assessee and deleted the addition in all the years.

On revenue’s appeal :

For the assessment years 1974-75 and 1975-76, the assessee declared the gross annual letting value of a building (constructed in 1938) at Rs. 6,000 each, but the ITO valued the same at Rs. 12,000. The assessee's appeals before the AAC and the Tribunal were unsuccessful. Relying on the Supreme Court's decision in the case of M.M. Chawla v. J.S. Sethi [1970] 2 SCR 390, the Tribunal rejected the assessee's contention that, in view of the provisions of the East Punjab Urban Rent Restriction Act, 1949, he could not charge more than fair rent determined there under and the annual letting value could not, therefore, exceed the rent he could get in law if the premises were rented out.

On reference:

■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of running resorts and hotels. It had devised concept of time shares wherein a person acquiring membership of such time share was assured of stay facility in resorts/hotels over period of membership. It followed a consistent accounting policy of recognizing a portion of time-share membership fee receipts as income in year of receipt and deferring balance to be recognized over tenure of services.

■

The Assessing Officer was of view that entire amount should be taxed in year of receipt and added deferred income to assessee's taxable income

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the additions made on account of deferred income.

■

On revenue's appeal to the Tribunal:

The land of the assessee was acquired by the State Government almost 15 years back. As per court’s order, during the relevant year, the assessee received enhanced compensation along with interest in respect of this land. The assessee filed return of income for the assessment year 2001-02 declaring income of Rs. 34,392 and vide this return, refund of Rs. 65,646 was claimed. The Assessing Officer noticed that total interest shown was Rs. 13,05,585 whereas the returned income was declared by the assessee at Rs. 34,392 only and that the assessee had allocated its interest receipts from the financial year 1986-87 to financial year 2000-01 but no tax payable was shown for the assessment years 1987-88 to 1991-92 on the plea that the assessment years 1987-88 to 1991-92 were beyond ten years and, therefore, were not within the purview of tax. The Assessing Officer held that the assessee was liable to pay tax for all these years in which he had earned income on account of interest and accordingly, he worked out the tax payable by the assessee.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) sustained the impugned addition on ground that the assessee could not be allowed double benefit, i.e., on one hand he could not deny payment of tax on interest either during the year of receipt or the year of accrual and, on the other hand, he could not claim benefit of whole amount of TDS.

On second appeal:

The assessee-company filed its return and claimed for carry forward and set off of unabsorbed depreciation of Rs. 17.73 crore.

The return and same was accepted by the Assessing Officer. Thereafter, the Assessing Officer proposed to rectify the same under section 154 so as to withdrew depreciation allowed to be carried forward to the tune of Rs. 13.71 crore on the ground that unabsorbed depreciation relating to the assessment years 1989-90 to 1998-99 was not eligible to be carried forward beyond a period of eight assessment years. However, in the light of the reply filed by the assessee, the proposed rectification was dropped.

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer issued a notice under section 148 and completed the assessment by withdrewing a sum of Rs. 13.71 crores from unabsorbed depreciation eligible for carry forward and set off.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) dismissed the same.

On second appeal:

The assessee won the first prize of Tripura State lottery in the draw held on 14-6-1983. One ‘S’ filed suit claiming a share in the lottery amount as joint owner. The Munsif Court ordered stay of the disbursement of the prize amount to the assessee due to which a delay of three years was caused in the disbursement of the lottery prize to the assessee and the prize amount was disbursed to him in October 1987. For the assessment year 1984-85, the assessee filed return on 18-12-1987 declaring lottery income. The return was rejected as time-barred and the petition for condonation of delay was also rejected. However, while completing the assessment for the assessment year 1988-89, the Assessing Officer also included the income from lottery because the assessee had received the lottery amount during the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1988-89. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee did not main- tain any books of account and, therefore, the income from the lottery winning would be assessed in the assessment year 1988-89 on receipt basis.

The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the Assessing Officer himself had determined the tax to be deducted at source in respect of the lottery amount as early as in July 1983. From this fact, the Commissioner (Appeals) came to the conclusion that the Assessing Officer had recognized the assessee’s right to receive the amount during a period much earlier than the accounting period relevant for the assessment year 1988-89. The Commissioner (Appeals) considered that the assessee, in accordance with the method of accounting followed by him, accepted the right to receive the lottery amount as an accrual of income and accordingly filed a return of income for the assessment year 1984-85 and, hence, the same amount could not be assessed in a subsequent year.

On appeal by the revenue :

For the assessment years 1982-83, 1983-84, 1984-85 and 1985-86 the assessments were completed on 7-10-1982, 25-4-1984, 24-4-1985 and 15-10-1985, respectively. Thereafter, the assessee filed returns under the Amnesty Scheme announced by the CBDT and disclosed the value of gold ornaments and jewellery. The Assessing Officer, after regularising the returns by the issue of notices under section 17, completed the assessments for all the years in question on 30-3-1990. Thereafter, the Commissioner formed an opinion that the value of the shares held by the assessee in various companies were not correctly valued by the Assessing Officer and. therefore, he issued notices under section 25(2). The assessee objected the proceedings under section 25(2) on the ground that the same was barred by limitation inasmuch as the valuation of shares was concluded by orders passed on 7-10-1982, 25-4-1984, 24-4-1985 and 15-10-1985, respectively.

On second appeal:

■

The assessee was supposed to repay Rs. 1.83 crores which was kept by them for a period of ten years as sales tax collected from customers. The assessee was given a benefit or incentive by State Government to keep this money with them for setting up an industry in a backward area. Otherwise, the assessee had to pay entire sales tax collected from customers, to the Government immediately as per the due dates mentioned under Maharashtra Sales Tax Act.

■

Over a period of 10 years, the assessee had collected and kept with it an amount of Rs. 1.83 crores and this amount had to be repaid in subsequent 5 equal installments. The Maharashtra State Government had come out with a 'Scheme of Incentive' as per which they scientifically calculated the Net Present Value of sales tax collected. In simple words, if the assessee prepays i.e., before five years, they would be paying lesser amount.

■

The assessee opted to repay its sales tax liability of Rs. 1.83 crores during the year under consideration at its NPV of Rs. 93.57 lakhs and this NPV was arrived at scientifically by State Government. Thus, the assessee had collected and kept sales tax of Rs. 1.83 crores for 10 years and repaid (prepaid) only Rs. 93.57 lakhs as final payment in this year i.e., no further payment was to be done by assessee. Thus, the assessee had got benefit of Rs. 90.22 lakhs.

■

The Assessing Officer considered it as 'income' in this year invoking section 2(24)(xviii).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

The assessee was engaged in construction activity. During the course of search at the premises of the directors of the assessee company, certain documents related to the assessee were found and seized which indicated that certain sum was paid on behalf of assessee by 'A' for construction work to B for construction regarding hotel.

Thereafter, the assessee was issued with show cause notice on 30-3-2021 requiring to show cause as to why the said amount should not be treated as undisclosed income by treating the same as unexplained money under section 69A and Assessing Officer called for report from DVO for estimation of said construction expenditure.

Thereafter, the AO made addition in hands of assessee on account of expenditure incurred towards hotel.

Addition made in the hands of the assessee was restricted to the difference in the cost estimated by the DVO and the cost declared by the assessee in its books by Commissioner (Appeals).

The assessee submitted that the addition made by the Commissioner (Appeals) on the basis of valuation report could not be sustained particularly considering the fact that the DVO report relied upon by the Commissioner (Appeals) was barred by limitation by taking into consideration section 142A(6).

The assessee-firm was running a nursing home. According to the assessee, the construction of the nursing home was started in 1978 and completed in 1985. The ITO on the basis of materials, seized in a search on 19-12-1985 from the assessee and its managing partner, held that the cost of construction of the nursing home admitted by the assessee at Rs. 53,860,020 for the entire period covered by the assessment years 1980-81 to 1985-86 was an understatement and, consequently, he referred the question of the cost of construction of the nursing home to the Valuation Officer. The Valuation Officer did not submit his report to the ITO till the date of assessments on 23-12-1986. Since, it was necessary for the ITO to complete the assessments, he had started making his own enquiries regarding the probable cost of construction and estimated the cost of construction of the building. The assessee filed appeals before the Commissioner (Appeals). When the appeals were pending, the Valuation Officer gave his report estimating the probable cost of construction of the building together with the cost of lift at Rs. 45.86 lakhs. Before the Commissioner (Appeals) both the revenue as well as the assessee agreed that this method of valuation adopted by the ITO ‘might be discarded and the more preferable method of the adoption of a rate per square feet of plinth area would be ideal. Thus, the entire exercise which was so far taken was discarded and a new proposal was placed by the ITO before the Commissioner (Appeals). In the new proposal, the ITO stated (i) that the building in question consisted of a front block, a rear block and a central block and all of them had ground floor with four floors above and the front block had three more floors completed, (ii) that in the accounting year 1983-84 construction of third floor of central block and second floor of rear block was completed, (iii) that in the accounting year 1984-85 construction of fourth floor of central block and third and fourth floors of rear block was completed, (iv) that in the accounting year 1985-86 construction of fifth to seventh floors of front block and fitting of elevator and other fittings were completed, (v) that the cost of construction of the building adopted by him was based on the Valuation Officer’s report which was based on CPWD rates for each year, (vi) that in the cost of construction of the nursing home certain amounts representing expenses on water and sanitary fittings, etc., were added, and (vii) that the total cost of the building and fittings were, thus, estimated at Rs. 66.1 lakhs. The Commissioner (Appeals) practically accepted these estimates, but by making only certain marginal adjustments in expenses, fixed the cost at Rs. 63.74 lakhs. Further he approved the spread over of the additions to be made in three assessment years. However, he reduced the estimated cost of lift, medical equipments and furniture and fittings by Rs. 97,000, Rs. 30,000 and Rs. 1,20,000 respectively.

pay Rs. 2,72,25,000 instead of Rs. 4,45,50,000 and, thereby save Rs. 1,73,25,000. It was contended that under the circumstances, the discounted value of interest cannot be taken into account. That, in other words, the assessee got rid of annual liability of Rs. 89,10,000 by making immediate payment of Rs. 2,72,25,000 in first year. 13. Mr. Dastur next contended that in this case, the assessee is claiming interest to the extent of Rs. 2,72,25,000 which the Assessing Officer disallows but, while disallowing, the Assessing Officer gives deduction to the assessee at the rate of Rs. 89,10,000 amounting to Rs. 4,45,50,000 over five years and, therefore, even the Assessing Officer accepts the contention of the assessee that Rs. 2,72,25,000 did not constitute capital expenditure but it constituted revenue expenditure. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has given to the assessee deduction of a larger amount by Rs. 1,73,25,000. However, Mr. Dastur concedes that in absolute terms, the Assessing Officer has given to the assessee more deduction but not in terms of the present value. He contended that the present value was Rs. 4,45,50,000 spread over five years which was the same as Rs. 2,72,25,000 in the first year. Therefore, there is no loss to the revenue. Therefore, the entire question is academic. Mr. Dastur contended that it was not open to the Assessing Officer to insist on the spread over particularly when the liability under the contract arose to the assessee in the first year unless the Assessing Officer holds that the contract was a sham. However, in this case there is no such findings and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was not entitled to change the terms of the contract. In the circumstances, the Assessing Officer was bound to proceed on the footing that the liability had accrued in the assessment year in question i.e. the assessment year 1997-98. That, if the assessee pays rent in advance in the first year under a contract which states that there shall be no refund of the rent paid then the assessee must get deduction in the first year itself and, therefore, the only question which the Assessing Officer was required to decide was whether there was a liability to pay interest during 1996-97 itself and if so the assessee was entitled to obtain full deduction during the assessment year 1997-98. He contended that the Courts should not take into account extraneous factors while deciding the claim of the assessee. In this case, he pointed out that the Tribunal has proceeded on the footing that the entire measure was adopted because, the assessee had surplus income whereas Maliram Makharia Stock Brokers Private Limited had brought forward losses. He contended that the assessee paid Rs. 2,72,25,000 up-front and further after five years the assessee repays the full face value of the debenture, with premium and, therefore, payment of Rs. 2,72,25,000 represented interest. Mr. Dastur relied upon the balance sheet to show that the entire amount of Rs. 6,00,00,000 continued to be the liability of the assessee right up to 31-3-2001. In the circumstances, the assessee was entitled to deduction for the full amount in the first year. Mr. Dastur, therefore, contends that in this case the spread over should have been refused because the liability arose in the very first year. Mr. Dastur contended that good accounting is not always the correct law. He relied upon the judgment of the Supreme Court in the case of Tuticorin Alkali Chemicals & Fertilizers Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 227 ITR 1721 and he contended that if the assessee was entitled to deduction for the full amount of Rs. 2,72,25,000 in the first year and that if the deduction depended on the terms of the contract, then it cannot be denied on the ground that the assessee has not debited the full amount to the Profit & Loss Account because according to the Supreme Court judgment, deduction does not depend on what the assessee debit but it depends on the provisions of the law. That, in this case the assessee has not debited Rs. 2,72,25,000 in the first year but that cannot be the ground for disallowing the deduction. He contended that tax cannot be levied on the basis of the entries which an assessee makes. He relied upon the judgment of the Gujarat High Court in the case of CIT v. Gujarat Mineral Development Corpn. [1981] 132 ITR 3772 . He also relied upon the judgment in the case of Buckau Wolf New India Engg. Works Ltd. (supra). The assessee was a partner with 50 per cent share in a firm 'MH' and as per agreement notwithstanding his retirement from partnership on 24-10-1963 he continued to hold 50 per cent share in the goodwill of the firm and for the user of his share of goodwill by the firm, he was entitled to receive a sum of Rs. 50,000 per annum. For the assessment year 1983-84, the assessee, a partner in a registered firm, earned certain amount as her share of income. As a result of search conducted on 5-9-1985 by the department in the business and residential premises of the said firm and others, the revenue came to know that the assessee had constructed a house between 1981 and 1982. As regards the amount of Rs. 70,000, it was held that the assessee being a lady from a business family, and a partner in a registered firm, she could not have kept a cash balance of Rs. 70,000 for a decade in an almirah when she had taken loans for construction of the property and even for the purchase of the land in January 1980 which she would not have done if she had really a saving of Rs. 70,000 with her.

The appellants filed a refund claim against provisionally approved price list for the period from 30.3.76 to 13.7.1976 The price list was finalised on 14.6.1982. held.text: Explanation 8 under section 43(1) which clarifies that where any amount is paid or is payable as interest in connection with the acquisition of an asset, so much of such amount as is relatable to any period after such asset, is first put to use shall not be included, and shall be deemed never to have been included in the actual cost of such asset, was inserted by the Finance Act, 1986 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1974. This provision, no doubt, was not before the Tribunal when it dealt with the question. Therefore, it would have been proper if the Tribunal had considered the effect of this insertion and decided the claim of assessee. The matter was, accordingly, remanded back to the Tribunal for fresh adjudication. While deciding the matter afresh, the principles laid down by the Apex Court in Challapalli Sugars Ltd. v. CIT [1975] 98 ITR 167 should be kept in view by the Tribunal.

■

The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed relief to the assessee by taking view that the assessee is in the business of four luxury resort in Goa. The assessee introduced unique project for fractional ownership. Such unique concept was also known as time share vacation facilities which were sold to various members. To keep the maintenance of resort, the maintenance was interested to associated group companies. The assessee in earlier years credited sale proceeds of timeshare in accounts and charge of construction against such sale proceeds. Many of members not utilized whole week to said resort but only spent a part of week. Such timeshare weeks were converted into sometime share point. The assessee also engaged 3 group companies and allotted certain timeshare points to such group entities for marketing on identical term and condition. Contract with such companies who are also having forfeiture clause. In case purchaser failed to make the payment against membership and maintenance fees their membership were forfeited. The legal ownership of resort building was with assessee. The assessee retained the building at zero cost. In the balance sheet of assessee company, the building or the land were not reflected in earlier years despite retaining legal ownership of resort building. On coming to know that many members are failing to make payment of their annual maintenance and membership charges. Such unrealized charge was in respect of 1721 members who failed to clear their dues and on forfeiture of such timeshare; dues of group companies were reimbursed. The Commissioner (Appeals) on appreciation of fact also held that the assessee has shown forfeiture rights in their balance sheet as trading asset. The total recovery of Group Companies which was engaged in management and maintaining of selling of time share at the end of relevant financial year was of 15203 timeshare weeks which were forfeited. The assessee was having total payment for forfeiture which was free from all encumbrances were of Rs. 22.28 crores. The valuation of all 4 resorts through valuer on capitalization of 292 forfeited units which were from all encumbrances was for a sum of Rs. 22.28 crores. The assessee capitalized as per actual payment made to 4 group companies at Rs. 3.37 crores and improvement against land at Rs. 18.91 crores as a cost improvement trade building. Since capitalization was made at the end of year, the assessee claimed 1/2 of 10 per cent which is of Rs. 94.57 lakhs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also held that entire consideration paid by assessee to its group companies for getting the identifiable unit from all encumbrances were to be treated as cost of improvement of capital asset which has to be incorporated in the balance sheet as tangible asset and thus, the assessee was right in claiming depreciation over the building block. The assessee vehemently argued that timeshare weeks so acquired by assessee in the relevant financial year were capitalized as a part of cost of building were subsequently sold in the form of fractional ownership of the apartments. The fractional ownership gains have been offered to tax. In subsequent years, the assessee offered from capital gain on transfer of such ownership of the resort apartment aggregating of Rs. 170 crores. To support such claim, the assessee furnished copy of financial statement and computation of income from assessment year 2018-19 to 2023-24. It is found that all such facts are duly acknowledged by the Commissioner (Appeals) at page no. 9 of his order. The assessee also furnished the copy of assessment order passed under section 143(3) read with section 143(3A) and 143(3B) or 144B for assessment year 2018-19 from 2022-23 and 2023-24. No counter arguments were made before that the fractional ownership gains have been offered to tax in subsequent years. It is also found that similar claims have been allowed in subsequent assessment years. Thus, on independent appreciation of facts, no reason is found to interfere with the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 34]

In a taxing law, one is not concerned with the policy of the Government relating to credit control, etc. The court has to go by the plain words in the statute. The words in the statute say that the amendment by which section 40A(8) was inserted will take effect from 1-4-1976, meaning thereby the assessment year 1976-77. If that is so, the income for the previous year ending 30-4-1975, alone has to be taken into account irrespective of the consequences. In this view of the matter, the income for the year ended on 30-4-1975, was rightly taken into account by the AO and the Commissioner (Appeals), while rejecting the claim of the assessee that the sum should not have been added to the income for the assessment year 1976-77.

There is, no scope for taking into account the interest income of the assessee and setting off the same against the expenditure by way of interest, before applying section 40A(8). This is because the section itself does not use the word ‘net interest’.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

on 31- 3-1983, some flats in the ground floor, upper ground floor first, second and other floors were not booked, then the most proximate rate at which invitation was advertised should be adopted as the value for those flats. White adopting the rates, care must be exercised to ensure that the rates adopted were for those respective floors, i.e., the rates of second floor could not be adopted for valuing the third floor, unless both the floors had the same rate. The rates at which the flat space was sold were similar to recoverable debt and since the flat price was payable in instalments spread over a few years, the instalments that became due after the valuation date needed to be discounted to arrive at the present worth of the space involved. Further, since the building in which the space was allotted to the several buyers required the sanction of the L & DO on payment of commercialisation charges, it was very much a charge on the present value of the flat space. Similarly, the settlement with the tenant, who had carried the matter to the High Court that was ultimately settled in 1986, was also a charge on the present value of the flats. Since the property was under construction as on the relevant valuation dates, and some more cost had to be incurred, as the construction got completed in 1987, i.e., almost four and three years from 31-3-1983 and 31-3-1984, respectively this element equated as interest also required to be allowed deduction of for arriving at the present value of the flat space.

The Assessing Officer was, accordingly, directed to recalculate the value of the space on the two valuation dates separately, as above.

The appeals were, accordingly, partly allowed.

The question whether Schedule III inserted with effect from 1-4-1989 was applicable to earlier years, had been decided on the basis of well-settled principles of law as enunciated by the Supreme Court in CWT v. Sharvan Kumar Swarup & Sons [1994] 210 ITR 886. Hence, no referable question of law arose from the Tribunal’s order directing the Assessing Officer to apply Schedule III while valuing the cinema houses in question. Further, there was merit in the assessee’s submission that profit-yielding method is a recognised method of valuation. In the case of S. Paramjit Singh v. WTO [1995] 55 ITD 331 (Chd.), the department’s own Valuation Officer had applied the same method in the context of cold storage. It was not understood as to why the same method could not be applied in the case of a cinema theatre. Hence, no referable question of law arose from the Tribunal’s order in directing the Assessing Officer to apply the yield method for valuation of the two cinema houses if rule 8 barred the application of Schedule III.

R. P. Singh for the Appellant. Sudhir Sehgal for the Respondent.

It is observed that as per the provisions of section 36(1)(viii) and relevant explanation clause (h) provides that any loan/ advance where the terms under which money is loaned/ advanced provide for repayment along with interest thereof, during a period of not less than 5 years. It is noticed that the Assessing Officer interpreted the same to include only those loans which are provided for the period 5 year or more only, accordingly he excluded all those loans which are preclosed in 5 years or less are not eligible to claim deduction u/s 36(1)(viii). He excluded the eligible profit on the loans which are repaid in 5 years or less than 5 years. Accordingly he recalculated the 20 per cent of the eligible interest instead of eligible profit earned from the long term finance business. After considering the submissions of both the parties and detailed findings of Commissioner (Appeals), it is observed that Commissioner (Appeals) had placed reliance on the decision of Gujarat High Court in the case of Principal Commissioner of Income-tax-2 v. Gruh Finance Ltd. [2017] 81 taxmann.com 388/248 Taxman 26 (Gujarat) wherein it was held that the nature of Long Term finance for the purposes of section 36(1)(viii) was to be seen at the time of sanction of loans and in case of no change in the character of account i.e. tenure being more than 5 years even after assignment, the same was held eligible for deduction with section 36(1)(viii). Since Commissioner(Appeals) had followed the decision of High Court, the Court is inclined to respectfully follow the same, hence the ground raised by the revenue is accordingly dismissed.

- in that case of valuation. In the case before the Supreme Court, the rule under the Wealth-tax Rules, 1957 had adopted the method of capitalizing income on a number of years' purchase value. The Supreme Court emphasized that this was essentially a rule of evidence as to the choice of one of the well-accepted methods of valuation to achieve uniformity in valuation resulting from the application of different methods to properties of a similar nature and character. Rule 8D is reasonable in its nature . That, however, is not dispositive of the question as to whether the rule can be regarded as prospective or retrospective in nature. In determining as to whether a rule in a piece of subordinate legislation is to be regarded as prospective or retrospective, an important aspect that has been emphasized by the Supreme Court in the aforesaid decision is as to whether the rule embodies what is essentially a well-known, a well-settled or well-accepted method. As a matter of fact in the instant case there can be no doubt about the position that rule 8D has essentially put into place an artificial method of estimating the expenditure that can be regarded as being relatable to income that does not form part of the total income under the Act. Before the insertion of section 14A, there was no specific method of determining the expenditure incurred in relation to non-taxable income. Looking at the totality of the circumstances, the measure of 0.5 per cent is reasonable. Hence, while the method of computation provided in rule 8D is fair and reasonable to pass muster under article 14, the method must take effect prospectively. [Para 66]

Section 7(1) as it stood in the relevant the provided that the value of period the asset, other than cash, shall be estimated on the basis of the open market value. Rule 1BB referred only to valuation of residential building. If that be so, there was no illegality in valuing a commercial building which was rented out on the basis of a rental receipt by the assessee.

When a new Schedule is inserted and there is no indication in the section that it has to be given retrospective effect, the provisions contained under the Schedule, in the ordinary course, cannot be given retrospective effect.

On an examination of the relevant section as well as the provisions contained in the Schedule one does not understand rule 8(c) read with rule 20 as clarificatory in nature so as to be given retrospective effect. In view of the above the Tribunal was fully justified in upholding the method of valuation on rental capitalisation.

Note : The case was decided against the assessee.

In the case of CIT v. Alcock Ashdown & Co. Ltd. [1997] 224 ITR 353/ 90 Taxman 521, the Supreme Court observed that the moment an asset is acquired or purchased for the purpose of the business, it is capital employed, though the asset as such is not actually utilised or used during the accounting year. In the chain of events, the earliest act or event is the purchase or acquisition of the asset. That by itself entitles the assessee to get the relief. The 'employment' of capital is done or over. The subsequent or later events, including the actual user of the asset, have nothing to do with the matter.

Considering the view taken by the Apex Court, there was no justification to interfere with the Tribunal's view that the benefit of section 80J was to be allowed to the assessee on the value of incomplete job.

In the case of CIT v. New India Industries Ltd. [1995] 212 ITR 653/ 80 Taxman 86, the Supreme Court observed that when the terms of the agreement were modified and provided for repayment beyond seven years, then that should be included in the capital computation for the purposes of the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964. Therefore, following the above view, there was no infirmity in the Tribunal's view in the instant case that borrowed capital payable beyond seven years after amendment in the original agreement should be taken into account for capital computation for the purpose of relief under section 80J.

In the instant case, assessee’s half share in the capital gain was Rs. 54,118. Out of this, deduction of Rs. 5,000 under section 80T had to be allowed. If that was allowed, the capital gain would come to Rs. 49,118. This deduction under section 80T had not been allowed in the original assessment as the capital gain assessed was Rs. 3,259 which was below Rs. 5,000. Hence, after deduction of Rs. 5,000 under section 80T, capital gain was only Rs. 49,118. Since this was below Rs. 50,000 even the CBDT could not accord sanction for reopening the assessment beyond the period of eight years. Thus, the reassessment proceedings were invalid and the reassessment order dated 24-12-1983 could not stand.

In view of the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladin & Sons v. CIT [1969] 74 ITR 651 , the enhanced compensation of Rs. 60,112 in which the assessee had half share which was awarded by the District Judge on 18-8-1972 was assessable only in the assessment year 1973-74 and not in the assessment year 1966-67. Thus, the ITO was wrong in assessing the above amount in the assessment year 1966-67 by his order dated 24-12-1983. This principle was applicable even in respect of Rs. 41,606 in which the assessee had half share, awarded by the District Judge on 18-8-1972 for severance of land resulting in injurious effect on the remaining land. Hence, this amount was not assessable in the assessment year 1966-67.

Further, in view of the decision of the Kerala High Court in CIT v. Smt. M. Subaida Beevi [1986] 160 ITR 557 the sum of Rs. 41,606 in which the assessee had a share had been awarded only by way of damages for injurious effect on the balance of the land belonging to the assessee and it was not related to the transfer of the acquired land. Thus, it could not be treated as part of the capital gain.

In CIT v. Smt. Sankari Manickyamma [1976] 105 ITR 172 , the Andhra Pradesh High Court had held that the right to receive compensation or interest accrues to the person from the date when the statutorily designated authorities determine the same. In the instant case also, the District Judge awarded the interest in his judgement dated 18-8-1972 and so it was assessable only in the assessment year 1973-74. In the result the assessee’s appeal was to be allowed and the departmental appeal was to be dismissed.

The wooden staging in the petitioner's cold storage could not be regarded as a part of the building. If the value of wooden staging estimated by the Valuation Officer was excluded, the total investment on the buildings of the cold storage, even according to the valuation officer, would be only Rs. 82,178. Hence, there was no basis for any reasonable belief by the ITO that the petitioner's investment on buildings during the relevant assessment year exceeded the amount shown by him, i.e., Rs. 54,852, by more than Rs. 50,000. Hence, he could not issue a notice under section 148 beyond 8 years from the date of the close of the relevant assessment year. That notice was clearly beyond time and invalid.

Hence, the petition was allowed and the notice was quashed.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

There is a difference between the purchase price of the flat and the value as per Stamp Valuation Authority. However, as a matter of fact the property was purchased in the earlier year in view of the payments being made in entirety in the earlier financial year and the details of payments have already been extracted. The first payment of the flat was made on 12-6-2012 and all the payments were completed till the financial year 2018-19. So far as the observation of the Assessing Officer is concerned that the difference between the purchase consideration and the value as per stamp valuation authority is to be taxed at section 56(2)(x), it is noted that the provisions of clause (x) of sub-section (2) of section 56 were inserted by Finance Act, 2017, with effect from 1-4-2017 and was not applicable because this flat was brought prior to that. Moreover, as per the first proviso to section 56(2)(x), it is stated that when the date of agreement fixing the amount for transfer of immovable property and the date of registration are not same. The stamp valuation on the date of registration may be taken for the purpose of this sub-clause but in any case, the insertion of this clause was made by the Finance Act, 2017 and was not applicable when the flat was bought. So far as the provisions of section 56(2)(vii)(b) are concerned, the clause (b) was inserted by Finance Act, 2015 with effect from 1-4-2014, which provides that in case consideration which is less than the stamp value of the property by an amount exceeding Rs. 50,000, then the stamp value of such property as exceeded amount shall be added to the income of the assessee. However, the proviso provides that the stamp value of the property on the date of agreement may be taken for the purpose of this consideration. Even this clause does not apply to the assessee as this is applicable for assessment year 2014-15 and therefore, these provisions are not applicable to the present transaction which was agreed to in assessment year 2013-14. It is also noted that this new charging section brought under statute book is applicable prospectively not retrospectively. [Para 10]

■

Considering the facts of the case in the light of decision of the coordinate Bench, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) is to be set aside and the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the addition. [Para 11]

■

In the result, the appeal of the assessee is allowed.

■

For an identical question of law, this Court has decided in favour of the assessee and dismissed Tax Case (Appeal) No.1419 of 2010, arising out of I.T.A.No.1705/Mds/2008 dated 06.07.2010, for the assessment year 2003-2004 in the assessee's own case. [Para 14]

■

In Tax Case (Appeal) No.1419 of 2010, this Court has held that the dictum laid down by the Andhra Pradesh High Court in CIT v. Treasure Island Pvt Ltd. ([I.T.T.A.No. 241 of 2012, dated 10-7-2013]) was confirmed by the Supreme Court in respect of Time-Share business. The judgment of the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Shyam Telelink Ltd. [2019] 101 taxmann.com 218 / 260 Taxman 402 / 410 ITR 31 (Delhi) and the judgment of the Gujarat High Court in CIT v. Winner Business Link (P.) Ltd. [2015] 55 taxmann.com 468 / 230 Taxman 399 (Gujarat), following the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Treasure Island Pvt Ltd (supra) and the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Dinesh Kumar Goel [2011] 9 taxmann.com 188 / 197 Taxman 375 / 331 ITR 10 (Delhi), also confirmed by the Supreme Court. Thus, the Courts have clearly established the legal position, approving the method of accounting adopted by the assessee. Courts have given legal sanctity to the concept of deferred income as matching principle. [Para 15]

■

Hence, this Court has no doubt that the accounting method adopted by the assessee has been approved by the Supreme Court. Therefore, there is no necessity to interfere with the order passed by Income Tax Appellate Tribunal, Chennai, in the batch of Tax Case Appeals disposed through combined order dated 15.07.2005. [Para 16]

■

For the reasons stated above, the substantial questions of law are held against the appellant/Revenue. [Para 17]

■

As a result, Tax Case (Appeal) Nos.1465 to 1469 of 2010 stand dismissed. There shall be no order as to costs. [Para 18]

issued by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor and promoters, demanding the payment of amount due under the consent award. No payments having been made by the corporate debtor, an application under section 7 was filed by the financial creditors. [Para 19]

The instant Tribunal noticed the relevant clauses of share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement and consent terms, The issue was as to whether the amount invested by the financial creditors can be said to be 'financial debt' or not. [Para 22] The Supreme Court has emphasized the Judgment of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 747/155 SCL 622, that in the various categories under (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5, the Legislature has only given instances, which could be included in the term 'financial debt'. However, the list is not exhaustive but inclusive. One may first consider as to whether the investment made by the financial creditors have commercial effect of borrowing or not. One would have noticed that raising of amount by the company through share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement was a commercial borrowing, since the said transaction has direct effect with the business, which was carried out by the corporate debtor, i.e. construction of building and township. The supplementary share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 12-7-2008, where the agreement clearly noted that 'the Company now requires further funding to the extent of Rs. 50 in order to carry out objectives of the Business Plan, i.e. approval of township, and actual execution of the township as per the designs prepared by the Company architects'. Thus, the raising of the amount through the said agreement has the commercial effect of borrowing, which is clearly demonstrated by the statements contained in the supplementary agreement. The use of expression 'further funding' indicates that transaction has commercial effect of borrowing. Now the question remains to be considered is as to whether the investment by the financial creditors can be said to be an investment by disbursal against consideration of time value of money. The expression 'time value of money' encompasses in itself the concept of time value of the disbursement. One would have already noticed the various clauses of amended and restated share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 14-5-2008 and would have extracted the relevant clauses, where company and promoters were obliged to purchase all the shares held by the non-defaulting shareholders at a price that provides the non-defaulting shareholders at an internal rate of return of 15 per cent per annum compounded annually or the Fair Market Value, whichever is higher. Clauses 19.1(a) and 19.6(a) as extracted, contains clear indication that investment was with an eye to earn profits and the investment was for consideration for the time value of money. Binding term sheet, which one would have also noticed above also contains several clauses, which indicate that proposals were given by the promoters to develop the project and provide an exit to the investors and the exit consideration was carrying IRR of 17 per cent. [Para 30]

It is further relevant to notice that section 7 application filed by the financial creditor was not based only on the consent award passed by the arbitrator on 19-1-2021, but all previous transactions were also basis of the application. The application filed under section 7 cannot be said to be an application for execution of consent decree, rather section 7 application was filed on account of default committed by the company in not honouring its obligation under different agreements. [Para 31]

Certain judgments, have been relied by the appellant in support of his submission that in the application filed under section 7, there was no 'financial debt' and the application deserved to be rejected. The appellant has relied on judgment of the Supreme Court in Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. v. K.P. Jayaram [2020] 118 taxmann.com 560/[2021] 163 SCL 210 (SC). The case of Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), arose out of an application under section 7, which was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. However, appeal against the same was allowed and the application filed under section 7 stood rejected as barred by limitation. In the Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), the respondent had requested the company to convert a sum of Rs. 90 lakhs from out of the said outstanding loan as share application money for issuance of shares in the name of the respondent No. 2. [Para 32]

■

From the close scrutiny of rule 5(1A) as well as rule 17(1) of the Rules, it is evident that the aforesaid provisions are pari materia provisions. [Para 8]

■

In the instant case, admittedly, the return was filed on behalf of assessee, within the extended period of time provided under section 139(4), and the assessee has claimed depreciation. [Para 9]

■

However it is pertinent to mention here that the Tribunal while taking into account section 32, has held that since section 32 does not provide any specific provision for exercising the option within the time limit, therefore, the condition imposed in the second proviso of rule 5(1A) to the extent that such an option has to be exercised at the time of filing of the return under section 139(1) is invalid cannot be upheld. It is trite law that the Tribunal is bound by the provisions of the Act and the Rules and has no power to declare any provisions of either the Act or Rules to be invalid or ultra vires. Therefore, the substantial question of law framed by this Court is answered in favour of the revenue and it is held that the Tribunal was not correct in holding that in the absence of prescription of any time limit under section 32, the condition mentioned in the second proviso to rule 5(1A) to exercise the option with regard to depreciation at the time of filing of the return under section 139(1) is invalid. [Para 10]

■

In the result, the impugned orders passed by the Tribunal insofar as it pertains to the finding that the second proviso to rule 5(1A) are ultra-vires is hereby set aside. Though the substantial question of law has been answered in favour of the revenue, however in view of the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Nagpur Hotel Owners’ Association [2001] 114 Taxman 255/247 ITR 201 (SC), no relief can be granted in favour of the revenue. Accordingly, both the appeals filed by the revenue are disposed of. [Para 11]

The interest was not charged at the time of the original assessment because there was no taxable income at the time of original assessment. Had there been a taxable income at the time of original assessment, the assessees would not have challenged the levy. In other words, in terms of the Supreme Court decision in the case of Central Provinces Manganese Ore Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 160 ITR 961/ 27 Taxman 275 the jurisdictional fact attracting the levy was not disputed. As per the decision of the Supreme Court in Modi Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 216 ITR 759/ 82 Taxman 377 it is true that regular assessment would mean only the first/original assessment and interest would be levied only up to the date of such assessment. But the Supreme Court has further held that interest so levied will be increased or reduced on account of the variations in income brought about by orders passed as a result of various proceedings that may take place subsequent to the original assessment. The orders mentioned therein include the one passed under section 155. Thus, once when order under section 155 was passed to include the share income in the partner’s income, clause (b ) of section 139(8) would be pressed into operation, provided the jurisdictional fact of levy was not denied. Simultaneously, interest shall be levied only up to the date of the original assessment and not up to the date of the order made under section 155. Therefore, the levy of interest under section 139(8) and under section 215 should be calculated up to the date of original assessment in the case of the assessee.

Urban agricultural land was included in the definition of ‘capital asset’ by the Finance Act, 1970 only with effect from 1-4-1970. However, there did exist a controversy regarding the taxability of income earned on transfer of capital gains on account of the definition of the term ‘agricultural income’ given in section 2(1A). This controversy was set at rest by the insertion of an Explanation in section 2(1A) by the Finance Act, 1989 with retrospective effect from 1-4-1970. In view of the ruling of the Supreme Court in Central Provinces Manganese Ore Co. Ltd. case (supra ), the assessees could approach the Assessing Officer for waiver or reduction under rule 117A of the Income-tax Rules, 1962.

Admittedly, the action was under section 147(a ) and could not have been under section 147(b). The action was being taken after the expiry of eight years. Action under clause (a) of section 147, could, therefore, be taken only in cases where the income that escaped assessment was in the sum of Rs. 50,000 or above. In this case, the proposal submitted by the ITO to the Board clearly said that the assessee received Rs. 2,05,000 as compensation and Rs. 12,500 towards interest thereon. The Tribunal had held that the sum of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt and only the interest of Rs. 12,500 constituted income (revenue receipt). Even in the earlier assessment proceedings, there was a controversy as to whether the whole or any part of the compensation amount constituted revenue receipt. The AAC had opined that out of the amount received, only an amount of Rs. 91,004 constituted revenue receipt. Evidently, the ITO had not applied his mind to the relevant facts. He seemed to have proceeded on the assumption that the entire compensation amount constituted a revenue receipt. In this, he was evidently wrong.

The Tribunal had subsequently found that only the sum of Rs. 12,500 representing the interest was includible in the income and that the remaining amount of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt. If so, the reopening of the assessment after eight years was clearly unsustainable under section 149 as it then stood.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

reassessment by issuance of reassessment notice under section 148, which as per the provisions of section 149, provided for an outer time limit of six years from the end of the relevant assessment yeari.e. till 31-3-2023, particularly when the assertion of the source of cash deposit tracing it to closing balance as on 31-3-2016 was well before him in the regular assessment proceedings ongoing in the year 2019 itself. [Para 17]

■ Not only this, the provisions of section 69A contemplate that the 'money' (cash deposit in the present case) could be deemed to be in the nature of income only in the financial year in respect of which the assessee is found to be the owner and in the instant case, by offering plausible explanation tracing the source of money to closing balance of preceding year, the assessee was found to be the owner of the 'asset'/cash in the assessment year 2016-17 and hence, the explanation of nature and source of such money and invocation of deeming fiction engrafted under section 69A could have been sought/examined by the Assessing Officer in the assessment year 2016-17 and could not have been done in the assessment year 2017-18 going by the express language contained in section 69A and not otherwise. Furthermore, the factum of liquidation/refund of short term loans and advances and its consequential accumulation as cash-in-hand as on 31-3-2016 could have been examined in the assessment year 2016-17 only particularly when the Assessing Officer has not discharged the burden cast upon him to implicate the assessee into the sweep of section 69A. As such, the Assessing Officer has made addition on pure guess. It is well settled principle of law that while making an assessment under the provisions of the IT Act, the Income Tax Officer is not entitled to make a pure guess and to resort to an assessment without reference to any evidence or any material at all and that suspicion howsoever strong cannot take the place of proof beyond reasonable doubt. [Para 20]

■

In view of the aforesaid analysis, it is opined that the Tribunal is absolutely unjustified in dismissing the appeal partly upholding the addition of Rs. 20.50 lakhs treating it as unexplained money invoking the deeming fiction engrafted under section 69A charging the same to higher rate of tax as prescribed under section 115BBE. As such, the impugned order passed by the Assessing Officer affirmed by the Commissioner (Appeals) and further partly affirmed by the Tribunal is hereby set aside. It is hereby held that Rs. 20.50 lakhs cannot be said to be unexplained money under section 69A. Accordingly, the substantial question of law is answered in favour of the assessee and against the revenue. [Para 22]

Section 32(2) pursuant to the amendment in Finance Act, 1996 curtailed the benefit of carry forward of unabsorbed depreciation loss to a period of 8 years and brought the said provision at par with the unabsorbed business losses. This provision was in force till assessment year 2001-02. Again the Finance Act, 2001 with effect from assessment year 2002-03 amended section 32(2) and restored back to the original version of the section as it stood prior to amendment by Finance Act, 1996, allowing the benefit of carry forward of losses to an infinite period and treating the same different from that of unabsorbed business losses. The explanatory memorandum to Finance Act, 2001 clearly spells out the intention of the legislature to provide the benefit of brought forward unabsorbed depreciation to be allowed to be eternally carried forward for an infinite period irrespective of the years to which it pertains. Though it is stated that the proposed amendment will take effect from 1-4-2002, going by the intention behind the amendment to this section vide Finance Act, 2001 restoring back to the same old provisions as it was then existing prior to 1-4-1997, it could only be logical to conclude that the legislature in its wisdom thought it fit not to disturb any of the unabsorbed depreciation losses to be made available for set off for an infinite period. In other words, the same has to be understood as the legislature only intended that any unabsorbed depreciation available to an assessee as on 1-4-2002 will be dealt with in accordance with the provisions of section 32(2) as amended by Finance Act, 2001 and not by the provisions of section 32(2) as it stood before the said amendment.

No specific provision has been incorporated by the Finance Act, 2001 in section 32(2) restricting the allowability of carry forward of unabsorbed depreciation loss upto assessment year 1996-97 as available to be set off only for a period of 8 years. Hence the purposive and harmonious interpretation has to be taken keeping in view the intention of the amendment of section 32(2) by Finance Act 2001. While construing taxing statutes, rule of strict interpretation has to be applied, giving fair and reasonable construction to the language of the section without leaning to the side of the assessee or the revenue. But if the legislature fails to express clearly and the assessee becomes entitled for a benefit within the ambit of the section by the clear words used in the section, the benefit accruing to the assessee cannot be denied. As per provisions of section 55(2)(b )(ii), the indexing has to be allowed if transferred capital asset became property of the assessee or of the previous owner before the first day of April, 1981. In the instant case, it was an admitted position that construction of flat was completed in about 1988 as per valuation report submitted by the assessee. The most important point was that building was not even in existence as on 1-4-1981 because admittedly, construction of the building was completed in about 1988 and, hence, till construction of the building was completed and possession was handed over to the previous owner, i.e., the HUF, what was held by HUF, was the right to obtain title and possession of the flat and it could not be said that the flat itself became property of the HUF prior to that date and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in holding that the assessee was entitled to adopt market value of the flat as on 1-4- 1981. For the purpose of section 255(2)(b)(ii ), the capital asset, i.e., flat in the instant case, should have become the property of the previous owner before 1-4-1981 to make the assessee entitled to this benefit, i.e., adopting market value as on 1-4-1981, but since in instant case, the flat was not even in existence till 1988, the assessee could not be given this benefit. Till 1988, the previous owner, i.e., HUF was not owner of the flat but was owner of right to get possession and title of the flat. In view of the above, the assessee could not be given benefit to adopt market value of the flat as on 1-4-1981 and order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and that of the Assessing Officer was to be restored to that extent. Regarding indexation, cost inflation index for the first year in which the asset was held by the assessee had to be considered. In the instant case, there was no dispute that the asset in question, i.e., flat was held by the assessee only from the financial year 1991-92, i.e., when the partition of the HUF took place. As per provisions of section 2(42A ), read with Explanation 1(i)(b ), the period for which the asset was held by the previous owner has to be added to decide as to whether the asset was short-term capital asset or long-term capital asset and since, admittedly, construction of the house was completed in 1988, the asset was a long-term capital asset in view of the Explanation to section 2(42A), but in view of the specific provisions of Explanation (iii) to section 48, indexing had to be allowed from financial year 1991-92, i.e., the year from which flat was held by the assessees on partition of the HUF and, hence, on that issue also, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and that of the Assessing Officer was to be restored. [Para 6]

In the case of K.S. Krishna Rao v. CIT [1990] 181 ITR 408. The Supreme Court has held that interest on enhanced compensation cannot be taxed all in a lump sum as having accrued on the date on which the Court passes the order for enhanced compensation : the interest has to be spread over on an annual basis right from the date of delivery of possession till the date of the order of the Court on a time basis . In Madras Industrial Development Corpn. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802 / 91 Taxman 340 the liability of the company with reference to the debentures existed for a span of 12 years. It was in the light of the subsistence of the corresponding liability for the 12 year period that the Supreme Court had held that the discount paid for selling those debentures had to be divided proportionately for the entire span of 12 years and the per year deduction should be on that pro rata basis. It was on the basis of the principle of ‘matching liability’ that the Supreme Court had held in that case that the assessee was entitled to claim a pro rata deduction of the discount element suffered by the company in issuing the debentures. The above ratio declared by the Supreme Court would not help the case of the assessee here. By exercising the option to receive the interest in lumpsum at a discounted rate, the assessee had foregone its right to receive the interest for the remaining two years. The assessee had no right at all for any interest for the remaining two years. When no such right to receive the interest existed for those two years, correspondingly there was no question of interest accruing or being received for those two years. Here, it was not a case of ‘interest received in advance’. It was a case of interest received at discounted rate. The right of the assessee to receive the interest for the future years was liquidated. Therefore, it was not possible for the assessee to divide the interest in three parts and offer only one part for assessment in the first year.

Hence, the Assessing Officer’s action was to be upheld, and the revenue’s appeal to be allowed.

Further, sub-section (6) of section 32A deals with the situation of carry forward and adjustment of the unabsorbed investment allowance of the amalgamating company in case of amalgamation. [Paras 15 and 16] On going through the provisions of sections 72A and 32A, it is evident that section 72A deals with carry forward and set-off of accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation allowance in case of amalgamation. According to this section, accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation allowance of the amalgamating company shall be deemed to be the loss, or as the case may be, of the amalgamated company for the previous year in which amalgamation was affected and other provisions of this Act relating to set-off of any carry forward of loss allowance for depreciation shall apply accordingly. Hence, the amalgamated company would get the original period for its carry forward and set-off. But in case of investment allowance, the unabsorbed/balance of investment allowance of the amalgamating company shall be deemed to be the unabsorbed investment allowance of the amalgamated company and it shall be entitled to claim its carry forward and adjustment against the total income subject to fulfilment of other conditions for the remaining period of 8 years. In any case, the total period of its carry forward would not exceed the period of 8 years specified in sub-section (3) of section 32A. Therefore, if the amalgamating company has availed the benefit of carry forward of three assessment years, the amalgamated company can claim the carry forward only up to 5 years and not full 8 years, as in the case of carry forward of accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation. In the instant case, nowhere either under the rehabilitation-cum-amalgamation scheme sanctioned by the BIFR or the BIFR order, it had been mentioned that investment allowance shall be carried forward up to the full period of 8 years, contrary to the provisions of section 32A(6). Therefore, there was no force in the argument of the assessee that it had been specifically specified in the BIFR order or the scheme that amalgamated company would be entitled to carry forward of the unabsorbed investment allowance up to 8 years. Therefore, the amalgamated company would only be entitled to the carry forward of unabsorbed investment subject to fulfilment of other conditions upto the remaining period of eight years. [Para 18]

Therefore, the revenue’s stand was correct and the assessee was not entitled to set-off of unabsorbed investment allowance for the impugned assessment year as it fell beyond the period of 8 years. [Para 19]

The cheque discounting charges are different from interest payments and are not attracted by the provisions of section 201(1A).

Even if the same is to be considered as interest, the case is not attracted by the provisions of section 201(1A). Two dates are crucial for arriving at the amount of interest chargeable under section 201(1A), that is, the date of deduction of tax and the date of actual payment of such tax to the credit of the Government. In the instant case, the date on which such tax was actually paid was not available for the Assessing Officer to work out interest. In such circumstances, machinery section failed in the instant case. The Assessing Officer was not right in substituting ‘the date of assessment order’ in place of ‘the date on which such tax was actually paid’ for computing the impugned interest as it is not permissible to read into a taxing provision any words which are not there or exclude any which are there. The words found in the provisions must be given their natural meaning. [Para 5]

Further, the Assessing Officer could not charge interest under section 201(1A) in stages, i.e., one up to the date of the assessment order and the other from the date of assessment order to the date of actual payment of tax. In all, the application of section 201(1A) in the instant case, was impracticable inasmuch as one of the components required for the computation of interest, namely, ‘the date of payment of tax to the Government’ was not available on record. Therefore, no interest under section 201(1A) could be charged not only in respect of cheque discounting cheques, but also in case of TVK. [Para 6]
