On the revenue’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■ The Commissioner (Appeals) allowed relief to the assessee by taking view that the assessee is in the business of four luxury resort in Goa. The assessee introduced unique project for fractional ownership. Such unique concept was also known as time share vacation facilities which were sold to various members. To keep the maintenance of resort, the maintenance was interested to associated group companies. The assessee in earlier years credited sale proceeds of timeshare in accounts and charge of construction against such sale proceeds. Many of members not utilized whole week to said resort but only spent a part of week. Such timeshare weeks were converted into sometime share point. The assessee also engaged 3 group companies and allotted certain timeshare points to such group entities for marketing on identical term and condition. Contract with such companies who are also having forfeiture clause. In case purchaser failed to make the payment against membership and maintenance fees their membership were forfeited. The legal ownership of resort building was with assessee. The assessee retained the building at zero cost. In the balance sheet of assessee company, the building or the land were not reflected in earlier years despite retaining legal ownership of resort building. On coming to know that many members are failing to make payment of their annual maintenance and membership charges. Such unrealized charge was in respect of 1721 members who failed to clear their dues and on forfeiture of such timeshare; dues of group companies were reimbursed. The Commissioner (Appeals) on appreciation of fact also held that the assessee has shown forfeiture rights in their balance sheet as trading asset. The total recovery of Group Companies which was engaged in management and maintaining of selling of time share at the end of relevant financial year was of 15203 timeshare weeks which were forfeited. The assessee was having total payment for forfeiture which was free from all encumbrances were of Rs. 22.28 crores. The valuation of all 4 resorts through valuer on capitalization of 292 forfeited units which were from all encumbrances was for a sum of Rs. 22.28 crores. The assessee capitalized as per actual payment made to 4 group companies at Rs. 3.37 crores and improvement against land at Rs. 18.91 crores as a cost improvement trade building. Since capitalization was made at the end of year, the assessee claimed 1/2 of 10 per cent which is of Rs. 94.57 lakhs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also held that entire consideration paid by assessee to its group companies for getting the identifiable unit from all encumbrances were to be treated as cost of improvement of capital asset which has to be incorporated in the balance sheet as tangible asset and thus, the assessee was right in claiming depreciation over the building block. The assessee vehemently argued that timeshare weeks so acquired by assessee in the relevant financial year were capitalized as a part of cost of building were subsequently sold in the form of fractional ownership of the apartments. The fractional ownership gains have been offered to tax. In subsequent years, the assessee offered from capital gain on transfer of such ownership of the resort apartment aggregating of Rs. 170 crores. To support such claim, the assessee furnished copy of financial statement and computation of income from assessment year 2018-19 to 2023-24. It is found that all such facts are duly acknowledged by the Commissioner (Appeals) at page no. 9 of his order. The assessee also furnished the copy of assessment order passed under section 143(3) read with section 143(3A) and 143(3B) or 144B for assessment year 2018-19 from 2022-23 and 2023-24. No counter arguments were made before that the fractional ownership gains have been offered to tax in subsequent years. It is also found that similar claims have been allowed in subsequent assessment years. Thus, on independent appreciation of facts, no reason is found to interfere with the finding of the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 34]

Thus, the assessee itself treated the developmental rights as immovable property and took necessary clearance from the appropriate authority. Under these circumstances, the developmental rights constituted capital assets and provisions of section 45(2) were applicable to the transaction as the capital asset was converted into stock-in-trade along with land, which was later transferred to developer. [Para 14] With regard to computation of capital gains under section 45(2), the assessee’s contention was that the Assessing Officer was not justified in resorting to backward interpolation of sale consideration with reference to cost inflation index. The assessee’s alternate contention was that if the Assessing Officer’s action in regard to computation of fair market value as on 1-4-1994 was to be upheld, the same system should be applied for computing the fair market value as on 1-4-1981, and then cost inflation index should be applied on that value. The assessee had also submitted the computation in that regard and had pointed out that the capital gains if so computed would be nil. These contentions were well-founded. [Para 17]

In the present circumstances, therefore, the matter should be set aside to the file of the Assessing Officer with a direction to refer the matter back to the departmental valuer for valuing the fair market value of the developmental rights as on 1-4-1981, in the form of non-transferable rights. While doing so, the valuer should take into consideration the effect of all the depressing factors on the value of land as prevailed on 1-4-1981, and also the fact that actual right to transfer industrial galas was received by the assessee as on 14-2-1996, and, thus, there was some clog on the rights of the assessee on 1-4-1994, which could be construed to be a depressing factor. The DVO was directed to ascertain the value after providing discount on account of the depressing factors. [Para 17]

As regards non-allowability of set-off of capital gains against brought forward business loss, there was no infirmity in the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) that when the Supreme Court rendered its judgment in the case of CIT v. Cocanada Radhaswami Bank Ltd. [1965] 57 ITR 306, the provisions of section 45(2) were not there, which were introduced with effect from 1-4-1985 by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1984. The income was assessable under capital gains and provisions of section 71 specifically prohibit set-off of income from capital gains against the business income. That ground was to be dismissed as such. [Para 20]

It is an admitted fact on record that an amount reflected in the books of account of appellant as outstanding as on 10-5-2008, were towards services received from abroad from the associated companies. Since on the date of amendment of section 67 and rule 6, such amounts were reflected under outstanding receipts, the appellant is liable to pay service tax on such amount under reverse charge mechanism as per section 66A. Therefore, it is opined that service tax amounting paid by the appellant and appropriated in the impugned order are in conformity with the service tax statute. Since, the appellant had delayed in making such payment, interest amount thereon are required to be paid, since the same is compensatory in character. [Para 12]

Thus, the appeal is partly allowed and the impugned order is set aside to the extent of confirmation of service tax demand along with interest and imposition of penalties under 'Franchise Service'. [Para 13]

in ‘F’ at the same time again, it appeared that those shares were not actually transferred by the assessee in favour of IHCL. The Tribunal in its order also found out that all along the assessee contended that there was no income as capital gains as there was no transfer of the shares. The Tribunal noted that on this argument, no doubt, the assessee succeeded. This finding was not challenged by the department and, hence, the same could be considered to have become final. As regards the taxability of the receipts under the award, both the lower authorities had held that the receipt was connected with parting by the assessee of its intangible rights of possession and enjoyment of the property belonging to ‘F’. It appeared that both the lower authorities pierced the corporate veil and held that even without transfer of shares of ‘F’ to IHCL, its rights in the property was handed over by the shareholders of that company, one of such shareholders being the assessee company. A perusal of the award also supported this contention. Certainly, IHCL received certain benefits by way of transfer of certain rights in the property although the said property did not belong to ‘F’ or even its shareholders in the true legal sense. The payment of as high a sum as Rs. 25 lakhs was on that account alone. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that in the process what was transferred was the goodwill of the business which was being run by the company ‘F’, could not be accepted. There was no doubt about the fact that ‘F’ was running a hotel on that property. IHCL, on acquisition of the property, however did not continue to run on that business. On the other hand, it dismantled that entire structure and built up a very big five star hotel under different name and style on the property. It was, therefore, clear that what IHCL did actually acquire was not the goodwill of the earlier hotel, but merely the uniteruppted right of possession and enjoyment of the property, coupled with the withdrawal by the assessee and its associate their rights to repossess the property at the end of the Director of Estates. The question would arise therefore, as to whether this intangible right of possession and enjoyment of the property had been acquired by the assessee and/its associate by incurring any cost or otherwise. The matter could not be answered simply by looking into the fact that the Assessing Officer in the assessment did not choose to tax the receipt either as business income or even as capital gains. Only by acquiring the shares of ‘F’ the assessee came into the joint possession and enjoyment of the property under consideration. The cost of acquisition of such intangible rights should therefore be equated with the cost of shares of ‘F’. Accordingly, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and it must be held that inasmuch as the assessee had acquired the intangible rights which were ultimately parted with by it in favour of the IHCL, by purchasing the shares of ‘F’, capital gains tax would surely arise, the cost of acquisition of the capital asset being referable to the cost of the shares of ‘F’ in the hands of the assessee.

As regards the question of year of taxability of the capital gains, it could not be said that it was the award which ultimately led to the transfer of the capital asset under consideration. The award merely confirmed and vindicated the standpoint of the assessee and its associates about having intangible rights in the property. Such rights were however transferred in terms of the memorandum of agreement dated 13-3-1975. The facts of the case also showed that almost immediately after arriving at this memorandum, the assessee and its associates handed over the possession of the property in favour of IHCL, which started developing the same into a full- fledged five star hotel. Therefore, the transfer of the intangible rights belonging to the assessee did take place in assessment year 1976-77 and not in the assessment year 1980-81. Ultimately, therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in deleting the capital gains from the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1980-81 was to be upheld on this ground alone.

The instant Tribunal noticed the relevant clauses of share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement and consent terms, The issue was as to whether the amount invested by the financial creditors can be said to be 'financial debt' or not. [Para 22] The Supreme Court has emphasized the Judgment of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 747/155 SCL 622, that in the various categories under (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5, the Legislature has only given instances, which could be included in the term 'financial debt'. However, the list is not exhaustive but inclusive. One may first consider as to whether the investment made by the financial creditors have commercial effect of borrowing or not. One would have noticed that raising of amount by the company through share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement was a commercial borrowing, since the said transaction has direct effect with the business, which was carried out by the corporate debtor, i.e. construction of building and township. The supplementary share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 12-7-2008, where the agreement clearly noted that 'the Company now requires further funding to the extent of Rs. 50 in order to carry out objectives of the Business Plan, i.e. approval of township, and actual execution of the township as per the designs prepared by the Company architects'. Thus, the raising of the amount through the said agreement has the commercial effect of borrowing, which is clearly demonstrated by the statements contained in the supplementary agreement. The use of expression 'further funding' indicates that transaction has commercial effect of borrowing. Now the question remains to be considered is as to whether the investment by the financial creditors can be said to be an investment by disbursal against consideration of time value of money. The expression 'time value of money' encompasses in itself the concept of time value of the disbursement. One would have already noticed the various clauses of amended and restated share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 14-5-2008 and would have extracted the relevant clauses, where company and promoters were obliged to purchase all the shares held by the non-defaulting shareholders at a price that provides the non-defaulting shareholders at an internal rate of return of 15 per cent per annum compounded annually or the Fair Market Value, whichever is higher. Clauses 19.1(a) and 19.6(a) as extracted, contains clear indication that investment was with an eye to earn profits and the investment was for consideration for the time value of money. Binding term sheet, which one would have also noticed above also contains several clauses, which indicate that proposals were given by the promoters to develop the project and provide an exit to the investors and the exit consideration was carrying IRR of 17 per cent. From the above it is noted that, "or", is dividing the two clauses under Explanation to Section 80IA which clearly indicates the intention of the legislature to give an option to the assessee entitled to claim deduction u/s 80IA(8) to choose either of the two mechanisms. [Para 13.4]

■ If in a scenario, the availability of the market value that one would ordinarily fetch in the open market is not possible to be determined then, the second option is always available with the assessee. For instance, if there are certain unique services which have been transferred or any unique goods or goods produced with patented IPR or intangibles where the market rate which can ordinarily fetch in the open market is not available, or where market value is not available in the open market, then market value has to be determined in terms of Sub-Clause (ii). If such option is not available then the AO cannot ascertain the market value of goods and services. However, if market value is available on such goods and services which are available in the open market, then same can be adopted for the purpose of Section 80IA(8). [Para 13.5]

■

Further, the different manner of treatment for determination of "market value" becomes evident glaring when Explanation to section 80IA (8) is juxtaposed with section 80A(6). Explanation to Section 80A(6) does not provide the word "or" and all the 3 clauses therein used for situation specific have been made separate and disjunctive from other clauses. [Para 13.6]

From the plain reading of the aforesaid Explanation hereinabove, one can clearly note the difference in Explanation to Section 80IA (8). In Section 80IA(A) the expression "market value" has been elaborated in the Explanation in three sub-clauses word "or" used, albeit the three clauses are separated by using semicolon, which means in these specific transactions „market value" has to be ascertained and determined in that particular manner only and there is no option for "or". Thus, difference in treatment in different sections cannot be lost sight of while interpreting the provisions. [Para 13.7]

■

The word "or" appearing between two sub-clauses in Explanation to Section 80IA (8) cannot be inferred that after the introduction of SDT from A.Y.2013-14 only sub-clause (ii) alone can be applied. The use of the word "or" can be interpreted as: "(a) both manner are available with the assessee to demonstrate that market value of the goods and services has to be either by showing that the price of such goods and services is in consonance with the price available in the open market; or" "(b) if assessee is not able to establish the price available in the open market, then the price of goods and services has to be established through arm's length principle u/s 92CA/92F. It also means that, if the price of the transfer of goods and services is in consonance with the price available in the open market then the profits of the eligible business shown as per this price is eligible for deduction and in that case the second option may not be necessary." HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual of - Assessment years 1998-99 to 2002-03 - Whether where assessee was engaged in business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts, entire amount of timeshare membership fee receivable by it at time of enrolment of member was not income chargeable to tax in initial year on account of contractual obligation that was fastened to receipt i.e., to provide services in future over term of contract - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was in the business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts. During relevant assessment years, the assessee collected revenue from timeshare members but same was not recognised as revenue for the current year. The explanation of the assessee was that it had considered only 40 per cent of the membership fees collected as income and the balance 60 per cent was treated as deferred income. It was stated that the balance amount was to be spread over the next 33 years during which the assessee was expected to provide timeshare facilities to the members. It was also stated that in order to provide various facilities during the next 33 years, it had to incur many costs. Further explanation of the assessee was that the AMC was exclusively meant to cover the maintenance of various facilities which were an integral part of the timeshare property. These charges were for the maintenance of various electronic gadgets made available in the accommodation, furniture, kitchen equipments, central air-conditioning etc. On the other hand, the consideration for future obligations received in the initial stages was towards transfer facility from one resort to another, split, accumulation and advancing facility, domestic and international exchange, transmission, upgradation etc. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and, hence, income had to be accounted for on accrual basis. He was of the view that the receipt was undisputedly income as the assessee itself had shown it as deferred income. However, the Act does not recognise the concept of deferred income and, hence, the assessee’s explanation could not be accepted. Considering all these aspects, the Assessing Officer added certain amount being 60 per cent of the receipts shown by the assessee as advance subscription. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee had to construct holiday resorts and provide timeshare facilities over a period of time. Further, the annual subscription fee collected met only the maintenance of the resorts. The utility charges collected ‘were as per actual consumption of things like electricity, water etc. It did not cover major renovation and repairs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also took note of the fact that over a period of 24 years, the assessee had to incur about 171 per cent of the original investment for major renovation and replacement of assets. Accordingly, he upheld the contentions of the assessee and deleted the addition in all the years.

On cross-appeals : HELD: In the instant case, assessee’s half share in the capital gain was Rs. 54,118. Out of this, deduction of Rs. 5,000 under section 80T had to be allowed. If that was allowed, the capital gain would come to Rs. 49,118. This deduction under section 80T had not been allowed in the original assessment as the capital gain assessed was Rs. 3,259 which was below Rs. 5,000. Hence, after deduction of Rs. 5,000 under section 80T, capital gain was only Rs. 49,118. Since this was below Rs. 50,000 even the CBDT could not accord sanction for reopening the assessment beyond the period of eight years. Thus, the reassessment proceedings were invalid and the reassessment order dated 24-12-1983 could not stand.

In view of the decision of the Andhra Pradesh High Court in Khan Bahadur Ahmed Alladin & Sons v. CIT [1969] 74 ITR 651 , the enhanced compensation of Rs. 60,112 in which the assessee had half share which was awarded by the District Judge on 18-8-1972 was assessable only in the assessment year 1973-74 and not in the assessment year 1966-67. Thus, the ITO was wrong in assessing the above amount in the assessment year 1966-67 by his order dated 24-12-1983. This principle was applicable even in respect of Rs. 41,606 in which the assessee had half share, awarded by the District Judge on 18-8-1972 for severance of land resulting in injurious effect on the remaining land. Hence, this amount was not assessable in the assessment year 1966-67.

Further, in view of the decision of the Kerala High Court in CIT v. Smt. M. Subaida Beevi [1986] 160 ITR 557 the sum of Rs. 41,606 in which the assessee had a share had been awarded only by way of damages for injurious effect on the balance of the land belonging to the assessee and it was not related to the transfer of the acquired land. Thus, it could not be treated as part of the capital gain.

In CIT v. Smt. Sankari Manickyamma [1976] 105 ITR 172 , the Andhra Pradesh High Court had held that the right to receive compensation or interest accrues to the person from the date when the statutorily designated authorities determine the same. In the instant case also, the District Judge awarded the interest in his judgement dated 18-8-1972 and so it was assessable only in the assessment year 1973-74. In the result the assessee’s appeal was to be allowed and the departmental appeal was to be dismissed.

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

On the revenues appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: There is a distinction between "receive of property being the shares of the amalgamating companies" and "underlying assets and transfer of said assets to the amalgamated company. For the purpose of attracting the rigours of section 56(2)(viia), the crucial date is the date of receive of any property being the shares of the amalgamated companies. Undoubtedly, the assessee received the property on account of approval of the scheme of amalgamation in the year under consideration and therefore, the income is required to be charged in the year under consideration. [Para 19]

The Assessing Officer was not certain about the year of chargeability i.e., whether it is to be charged on the year of receipt of property or it is to be charged in the year of the transfer of property pursuant to the scheme of amalgamation. [Para 20]

The year of chargeability would be the year in which the assessee received the properties i.e., the assessment year under consideration and therefore, the Assessing Officer had rightly charged the income under section 56(2)(viia). [Para 20.1]

In this regard, the above said principle is not universally applicable and is required to be applied with caution and on case to case basis. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer was wrongly harboring the view that the additions were required to be made on substantive basis in the year of transfer i.e., assessment year, 2012-13. Admittedly no proceedings were pending at the time of passing of assessment order dated 31-12-2016, therefore it is not possible to make the addition on substantive basis for Assessment year 2012-13. If the same is held then the Bench would be asking the Assessing Officer to do the impossible. Further, there is a time limit provided under the Act for the completion of assessment under section 143(3) for assessment year 2014-15 and the assessment proceedings for assessment year 2014-15, on the basis of protective addition, cannot be put in abeyance till the additions are made on substantive basis for assessment year 2012-13. In view of the above, the contention of the assessee that the substantive addition should precede the protective addition could not be accepted. [Para 21]

Further, though the assessee had made the plea on the submission that section 148 proceedings initiated against the assessee for assessment year 2012-13 had been dropped, which were initiated on substantive basis, but the said contention was not dealt by the CIT(A) while passing the impugned order. [Para 21.1]

It is clear that the assessee did not exist in the assessment year 2012-13. Therefore, no addition can be made in the hands of a non-est entity i.e., assessee for the assessment year 2012-13 as it was not in existence in that assessment year. Moreover if the contention of the assessee is accepted that the substantive additions were dropped for the assessment year 2012-13, then the protective addition made in the assessment year 2014-15 are required to be converted into substantive addition. Merely because some other High Courts have taken a different view, it is not correct to say that the issue, which has been subjected to rectification, is a debatable one in so far as that particular State is concerned. It is permissible for the income-tax authorities to resort to the provisions of section 154 for bringing a matter in consonance with the judicial pronouncements of the High Court of the State where such authorities are working. However, in the instant case, the unabsorbed depreciation was held to be eligible for being carried forward in the hands of the assessee in the assessment orders for the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78. It was, therefore, clear that the error existed in the assessment orders passed by the ITO for the assessment year 1975- 76 on 18-1-1977 and for the assessment year 1977-78 on 19-11-1989. The said error or mistake apparent from record could be rectified by passing appropriate orders under section 154 for the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78, provided such rectification orders had been passed within the time-limit of four years prescribed under section 154(7). Once a right had been extinguished under the provisions of law and once a matter had become barred by limitation of time, it could not be revived by such an indirect route of passing an order under section 154 for a subsequent year, namely, the assessment year 1980-81. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in holding that the proceedings of rectification pertaining to the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78, which had already became barred by limitation of time, could not be revived by allowing the ITO to pass an order under section 154 for the assessment year 1980-81.

As regards the interest under section 215, the provisions of section 215(3) as it existed prior to its amendment with effect from 1-4-1985 did not provide for any enhancement or increase in the amount of interest charged under section 215 where the amount payable increased as a result of an order of rectification or an order on appeal or revision, etc. The provisions providing for consequent increase or enhancement in the amount of interest charged under section 215 had for the first time been introduced by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1984 with effect from 1-4-1985. The very fact that the aforesaid amendment has not been made with any retrospective effect clearly showed that prior to the assessment year 1985-86, interest charged under section 215 could not be increased where as a result of an order under section 154 or 147 or 250 or 254, etc., such amount had been increased. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in directing the ITO to remit the interest charged under section 215.

[Para 8] It was also contended by the assessee that the Tribunal's order dated 14-6-2000, which had attained finality, related only to the original compensation and not the enhanced compensation with regard to which there was no finding or direction by the Tribunal and, therefore, the inclusion of the enhanced compensation in the reassessment order was bad and without justification. It was further contended that even if the notice of re-assessment was taken to refer only to the enhanced compensation, the notice was invalid because the enhanced compensation was assessable only on receipt basis under section 45(5) in the assessment year 1986-87. It was true that the decision of the Tribunal dated 14-6-2000 had become final inasmuch as neither party had filed an appeal against the same, but it was equally true that the reference to section 45(5) in the order of the Tribunal was an inadvertence. The Tribunal had referred to section 45(5) as a supporting reason for holding that the capital gain could be said to have arisen only by virtue of the order of the LAO dated 25-3-1980. The reference to the section did not however whittle down the effectiveness of the direction of the Tribunal. One should understand the direction of the Tribunal de hors the provisions of section 45(5) which were not applicable to the relevant assessment year 1980-81 under appeal. It was not contended by the assessee that the finding of the Tribunal that the capital gain was assessable in the assessment year 1980-81 was a finding which was not necessary for the disposal of the appeal and, therefore, the same could not be given effect to by reopening the assessment for the assessment year 1980-81. Even if such a contention was to be taken, the same would not have been accepted having regard to the provisions of Explanation 2 to section 153. The fiction contained in the Explanation removes the bar of limitation irrespective of the question whether the appellate authority has, in fact, given or can, in law, give a finding or direction that the income should be taxed in a specified assessment year other than the year for which the appellate authority hears the appeal. If this principle was applied to the instant case, one should determine the assessability of the receipt having regard to the law as it stood in relation to the relevant assessment year 1980-81. The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the impugned order that the Tribunal did not refer to the assessability of the enhanced compensa-tion directed by the order of the District Judge dated 25-2-1985, which was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, therefore, the Assessing Officer could not bring the enhanced compensation to tax while making the reassessment for the assessment year 1980-81. He had further referred to section 45(5) to support the above conclusion. This part of the decision of the Commissioner(Appeals) had been challenged as incorrect on the footing that section 45(5) came into effect only from 1-4-1988 and having regard to the provisions of section 45(1) read with section 155(7A), even the enhanced compensation was assessable only in the assessment year 1980-81. Section 45(5) was inserted by the Finance Act, 1987, only with effect from 1-4-1988 and, therefore, became applicable only from the assessment year 1988-89 onwards. The enhanced compensation ordered by the District Judge was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that the same could be assessed only in the assessment year 1986-87. This conclusion was obviously wrong, since the enhanced compensation could not have been assessed on receipt basis under section 45(5) for the assessment year 1986-87 for the simple reason that the section did not come into effect for that assessment year. This decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore unsupportable. The department referred to section 155(7A). Sub-section (7A) was inserted by the Finance Act, 1978, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1974 to empower the Assessing Officer to amend an order or award of additional compensa-tion in the case of compulsory acquisition of a capital asset. Sub-section (7A) was omitted by the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987, with effect from 1-4-1992. Thus, it had effect for the assessment year 1980-81. Sub-section empowered the Assessing Officer, in cases where the compensation for the acquisition was enhanced or further enhanced by any Court, Tribunal or any authority, to accordingly amend the computation of the capital gains made earlier on the footing that such computation shall be deemed to have been wrongly made

Prescription of the second proviso is admittedly fulfilled in the instant case inasmuch as the assessee paid a sum of Rs. 1 lakh as part payment prior to the date of the agreement in the year 2008 through banking channel. In view of the foregoing discussion, it is to be held that the mandate of the main part of section 56(2)(vii)(b) does not apply to the facts of the instant case as it is covered by the first and second provisos inasmuch as the assessee entered into an agreement fixing the amount of consideration for the purchase of the immovable property in the year 2008 but the actual registration took place in 2015 and, further, the assessee paid a part of the consideration by cheque in the year 2008 before the date of the agreement. In such circumstances, it is the stamp value on the date of agreement in the year 2008, which should be applied for the purpose of the sub-clause and not the stamp value as in the year 2015. Stamp value of the property as on the date of the agreement in 2008 was Rs. 23.75 lakhs. As such stamp value is obviously less than the actual consideration at Rs. 31 lakhs. ■ It is found that the Assessing Officer has adopted "look through approach" holding that the transaction is not for "sale of shares" but for "sale of underlying assets", and disregarded the substance of the transaction which is transfer of shares of UEM held by assessee and not the assets of the company without having any evidence or cogent material or information on record. In fact, the Assessing Officer determination of the full value of consideration at Rs. 484.13 crore, which is actually the value of the company in perpetuity on the basis of projected cash flow (not the underlying assets) as in financial year 2020-21, has no basis in law. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has wrongly adopted the total capitalised value of the company for perpetuity of 484.13 crore as in financial year 2020-21 as against value per share worked out for the financial year 2015-16. [Para 41]

■

Further, for determining the full value of sale consideration in cases of transfer of unquoted shares of a company, the Assessing Officer could have invoked the enabling provisions of section 50CA read with rule 11UA for determining the fair market value (FMV) of the shares and substitute the same with the sales consideration adopted by the assessee. Section 50CA provides that where consideration received or accruing as a result of transfer of a capital assets being unquoted shares of a company, is less than the fair market value determined in the manner as prescribed in rule 11 UA, then the value so determined shall, for the purpose of section 48, be deemed to be full value of consideration received or accrued as a result of such transfer. There is however legal difficulties in invoking the deeming fiction of section 50CA in the present proceedings, as the unquoted equity shares of UEM, were transferred in financial year 2015-16 prior to 1-4-2018. The provisions of section 50CA cannot be invoked for period before 1-4-2018 to determine the FMV for taking it as full value of consideration for the computation of capital gains under section 48. It is therefore opined that the full value of consideration received on transfer of shares cannot be substituted either by fair market value or by any other manner, at least in the concerned assessment year 2015-16. On the basis of discussion above, it is therefore held that the Assessing Officer’s invocation of section 50 to consider the 'sale of shares' as 'sale of asset' for calculating short-term capita gain, is invalid and not supported by any legal provisions. Therefore, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the additions made as short-term capital gain. [Para 42]

The assessee, a cellular mobile telephony service provider, received about Rs. 133.79 crores from prepaid customers during the year, disclosed as advances since services had not been rendered; it recognised revenue on the basis of actual usage within the validity period.

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

It is found that similar issue came up for consideration before the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in ACIT v. Shyam Telelinks Ltd. [2013] 31 taxmann.com 239 (Delhi - Trib.)/[2013] 141 ITD 416 (Delhi - Trib.), wherein the Co-ordinate Bench agreed with the similar mode of revenue recognition by the taxpayer. The Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal further directed the Assessing Officer to verify whether, in the subsequent year, the taxpayer has declared the revenue in respect of expired prepaid cards, and in case no discrepancy is found in this regard, the Co-ordinate Bench directed that no adjustment is called for with the assessee's mode of revenue recognition. In the Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), the respondent had requested the company to convert a sum of Rs. 90 lakhs from out of the said outstanding loan as share application money for issuance of shares in the name of the respondent No. 2. [Para 32] What was held by the Supreme Court is that payment received for shares duly issued to third party at the request of the payee cannot be a debt, not to speak of financial debt. There can be no quarrel to the proposition laid by the Supreme Court in the Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra). When shares are duly issued to a third party, on the basis of which amount, filing of an application under section 7 by the respondent was rightly rejected, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court has again reiterated that 'financial debt' means debt along with interest, if any disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. The instant is not a case regarding allocation of shares by payment of money on the basis of which money, section 7 application is filed. The transactions, which have come up for consideration contains several clauses which makes it clear that it is not a case of simple allotment of shares against payment of money. Hence, the judgment in Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), cannot help the appellant in the instant case. [Para 34]

What was held by the instant Tribunal in the Sushil Ansal v. Ashok Tripathi [2020] 118 taxmann.com 569 (NCL - AT), is that application by a decree holder would not fall within the definition of financial creditor. The judgment of Supreme Court in Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A Balakrishnan [2022] 138 taxmann.com 567/172 SCL 696, where the Supreme Court has clearly held that Legislature could never have intended to keep a debt, which is crystallized in the form of a decree, outside the ambit of section 5, sub-section (8). In view of the clear pronouncement of the Supreme Court it is opined that appellant cannot take any benefit from the above judgment of this Tribunal. [Para 36]

In the case of Raj Singh Gehlot v. Vistra (ICL) India Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Ins.) No. 6 of 2021, dated 2-8-2021], also a share subscription cum shareholders agreement was entered, which also contained various conditions. The financial creditor invested through the agreement. The agreement also contained clauses for distribution of revenue, cash flow etc. for which investment was made by the financial creditor in the SPV. Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor was admitted by Adjudicating Authority, which was challenged by Raj Singh Gehlot. The appeal was allowed by, thus, Tribunal, on which heavy reliance has been placed by the appellant. It is to be noticed that in the said case, there was arbitral award in favour of the financial creditor. The Tribunal in the Raj Singh Gehlot's judgment (supra), placed reliance on judgment of the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, in which the Supreme Court explained the meaning of concept of 'financial debt' under section 5, sub-section (8). When one looks into the judgment of this Tribunal in the above case, the basis of the judgment of this Tribunal is that section 7 application was filed on the basis of breach of settlement agreement, which is not permissible under section 7. [Para 38]

In Anuj Jain (supra), it was held that there has to be disbursal of fund by the financial creditor. The Tribunal held that award received under Arbitration and Conciliation Act or amount emerged from the settlement agreement will not come within the purview of section 7 application. [Para 40]

The ratio of the judgment Anuj Jain (supra) on the Tribunal, as noted above was that since section 7 application was filed alleging breach of settlement agreement, the application was not maintainable. The basis of judgment is that settlement agreement, which resulted into decree cannot be made basis for section 7 application. The judgment of the Supreme Court in Kotak Mahindra Bank (supra), which clearly says that mere fact that a decree had been obtained by the financial creditor, shall not take him out of section 7 proceedings and if ingredients of 'financial debt' are in existence, section 7 application is maintainable. The Tribunal in Raj Singh Gehlot's case (supra), has noticed the amendment made in the shareholder agreement. As per the judgment of the instant Tribunal, there was no consideration for time value of the debentures. [Para 41]

Section 2(45) defines ‘total income’ as ‘the total amount of income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in this Act. The principal charging section 4 makes the "total income of the previous year" subject to the charge of the income-tax. Thus the assessee’s income, which could be subject to tax, was the income of previous year and not the income which pertained to future 99 years. LD: Although the TRO had proceeded with the recovery proceeding by way of sale of the land, yet it transpired that necessary permission had been sought from the competent authority with regard to the reopening of the assessment proceedings but as it was apparent from the record, the assessee or her legal heirs had not been involved in the auction proceeding properly. Of course, in all fairness, the assessee could have agitated this issue before some civil court as it was a matter of administrative improprieties. In the instant case, one was not aware whether the concerned authority entrusted with the recovery proceeding, attachment and auction sale of the property of the assessee, was also entrusted with the payment of capital gains tax, if any, on the sale value so received by the auction seller. However, the contention of the assessee that capital gains tax would not be chargeable in his hands could not be accepted. The assessee’s contention that capital gains tax would not be chargeable in her hands because of the law laid down in case of J. Narayana Murthy (Supra) could not be simply accepted. It was because the facts of the cited case and the impugned case were totally different. The assessee had not been declared as insolvent rather, for recovery of the tax dues or resultant effect leading to attachment and auction sale, action was taken by the revenue. But there was serious infirmity in computing the capital gains tax because the Assessing Officer determined the cost of acquisition as on 1-4-1964 as per the balance sheet filed by the assessee and not the value as had to be determined on the basis of indexed cost of acquisition as has been envisaged under the Explanation (iii) to the proviso to section 48, i.e., the section related to mode of computation. However, the Assessing Officer did not enquire into the indexed cost of improvement, if any, made in between the period from 1-4-1964 to 1-4-1981 as per the provision of Explanation (iv) of the proviso to section 48. Therefore, in all fairness, the cost of acquisition had to be determined and adopted by the Assessing Officer on the basis of fair market value as on 1-4-1981. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to collect the value so adopted in a case of sale in the nearby vicinity as on 1-4-1981 or any nearby date next to 1-4-1981 or prior to 1-4-1981. In this connection, both the assessee and the revenue were directed to collect the requisite information from the DSR in order to arrive at the rate of computation of indexed cost as on 1-4-1981.

So far as the question of charging of interest under section 139(8) was concerned, there was plethora of judgments of the Supreme Court and various High Courts that in the case of reassessment, interest under section 139(8) could not be charged.

Further, since the new Explanation 2 to section 139(8)(a) is effective from the assessment year 1985-86, it did not apply to the preceding assessment year, i.e. , assessment year 1984-85.

Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in charging interest under section 139(8).

HEADNOTE: Section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Valuation of taxable services for charging service tax - Assessee was in business of operating hotels under its various brands - Any entrepreneur interested in running a hotel under assessee's banner signed an operating agreement with assessee to operate hotel under one of brands of assessee - Thereupon assessee sent its employees to such hotel for working therein and to ensure that proper standards were maintained in actual operation of hotel - Assessee directly paid salary to its above employees and same was reimbursed by hotel on actual basis without any markup to assessee - Adjudicating Authority levied service tax on expenses reimbursed by hotel to assessee under section 67 - Whether in terms of law declared by Delhi High Court in case of Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2012] 38 STT 75/28 taxmann.com 213, such reimbursable expenses collected by services provider (assessee) from service recipient (hotel) could not be held to be a part of value of services being provided by assessee and same could not be subjected to service tax - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Reimbursable expenses collected by services provider from service recipient could not be held to be a part of value of services being provided by services provider and same could not be subjected to service tax

FACT: The assessee was in the business of operating hotels under its various brands. Any entrepreneur interested in running a hotel under the assessee's banner signed an operating agreement with the assessee to operate the hotel under one of the brands of the assessee.

Thereupon the assessee sent its employees on secondment (deputation) to such hotel. Such employees were not employed by the hotel and they continued to be in the employment of the assessee. Though they continued to be on the rolls of the assessee, but in fact worked for the hotel in the actual day-to-day operation and running of the hotel. They also ensured that proper standards were maintained in the actual operation of the hotel so as to protect the valuable brand of the assessee. The salaries and expenses of such employees were continued to be paid by the assessee, but the same was reimbursed by the hotel on actual basis without any markup.

The Adjudicating Authority levied service tax on the expenses reimbursed by the hotel to the assessee under section 67.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: The Delhi High Court in the case of Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2012] 38 STT 75/28 taxmann.com 213 has held that reimbursable expenses cannot form part of the gross value of the services being provided by the service provider. In the instant case, the salary of the employees being sent by the assessee to the hotel is being paid by the assessee directly to the employees and the same is being reimbursed by the hotel without any markup. As such, in terms of the law declared by the High Court such reimbursable expenses collected by the services provider from the service recipient cannot be held to be a part of the value of the services being provided by the assessee and the same could not be subjected to service tax under section 67. [Para 4].

Apart from the fact that the issue is covered by the earlier decision of the Delhi High Court, the demand is barred by limitation having been raised by invoking longer period of limitation. The issue involved is a bona fide issue of interpretation of legal points which were the subject matter of various decisions. As such, it cannot be said that there was any suppression or misstatement with any mala fide intention to evade tax on the part of the assessee, thus justifying invocation of longer period of limitation. [Para 5]

In view of the aforesaid, the demand of service tax upon the assessee was liable to be set aside. [Para 6]

HEADNOTE: Section 147, read with section 149 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income escaping assessment - General - Assessment year 1955-56 - On basis of Tribunal's judgment, assessment for relevant assessment year was reopened under section 147(a) after a period of eight years - It was, however, seen from Tribunal's order that interest income of only Rs. 12,500 was required to be assessed - Whether, since, action under clause (a) of section 147 could be taken only in cases where income that escaped assessment was Rs. 50,000 or above, reopening of assessment in instant case was clearly unsustainable - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee entered into a contract with a German firm for purchase of machinery. The delivery was not within the time stipulated nor was it according to specifications. The assessee, therefore, instituted a suit against the said firm in 1935 for recovery of a sum of Rs. 2,05,000. The suit was ultimately decreed in December, 1953, for the said sum plus interest pendente lite. The assessee could however, recover only Rs. 2,20,192 from the Custodian of Enemy Properties. This amount was received by the assessee in the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1961-62. The assessee claimed that it was a capital receipt and hence not taxable. The ITO accepted the said claim only in respect of a small portion of the said amount and included the rest in the income of the assessee. On appeal, the amount to be included in the income was reduced substantially. Even so, the assessee filed a further appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the appeal on the only ground that the said amount could not be included in the assessment year 1961-62 for the reason that the assessee was maintaining its accounts on the mercantile basis and that the said amount must be deemed to have accrued on the date of the decree.

On the basis of the Tribunal's judgment, the ITO reopened the assessment for the relevant assessment year. However, on appeal, the Tribunal set aside the reassessment proceedings.

On reference:

HELD: Admittedly, the action was under section 147(a ) and could not have been under section 147(b). The action was being taken after the expiry of eight years. Action under clause (a) of section 147, could, therefore, be taken only in cases where the income that escaped assessment was in the sum of Rs. 50,000 or above. In this case, the proposal submitted by the ITO to the Board clearly said that the assessee received Rs. 2,05,000 as compensation and Rs. 12,500 towards interest thereon. The Tribunal had held that the sum of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt and only the interest of Rs. 12,500 constituted income (revenue receipt). Even in the earlier assessment proceedings, there was a controversy as to whether the whole or any part of the compensation amount constituted revenue receipt. The AAC had opined that out of the amount received, only an amount of Rs. 91,004 constituted revenue receipt. Evidently, the ITO had not applied his mind to the relevant facts. He seemed to have proceeded on the assumption that the entire compensation amount constituted a revenue receipt. In this, he was evidently wrong.

The Tribunal had subsequently found that only the sum of Rs. 12,500 representing the interest was includible in the income and that the remaining amount of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt. If so, the reopening of the assessment after eight years was clearly unsustainable under section 149 as it then stood.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

■ The basic dispute in the instant case is whether the valuation of shares at a premium of Rs. 90 per share is representative of the fair market value. According to the appellant the valuation of fair market value of the shares has been made on the basis of the DCF method which had been introduced as an alternative to the valuation based on Net Asset Value method during the assessment year under consideration. However, according to the Assessing Officer, the same could not have been adopted for valuation purpose because the shares in question had been subscribed and allotted on 29-9-2012 which was before the date of the coming into effect of the DCF method, in the Rules. The assessee, however, contends that the option to the assessee to adopt DCF method was available because the assessment in this case was pending on that date which was completed later on 29-3-2016. The DCF method could be applied for valuation purposes for the assessments pending at that time. Besides, the Circular stated that rule would apply from the date of its publication. This assessment was pending on that date. The benefit of the DCF method of valuation was thus even otherwise available to the assessee as per the Circular. Further rule 11UA(2)(b) provides for the acceptance of the valuation made by Chartered Accountant as an acceptable mode for determining the fair market value of shares. The assessee has filed a report of CA, which certifies the fair market value, higher than Rs. 100 at Rs. 106 per share. The attempt of the Assessing Officer to locate and establish discrepancies or errors in that report of the Chartered Accountant is not based on any acceptable principle or approved standards. The discrepancies as pointed out by the Assessing Officer are not relevant in the context of capital restructuring in the case of group companies. Valuation by itself is a specialized exercise which can be disputed only on the basis of the findings of another expert as recognized in law for that purpose. The valuation as proposed by the DCF method cannot, therefore, be faulted. There is no overvaluation of shares over the fair market value. Accordingly the invocation of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) by the Assessing Officer being erroneous cannot be upheld. Thus, the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 56(2)(viib) is directed to be deleted. [Para 6.1]

■

As to the other objection of the assessee, to the action of the Assessing Officer to add the share capital amount as collected by way of premium from the subscribing companies by invoking the proviso to section 68, it is viewed that the proviso provides for the scrutiny and assessment of the funds of the immediate subscribing company. The proviso does not extend that power to scrutinise the financial capacity of the secondary source which has provided funds to the subscribing companies. It is also noticed that in the case of some of the secondary sources, there are scrutiny assessment orders on record. Further the fact that the investments as made by the subscribing companies were out of funds which they possessed at the beginning of the year and no fresh infusion of funds by the subscribing companies during the assessment year under consideration and the source of funds are all proceeds of investments made in earlier years in the course of business and have been recalled/encashed was corroborated by the director of the subscribing companies in his statement recorded on oath. According to section 149(1)(b)(iii ), as it stood with effect from 1-4-1989 but before being amended by the Finance Act, 2001, with effect from 1-6-2001, if seven years had elapsed from the end of the assessment year 1980-81, but not more than ten years had elapsed, the notice under section 148 could be issued for the assessment year 1980-81, provided the escaped income was likely to be Rs. 50,000 or more. It could either be sold along with the flats or separately or might be retained for being leased to the flat-owners. The rates at which the flats were booked on various dates were to be considered for valuation of those flats. In case of any space earmarked for the appellant which had not been so agreed to be sold, but was intended to be retained by the appellant himself it had to be valued at the rate at which initial booking was started, because it was based on the initial understanding with the builder. However, upon the assessee deciding not to sell some flats at a later point of time, the rate that was prevalent then had to be adopted for those flats. The Tribunal being concerned with the market value of the flats and not their cost of construction, these need to be valued at the same rate at which it would be available to the public.

The adoption or estimate by the Commissioner (Appeals) of the rates at which some space could be made available to the buyers of the basements, upper ground floor, etc., was improper, because he did not consider the rates at which public was invited to buy the flat space. The rates were revised upwards more than once, which suggested that the public was slow in responding to the invitation but, all the same, it was those rates with which the flats were to be related and not any imaginery rate. If, as on 31- 3-1983, some flats in the ground floor, upper ground floor first, second and other floors were not booked, then the most proximate rate at which invitation was advertised should be adopted as the value for those flats. White adopting the rates, care must be exercised to ensure that the rates adopted were for those respective floors, i.e., the rates of second floor could not be adopted for valuing the third floor, unless both the floors had the same rate.

The rates at which the flat space was sold were similar to recoverable debt and since the flat price was payable in instalments spread over a few years, the instalments that became due after the valuation date needed to be discounted to arrive at the present worth of the space involved. Further, since the building in which the space was allotted to the several buyers required the sanction of the L & DO on payment of commercialisation charges, it was very much a charge on the present value of the flat space. Similarly, the settlement with the tenant, who had carried the matter to the High Court that was ultimately settled in 1986, was also a charge on the present value of the flats. Since the property was under construction as on the relevant valuation dates, and some more cost had to be incurred, as the construction got completed in 1987, i.e., almost four and three years from 31-3-1983 and 31-3-1984, respectively this element equated as interest also required to be allowed deduction of for arriving at the present value of the flat space.

The Assessing Officer was, accordingly, directed to recalculate the value of the space on the two valuation dates separately, as above.

The appeals were, accordingly, partly allowed.

Therefore, it can be said that there is every possibility of an obligating event arising which will result in an outflow of resources. [Para 29] A question may be raised that if the obligating event is sure to arise, the assessee could have made reasonable provision every year which would meet the matching concept also. However, it was not possible. In the case of Rotork Controls India (P.) Ltd. v. CIT 180 Taxman 422 (SC), the Supreme Court has observed that a provision is recognised when: (a ) an enterprise has a present obligation as a result of a past event; (b) it is probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation; and (c ) a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. If these conditions are not met, no provision can be recognised. In the instant case, as already observed that the assessee had a present obligation as a result of a past event. Thus, the first condition was satisfied. It was also observed that outflow of resources was probable to settle the obligation. The second condition was also satisfied. However, considering the nature of activity, it was the third condition which was difficult to satisfy. The demand for accommodation by the members was essentially tourism oriented. Tourism, in turn, depends on several factors. They may be social, political, climatic and so on. If wedding season is in full swing, tourism can get affected. If there is some commotion around a particular resort or if the law and order situation is not conducive, tourism can be affected. Sudden change in weather can also affect tourism. Further, availability of rail or air reservation can also affect tourism. The possibility of Leave Travel concession (LTC) getting lapsed can see sudden spurt in tourism. These are only a few illustrations which can affect the demand for accommodation either way. There may be many possibilities which may not come to mind but may put the assessee into tremendous pressure. All these factors are such which are twined with the normal human life and, hence, are not only certain to occur but also make it difficult to reasonably estimate the probable outflow of resources. Moreover, as mentioned earlier, most of the grievances are settled by consumer forum and it can be anybody’s guess as to what damages the forum will award. Considering the difficulty in estimating reasonably the obligation in monetary terms, no provision can be made. [Para 30]

As already have held that there was a definite liability cast on the assessee to fulfil its promise and, therefore, it could not be said that the entire fee received by it had accrued as income. Further, the peculiar nature of the activity along with the complexity attached to it was also considered as a result of which no reasonable provision for the liability could be made. Therefore, recognising the entire receipt as income in the year of receipt could lead to distortion. [Para 31]

As a result the proposition of the assessee that it was not justifiable to tax the entire income in a single year was to be accepted. [Para 31]

Accordingly, the entire amount of time share membership fee receivable by the assessee up front at the time of enrolment of a member was not the income chargeable to tax in the initial year on account of contractual obligation that was fastened to the receipt to provide services in future over the term of contract. [Para 32]

In the result, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be dismissed. [Para 33]

EDITOR’S NOTE

It is well established that each assessment year is a separate unit of assessment and the law relating to reopening of assessment has to be applied keeping the facts and circumstances of that year only in mind. Therefore, view taken in a particular assessment year cannot bind the Assessing Officer for subsequent assessment years.

Section 50C of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Capital gains - Special provision for computation of full value consideration (Land and building) - Assessment years 2004-05, 2006-07 and 2007-08 - Assessee sold a land and building for consideration of Rs. 17.50 crores vide conveyance deed dated 12-9-2005 and sale price had been approved by appropriate authority in financial year 2001-02 when agreement for sale was entered into - Stamp duty authorities determined market value of property at Rs. 26.02 crores - Assessing Officer invoked provisions of section 50C and computed long-term capital gains on basis of stamp duty valuation - Assessee contended that provisions of section 50C should not be applied to agreements entered prior to its introduction - However, no reason had been cited by parties for delay in completing registration and it was also not clear as to whether assessee had received any part of consideration in year 2001-02, when agreement was entered into as per conditions prescribed in proviso to section 50C - Whether since all relevant factual aspects, which were necessary for purpose of section 50C, had not been furnished by assessee, this issue required fresh examination at end of Assessing Officer - Held, yes [Para 22.6] [Matter remanded]INCOME TAX : Where assessee sold land and building for consideration of Rs. 17.50 crores determined as per sale agreement entered in year 2001-02 vide conveyance deed dated 12-9-2005 and Assessing Officer invoked provisions of section 50C and computed long-term capital gains on basis of stamp duty valuation of Rs. 26.02 crores, since no reason had been cited by parties for delay in completing registration and it was also not clear as to whether assessee had received any part of consideration in year 2001-02, this issue required fresh examination at end of Assessing Officer  INCOME TAX : Consistently followed method of valuation of stock, which has been accepted by departmental authorities earlier, should not be disturbed, since a stray departure in one year tends to upset calculations  INCOME TAX : Provisions of section 35DDA are related to lump sum compensation paid and, therefore, provisions of section 35DDA would not apply to pension payments, which are recurring in nature  INCOME TAX : Application software usually become outdated in no time and, hence, expenses incurred thereon are to be allowed as revenue expenditure  INCOME TAX : Where assessee claimed travel expenses incurred on foreigners who were executives specializing in business carried on by assessee and visited India for business purposes only, said expenses were to be allowed as revenue expenditure  INCOME TAX : Rule 8D came into effect from 1-4-2008 and hence could not be applied to assessment years 2004-05, 2006-07 and 2007-08  INCOME TAX : Value of closing stock as on 31-3-2004 should be determined by Assessing Officer by loading unutilised MODVAT credit and Assessing Officer should be directed to adopt same method for opening stock as on 1-4-2004  INCOME TAX : Where royalty income received was not connected with business of exports carried on by assessee, Assessing Officer was justified in excluding 90 per cent of royalty income from profits for purpose of computing profits of business as per Explanation (baa) to section 80HHC  INCOME TAX : Where assessee permitted demerged company to use some of its premises and recovered certain costs from it and Assessing Officer took view that Annual letting value had to be computed and assessed under head Income from house property and arrived at fair rental value by increasing 5% of rent determined in Assessment Year 2003-04 and assessed same in Assessment Year 2004-05, since Assessing Officer had adopted ad hoc rate for determining Annual letting value, determination of ALV required fresh examination  INCOME TAX : Where Assessing Officer referred matter of determination of fair market value as on 1.4.1981 to departmental valuation officer (DVO), since DVO did not furnish his report before completion of assessment but before Tribunal, matter was to be remanded back  INCOME TAX : Where assessee made provision for expenses on basis of estimates, Assessing Officer was not justified in making disallowance of adjustment by way of excess/short amount in respect of year end provision made for expenses, since, whatever may be degree of estimation, there was bound to be some difference when actual bill would be received and same would require adjustment on account of excess/short provision  INCOME TAX : Interest under section 234C is required to be computed on returned income

III. Section  32,  read with section  2(11),  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Depreciation  -  Allowance/Rate of  (Time share weeks) - Assessment years  2015-16 to 2016-17  - Assessee-company operated resort properties and sold time share rights - Due to member defaults in maintenance fees, 15,203 time share weeks were repossessed/forfeited - Assessee capitalised these weeks as removal of encumbrances/cost improvement to resort properties (Rs. 22.28 crores: Rs. 3.37 crores land, Rs. 18.91 crores building) - It claimed depreciation on building component - Assessing Officer disallowed depreciation, holding time share weeks were not building/tangible asset within section 2(11) - Whether since legal ownership of resort buildings remained with assessee and payments to group entities removed encumbrances on identifiable units and represented cost of improvement of existing capital asset, capitalised amount was to be treated as part of building block and depreciation was to be allowed - Held, yes [Para 34] [In favour of assessee]

Section  5,  read with section  263,  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 -  Income  -  Accrual of  (Advance business receipts) - Assessment year  2005-06  - Assessee was engaged in running of hotels, resorts and clubs - It offered holiday schemes for its card members to utilize 'room nights' at assessee's hotel against payment of some advance - In case of non-utilization of said facility, assessee would refund back said sum to card members along with surrendered value - High court held that assessee was required to refund advance in more than 99 per cent in cash, assessee incurred liability and no income could be said to have accrued to assessee on receipt of advance - It was stated at bar that in respect of assessment years in question, there had been no claim made by appellant-Department in Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP) proceedings, wherein plan was approved on 25.04.2024 and was implemented - In circumstances, appropriate orders might have been made in these appeals - Whether taking note of above submission and by following judgment Ghanashyam Mishra & Sons (P.) Ltd. v. Edelweiss Asset Reconstruction Co. Ltd. [2021] 126 taxmann.com 132 (SC), appeals and SLP’s were to be dismissed - Held, yes [Para 2] [In favour of assessee]

I Section 5, read with section 145, of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual Of (Time of accrual - Late payment surcharge) - Assessment year 2018-19 - Assessee was engaged in business of generation of electricity and distributed same through intermediaries - It had entered into Power Purchase Agreements (PPAs) with DISCOMS to regulate terms and conditions in respect of sale of power - Based on PPAs, assessee was eligible to claim sale prices of electricity and late payment surcharge (LPSC) of existing rate of 1.5 per cent per month in case sale considerations were settled beyond agreed period of settlement - Assessing Officer had made an addition of LPSC as income of assessee on ground that assessee followed mercantile system of accounting and same was chargeable to tax whether it was received or receivable - Whether as per accounting standard and norms, assessee had to declare its income not only based on accrual system but also supported by concept of certainty of recovery - Held, yes - Whether since assessee had not recovered any LPSC in past, impugned addition was to be deleted - Held, yes [Para 20] [In favour of assessee] II Section 36(1)(iii), read with section 43 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Interest on Borrowed Capital (Capital work-in-progress) - Assessment year 2018-19 - Assessee had made investments in three categories, viz., direct purchase of fixed assets, in-house development of project I (Bamnauli project) and in house development of project II (Bawana Project) - Assessing Officer observed that assessee had shown outstanding loan in Balance Sheet and had not capitalized any interest amount on fixed assets purchased during year and outstanding Capital work in progress (CWIP) - Accordingly, he proceeded to made addition to income of assessee being of view that interest expenditure relatable to amount invested had to be capitalized and could not be allowed as revenue expenditure - It was observed that Bawana Project was commissioned in financial year 2013-14 and interest was already determined and capitalized at time of commissioning of project itself - As regards Bamnauli Project, assessee had submitted evidence before Commissioner (Appeals) stating that this project was fully financed out of equity introduced by GNCTD and no borrowed funds were utilized during this assessment year, however, Commissioner (Appeals) had rejected same - As regards direct purchase of assets, it was observed that same was put to use on same date as that of acquisition and, therefore, there was no concept of further capitalization - Whether, in view of aforesaid, impugned addition made by Assessing Officer was unsustainable and Assessing Officer was directed to only verify Project Bamnauli since none of tax authorities have verified this aspect and then allow claim of assessee as per law - Held, yes [Para 26] [Partly in favour of assessee] III Section 80-IA of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Deductions - Profits and gains from industrial undertakings, etc., after certain dates (Computation of deduction) - Assessment year 2018-19 - Assessee had claimed unwinding of interest on retention liability project (IND-AS adjustment) as deduction under section 80IA(4) - Assessing Officer and Commissioner (Appeals) held that said amount was not profit derived from industrial undertaking and therefore, deduction under section 80IA was not allowable on this amount -
