CIT(A) was that the proceedings were initiated under section 158BD on 27-3-2003 in consequence upon a search proceedings started in the case of Purandhare group on 8-12-1999. According to him, the proceedings under section 158BD were not barred by limitation under the statute. In this manner, the legal objections of the assessee were dismissed which are now being challenged through this second appeal. 5. From the side of the appellant, Learned A.R. Mr. Sunil Pathak has appeared and on the basis of the facts mentioned herein-above, argued that the assessee has started a company namely LBCPL on 20-3-1994, in which he and his wife were the directors. The said company had acquired development rights of Gajanan Co-operative Society, Kothrud, Pune. The Purandhare group has purchased the said company on 1-7-1995, hence the assessee has transferred all his rights in favour of the transferee. A search was conducted on Shri Purandhare on 8-12-1999 and a chit was found mentioning 35 to Shri Lunawat for land. Highlighting the alleged mistakes of the Revenue Department, Ld. AR has vehemently relied upon a decision of the Assessing Officer, already taken in the case of the said company wherein, according to him, the Assessing Officer has thoroughly investigated the matter and recorded the statements and thereafter arrived at the conclusion that no such payment was made to the assessee and the claim by the said company of expenditure or deduction was disallowed. When the said company had gone in appeal, then again the statements were recorded, however, while deciding the said appeal, the Ld. CIT(A) has formed a different opinion that the amount was actually paid by Shri Purandhare and directed the Assessing Officer to issue notice under section 158BD/147 to the assessee. Accordingly, in the impugned order, the Assessing Officer has taken the action against the assessee. Coming to his main plank of argument, Ld. A.R. has drawn our attention on pages 243, 245 and 246 of the compilation containing the copies of the notices issued under sections 158BD and 147 by the Assessing Officer. Referring page 243 of the paper book which contains a notice issued by ACIT, Circle 5, Pune dated 14-5-2003, wherein vide para 2, it was clearly mentioned that the proceed- ings under section 158BD were initiated on the basis of the intimation received from the office of CIT(A)-I, Pune, during the course of appeal proceedings in the case of M/s. LBCPL. On page 244, there was a letter from the assessee addressed to the Assessing Officer wherein, the assessee has demanded "satisfaction recorded by the assessee". Next is the page 245 of paper book containing a notice under section 158BD dated 8-4-2003 wherein vide para 3, it was intimated by the ACIT, Circle 3, Pune that the CIT(A) during the course of appellate proceedings in the case of LBCPL had recorded the statement on oath and intimated the office to initiate proceedings under section 158BD of Income-tax Act. On the basis of those notices & correspondence, Ld. A.R. Mr. Pathak has stressed that the Assessing Officer has initiated the proceedings under section 158BD only on the basis of the direction of Ld. CIT(A) who was deciding an appeal of an another company which had already been sold by the assessee, namely M/s. LBCPL. According to him, now the situation is that on one hand, the Assessing Officer had made an addition of Rs. 35 lakhs by disallowance of expenditure in the hands of the said company by treating as non-genuine, however, on the other hand, also making an addition of the same amount held to be received by the assessee. One more fact has also been brought by Ld. A.R. that the revenue department has resorted to the assessment under section 158BD as well as under section 147 in the case of one Shri Pramod Lunawat, thus taxing the same amount on substantive basis in two hands. So, he has contested that the proceedings under section 158BD should not emerge out of the appellate proceedings carried out in an another case. He has also contested that the assessment was beyond a reasonable time because the action under section 132 was initiated out on Purandhare group on 8-12-1999 and the notices in the case of the assessee were issued after the lapse of 3½ years on 27-3-2003. In support of this objection of inordinate delay, Ld. A.R. has cited the case of Khandubhai Vasanji Desai v. Dy. CIT [1999] 236 ITR 73 (Guj.), and the decisions of H. Ajitbhai & Co. v. Asstt. CIT [1999] 45 ITD 262 (Ahd.) and Raymond Woollen Mills Ltd. v. ITO [1996] 57 ITD 536 (Bom.).

(i) the business of the hotel is not formed by the splitting up, or the reconstruction, of a business already in existence or by the transfer to a new business of a building previously used as a hotel or of any machinery or plant previously used for any purpose ; (ii) the business of the hotel is owned and carried on by a company registered in India with a paid-up capital of not less than five hundred thousand rupees ;

(iii) the hotel is for the time being approved for the purposes of this subsection by the Central Government ;

(iv) the business of the hotel starts functioning after the 31st day of March, 1981 but before the 1st day of April, 1985.

(5) The deduction specified in sub-section (1) shall be allowed in computing the total income in respect of the assessment year relevant to the previous year in which the industrial undertaking begins to manufacture or produce articles or things, or to operate its cold storage plant or plants or the ship is first brought into use or the business of the hotel starts functioning (such assessment year being hereafter in this section referred to as the initial assessment year) and each of the seven assessment years immediately succeeding the initial assessment year :

Provided that in the case of an assessee, being a co-operative society, the provisions of this sub-section shall have effect as if for the words "seven assessment years", the words "nine assessment years" had been substituted.

(6) Notwithstanding anything contained in any other provision of this Act, the profits and gains of an industrial undertaking or a ship or the business of a hotel to which the provisions of sub-section (1) apply shall, for the purposes of determining the quantum of deduction under sub-section (1) for the assessment year immediately succeeding the initial assessment year or any subsequent assessment year, be computed as if such industrial undertaking or ship or the business of the hotel were the only source of income of the assessee during the previous years relevant to the initial assessment year and to every subsequent assessment year up to and including the assessment year for which the determination is to be made.

(7) Where the assessee is a person other than a company or a co-operative society, the deduction under sub-section (1) from profits and gains derived from an industrial undertaking shall not be admissible unless the accounts of the industrial undertaking for the previous year relevant to the assessment year for which the deduction is claimed have been audited by an accountant, as defined in the Explanation below sub-section (2) of section 288, and the assessee furnishes, along with his return of income, the report of such audit in the prescribed form duly signed and verified by such accountant.

(8) Where any goods held for the purposes of the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship are transferred to any other business carried on by the assessee, or where any goods held for the purposes of any other business carried on by the assessee are transferred to the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship and, in either case, the consideration, if any, for such transfer as recorded in the accounts of the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship does not correspond to the market value of such goods as on the date of the transfer, then, for the purposes of the deduction under this section, the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking or the business of the hotel or the operation of the ship shall be computed as if the transfer, in either case, had been made at the market value of such goods as on that date :

Provided that where, in the opinion of the Income-tax Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking or the business of the hotel or the operation of the skip in the manner hereinbefore specified presents exceptional difficulties, the Income-tax Officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit.

Explanation: In this sub-section, "market value", in relation to any goods, means the price that such goods would ordinarily fetch on sale in the open market.

(9) Where it appears to the Income-tax Officer that, owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship to which this section applies and any other person, or for any other reason, the course of business between them is so arranged that the business transacted between them produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profits which might be expected to arise in the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship, the Income-tax Officer shall, in computing the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the ship for the purposes of the deduction under this section, take the amount of profits as may be reasonably deemed to have been derived there from.

(10) The Central Government may, after making such inquiry as it may think fit, direct, by notification in the Official Gazette, that the exemption conferred by this section shall not apply to any class of industrial undertakings with effect from such at as it may specify in the notification.]

32. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the provisions of this Chapter, the value in respect of supplies specified below shall, at the option of the supplier, be determined in the manner provided hereinafter.

(2) The value of supply of services in relation to the purchase or sale of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be determined by the supplier of services in the following manner, namely:—

(a)

for a currency, when exchanged from, or to, Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to the difference in the buying rate or the selling rate, as the case may be, and the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for that currency at that time, multiplied by the total units of currency:

Provided that in case where the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for a currency is not available, the value shall be one per cent of the gross amount of Indian Rupees provided or received by the person changing the money:

Provided further that in case where neither of the currencies exchanged is Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to one per cent of the lesser of the two amounts the person changing the money would have received by converting any of the two currencies into Indian Rupees on that day at the reference rate provided by the Reserve Bank of India:

Provided also that a person supplying the services may exercise the option to ascertain the value in terms of clause (b) for a financial year and such option shall not be withdrawn during the remaining part of that financial year;

(b)

at the option of the supplier of services, the value in relation to the supply of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be deemed to be—

(i)

one per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount up to one lakh rupees, subject to a minimum amount of two hundred and fifty rupees;

(ii)

one thousand rupees and half of a per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding one lakh rupees and up to ten lakh rupees; and

(iii)

five thousand and five hundred rupees and one tenth of a per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding ten lakh rupees, subject to a maximum amount of sixty thousand rupees.

(3) The value of the supply of services in relation to booking of tickets for travel by air provided by an air travel agent shall be deemed to be an amount calculated at the rate of five per cent of the basic fare in the case of domestic bookings, and at the rate of ten per cent of the basic fare in the case of international bookings of passage for travel by air.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-rule, the expression "basic fare" means that part of the air fare on which commission is normally paid to the air travel agent by the airlines.

(4) The value of supply of services in relation to life insurance business shall be,—

(a)

the gross premium charged from a policy holder reduced by the amount allocated for investment, or savings on behalf of the policy holder, if such an amount is intimated to the policy holder at the time of supply of service;

(b)

in case of single premium annuity policies other than (a), ten per cent of single premium charged from the policy holder; or

(c)

in all other cases, twenty five per cent of the premium charged from the policy holder in the first year and twelve and a half per cent of the premium charged from the policy holder in subsequent years:

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-rule shall apply where the entire premium paid by the policy holder is only towards the risk cover in life insurance.

(5) Where a taxable supply is provided by a person dealing in buying and selling of second hand goods i.e., used goods as such or after such minor processing which does not change the nature of the goods and where no input tax credit has been availed on the purchase of such goods, the value of supply shall be the difference between the selling price and the purchase price and where the value of such supply is negative, it shall be ignored:

Provided that the purchase value of goods repossessed from a defaulting borrower, who is not registered, for the purpose of recovery of a loan or debt shall be deemed to be the purchase price of such goods by the defaulting borrower reduced by five percentage points for every quarter or part thereof, between the date of purchase and the date of disposal by the person making such repossession.

(6) The value of a token, or a voucher, or a coupon, or a stamp (other than postage stamp) which is redeemable against a supply of goods or services or both shall be equal to the money value of the goods or services or both redeemable against such token, voucher, coupon, or stamp.

Attribution of income taxable under section 67(10)87 to capital assets remaining with the specified entity, under section 7288.

[R. 8AB of the 1962 Rules]

50. (1) For the purposes of section 72(5)89, the amount chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under section 67(10)87, shall be attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in the manner provided in this rule.

(2) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, chargeable to tax under section 67(10)87 relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90 shall be—

A= B×(C/D).

Where,—

A= the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90;

B= amount charged under section 67(10)91;

C= increase in, or recognition of, value of the asset remaining with the specified entity, because of revaluation or valuation; and

D= aggregate of increase in, or recognition of, value of all assets because of the revaluation or valuation.

(3) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, is in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 does not relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(4) Irrespective of anything contained in sub-rule (2) or sub-rule (3), where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 relate only to the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(5) The specified entity shall furnish the details of amount attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in Form No. 2792.

(6) The person who is authorised to verify the return of income of the specified entity under section 26593 shall verify Form No. 2792.

(7) Form No. 2792 shall be furnished on or before the due date referred to in section 263(1)(c)94 for the tax year in which the amount is chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91.

(8) For the purposes of this rule,—

(a)

the amount chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91 shall relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, if the revaluation is based on a valuation report obtained from a registered valuer as defined in rule 56(f)95;

the specified entity shall not be entitled for the depreciation on—

(i)

the increase in value of an asset on account of its revaluation; or

(ii)

the recognition of the value of a self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, due to its valuation; and

Time limit for sale of attached immovable property Rule 68B(1) of the Second Schedule prescribes that the sale of immovable property (attached for tax recovery) must be completed within 7 years from the end of the financial year in which the order for tax, interest, fine, penalty, or any other sum becomes final. However, the Board may extend this period by up to three more years, but only if they provide written reasons for doing so.

Further, if the property is required to be re-sold (because the highest bid was lower than the reserve price, or due to some specific circumstances mentioned in rules 57, 58 or 61), the above time limit is extended by one more year.

Rule 68B(2) prescribes that the period during which the proceedings are stayed by an order or injunction of any court shall be excluded in computing the time limit for conclusion of the proceedings.

However, there was an ambiguity regarding the commencement date and the end date of the period stayed by an order or injunction of any court which was required to be excluded.

With a view to removing such ambiguity, the Finance Bill, 2025 proposed to amend the said rule so as to exclude the period 'commencing on the date on which stay was granted by an order or injunction of any court and ending on the date on which certified copy of the order vacating the stay was received by the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner' while computing limitation period.

16. Other Amendments

The end date for notifying faceless schemes under Section 92CA (reference to TPO), Section 144C (reference to DRP), Section 253 (Appeal to ITAT), and Section 255 (procedure of ITAT) is proposed to be omitted. This would allow the central government to issue directions beyond the cut off of March 31, 2025.

Sections 72A and 72AA are proposed to be amended to limit the carried forward loss of a predecessor entity to be offset by the successor entity for a maximum of eight assessment years.

Section 132(8) is proposed to be amended to provide that the time limit for obtaining approval for retention is one month from the end of the quarter in which the assessment, reassessment, or recomputation order was made. Currently, the timeline is 30 days from the date of the assessment, reassessment, or recomputation order.

The word 'authorisation' is proposed to be replaced with 'authorisations' in Explanation 1 to Section 132 to align with other provisions of the Act.

It is proposed to amend clause (ii) of Explanation 1 to Section 132B to update the reference from Section 158BE to Section 158B, reflecting the changes made by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 2024.

Amendments are proposed to Sections 144BA, 153, 153B, 158BE, 158BFA, 263, 264, and Rule 68B of Schedule II to exclude stay periods in computing time limits for assessment/reassessment proceedings. The period from the date of the court's stay order to the date the jurisdictional Principal Commissioner or Commissioner receives the certified copy of the stay vacation order shall be excluded in computing time limits for assessment/reassessment proceedings.

1. Proposal to amend 'Plant or Machinery' under Section 17(5)(d) of CGST Act with 'Plant & Machinery'

In section 17 of the Central Goods and Services Tax Act, in sub-section (5), in clause (d) for the words 'plant or machinery', the words 'plant and machinery' shall be substituted.

This issue has been highly debated due to its significant impact on the availability of Input Tax Credit (ITC). It is to be noted that this amendment has been proposed to nullify the impact of decision as held in Safari Retreats1.

The issue in Safari matter was whether the phrase 'plant or machinery' in Section 17(5)(d) can be given the same meaning as, the explanation appended at the end of Section 17(5) which defines the term 'plant and machinery' & whether 'Building' could be held as 'Plant' on which ITC would be available.

After much deliberation, it was held by Supreme Court that 'plant or machinery' cannot be given the same meaning as provided for 'plant and machinery'. Also, it was observed that, ITC can be availed on goods and services used for construction of immovable property subject to its use, which is to be decided on a case-by-case basis by applying a functionality test, considering the unique business requirements and the role that immovable property plays in the said business.

The Court then referred to similar, phrase occurring in section 245E of the Act permitting the Settlement Commission to reopen proceedings where it thinks it "necessary or expedient", and quoted the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Paharpur Cooling Towers (P.) Ltd. [1996] 219 ITR 618: "Section 245E, which ...empowers the Commission to reopen any completed proceedings connected with the case before it but this power is circumscribed by the requirement expressly stated in the section that such reopening of completed proceedings should be necessary or expedient for the proper disposal of the case pending before it. There are two other limitations upon this power, viz., that this reopening of the completed proceedings can be done, even for the aforesaid limited purpose, only with the concurrence of the assessee and secondly that this power cannot extend to a period beyond eight years from the end of the assessment year to which such proceeding relates. These two features make it abundantly clear that the section contemplates reopening of the completed proceedings not for the benefit of the assessee but in the interests of the Revenue. It contemplates a situation where the case before the Commission cannot be satisfactorily settled unless some previously concluded proceedings are reopened which would normally be to the prejudice of the assessee. It is precisely for this reason that the section says that it can be done only with the concurrence of the assessee and that too for a period within eight years. This section cannot be read as empowering the Commission to do indirectly what cannot be done directly....The power conferred by section 245E is thus a circumscribed and a conditional power. It can be exercised only in accordance with and subject to the conditions aforementioned and in no other manner." [Emphasis supplied] (p. 627)

The exercise of the discretion by the Assessing Officer is required to be preceded by the formation of an opinion by the Assessing Officer of the necessity or expediency of making such a reference. However, the Court noted that provision does not make apparent the nature of such opinion. Is this a prima facie opinion or a considered opinion after examining all available materials? Court answered it thus: "A reading of section 92C and 92CA does not indicate that the Assessing Officer is required to form a prior considered opinion after considering all the available materials, even before making a reference to the TPO". The court noted that section 92CA (1) is in contrast with section 55A of the Act where the Assessing Officer is empowered to refer to the Valuation Officer (VO) the question of ascertaining the Fair Market Value (FMV) of a capital asset. The wording of section 55A is unambiguous that the Assessing Officer has to first form an opinion that the value declared is less than the FMV, before he can refer the question to the VO. If he does not, then the reference itself is bad. The question, in regard to section 92CA before the court: ‘Is reference to the TPO by the Assessing Officer to be made by the Assessing Officer only after he is satisfied by going through the steps enlisted in section 92C (1) to (3) that the price declared by the assessee is not to be accepted or can he make such a reference at an anterior stage? ’ The Court held that : "There is nothing in section 92CA itself that requires the Assessing Officer to first form a considered opinion in the manner indicated in section 92C(3) before he can make a reference to the TPO. It is not possible to read such a requirement into section 92CA(1). However, it will suffice if the Assessing Officer forms a prima facie opinion that it is necessary and expedient to make such a reference". The court’s reasoning was that the TPO is expected to perform the same exercise as envisaged under section 92C(1) to (3) while determining the ALP under section 92CA(3) by the Assessing Officer. The latter part of section 92CA(3) unambiguously states that the Assessing Officer shall by an order in writing, determine the ALP, in relation to the international transaction in accordance with sub-section (3) of section 92C. It will be pointless to have a duplication of this exercise at two stages one after the other. In the opinion of the court, the scheme of the provision is that after the TPO determines the ALP the matter revives before the Assessing Officer at the section 92C(4) stage where, in terms of section 92CA (4), the Assessing Officer will compute the total income "having regard to" the ALP determined by the TPO.

At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. It also provides that the time value of money is the difference in the value to be received today as compared to a greater value to be received in future. Also, the Insolvency Law Committee Report2 has the time value of money which means the compensation for the duration for which the money has been disbursed by the creditor to the debtor which can be in form of either interest or factoring of discount in payment. Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302/140 SCL 135 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Appellate Tribunal referred to the Black's Law Dictionary, 9th Edition to construe the meaning of time value of money and concluded that it is the compensation or the price paid for the time during which the money was disbursed, i.e., the time between lending and repayment.

Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

Liability of chit funds liable to pay service tax after 1-6-2015

Question - We understand that after enactment of Finance Act, 2015, chit funds are liable to pay service tax. Kindly advise.

Answer - In Delhi Chit Funds Association v. Union of India [2013] 32 taxmann.com 332/39 STT 955 (Delhi), the levy of service tax on chit funds has been held as invalid. It was (in effect) held that it is mere transaction in money and hence outside the definition of 'service' itself.

Departmental SLP against this decision has been dismissed by Supreme Court - Union of India v. Delhi Chit Fund Association [2014] 43 GST 524/42 taxmann.com 52.

In Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2008] 17 STT 491 (AP), the Board circular dated 23-8-2007 extending service tax to business chit funds has been held as invalid and has been squashed. - SLP against the order dismissed by SC - Union of India v. Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds [2015] 49 GST 274/53 taxmann.com 237 (SC).

However, in All Kerala Association of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2013] 40 STT 500/35 taxmann.com 620 (Ker.), validity of service tax on chit funds has been upheld.

Some changes were proposed in Finance Act, 2015 to get over these decisions. However, these changes have not been made effective so far, as explained below.

Proposed changes in definitions - Following definitions are proposed vide section 107 of Finance Act, 2015. However, these definitions have not been notified when other provisions of the Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, the following definitions are not effective.

'Transaction in money' shall not include any activity carried out for consideration by foreman of chit fund Service tax will be payable by foreman of chit fund on services provided by way of conducting a chit. - proposed Explanation 2(ii)(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 [which defines service] inserted by section 107(g) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this explanation is not effective.

Foreman of chit fund shall have the same meaning as is assigned to the term 'foreman' in section 2(j) of the Chit Funds Act - proposed section 65B(23A) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted by section 107(b) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this definition is not effective.

It was clarified that these amendments have been made as intention of law has always been to levy service tax on these activities. However, in view of contrary decisions of various High Courts, specific amendments are made in statutory provisions - para 5.1(ii) of MF(DR) letter DOF No. 334/5/2015-TRU dated 28-2-2015.

Interestingly, these amendments, though passed, have not been made effective when other provisions were made effective from 1-6-2015. Reason for this is not clear.

Conclusion - Since these changes, proposed in Finance Act, 2015 have not been notified and not made effective, in my view, the decisions of Delhi High Court and Andhra Pradesh High Court are valid and no service tax should be payable on chit funds.

A part of the gross amount collected by the appellants from the so-called ‘members’ was collected prior to 16-6-2005 and the remainder was collected on/after 16-6-2005. These amounts were determined on a pro rata basis out of large amounts which were collected by the appellants from the members on long-term basis. The service recipients had a variety of schemes provided by the appellants. Some of them could avail of the facilities in the resorts for a short period, say, 5 years, some others could avail of the same for a longer period, say, 25 years, and so on. The resort could be used, in this manner, even up to 99 years. The appellants collected various amounts from these time-sharers depending on the length of the time period. The gross amount for the purposes of levy of service tax was determined on pro rata basis for the relevant period (16-6-2005 to 30-9-2006). The authorities below taking view that the appellants were covered under the category of ‘club or association service’ under section 65(25a) confirmed demand of service tax of over Rs. 2.5 crores against them under proviso to section 73(1). Against said order, the instant appeal was filed wherein it was submitted that, on the terms and conditions of the agreement entered into between the appellants and a time-sharer, the latter received a right to stay in the former’s holiday resorts and avail of various facilities, amenities and advantages for the prescribed period. It could enjoy the benefit under a ‘Certificate of Membership’ issued by the company known as Trump Certificate. It was contended that as the Trump Certificate was freely transferable for a determinate value by a member to any other person at any stage, it qualified to be ‘goods’ within the meaning of this word defined under the Sale of Goods Act. An alternate argument was that the Trump Certificate should be regarded as a deed of conveyance of a right to reside in immovable property; that a major part of the amounts paid by the certificate-holder to the appellants was in the nature of rental for such right to reside in the resort; that such amount was not exigible to levy of service tax prior to 1-7-2007; and that, for the period of dispute, the appellants were not liable to pay any service tax in respect of the aforesaid amount. The appellants also pleaded limitation against the impugned demand. It was submitted that the taxable service in question was introduced only with effect from 16-6-2005 and, therefore, the appellants could not be held to have suppressed any fact material to that service before the department prior to that said date; it was, accordingly, argued that the extended period of limitation was not invocable in the instant case.

The Tribunal held that what had been referred to by the appellants as a saleable product appeared to be a ‘Certificate of Membership’, which signified the so-called time-sharer having been admitted to ‘membership’ for a specified period to enjoy a specified number of ‘Trump Units’ in the holiday resort. This document was issued upon an application for ‘membership’ having been filed by the person concerned. Expressions such as ‘number’, ‘membership’, ‘associate member’, etc., were seen oft-repeated in these records. Prima facie, it appeared that it could not be gainsaid that the time-sharers were members of the body into which they were admitted as members. The statutory definition would rule out the common parlance meaning of ‘club’ or ‘association’. What the statute lays down is the law. Prima facie, each holiday resort run by the appellants answered the definition of ‘club’ or ‘association’ given under section 65(25a) ibid. In this view of the matter, the appellants could not be said to have made out a prima facie case against the impugned demand of service tax on merits. In the same view of the matter, the plea of ‘goods’ and the alternate plea of ‘immovable property’ would not be sustainable.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

But the question is whether the accounting entries affect the allowability of expenditures? For example, if we do not make any entry in the accounts, whether the expenditure can be claimed under the Act? Generally, the accounting entries are relevant but not conclusive. Except where there is specific provision under the Act (for example in case of bad debts), the allowability is dependent on the provisions of law and accounting entries are not relevant. So, even if there are no accounting entries in the accounts then also the assessee can claim the expenditure if otherwise allowable under the Act.

3.3 In which year expenditure is allowable - If one comes to know that a particular expenditure is allowable, then the next thing is in which year it is allowable? Because if not claimed in right year, then that will not be allowable in the other year. It simply means, that whether the deduction can be claimed in the year different from the year of accrual? For example, as per agreement you have to pay rent for three years at the time of agreement, so the accrual is at that time. But the question is whether the total amount is allowable in one year or has to be allowed in three different years, though in other two years there will be not any accrual. Simply it means, whether the matching principle is applicable or not?

3.4 How to claim - The next point is how the deduction can be claimed? What is the method of making claim for deductions? It means whether the deduction can be claimed in the return of income only or it can be claimed during assessment or appeal, etc.? For example, if you come to know of a liability relating to the year at the time of its assessment or appeal, whether you can claim the same at that time even if you have not claimed it in the return? The answer is simply, yes. You can also claim it during assessment in certain cases. Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

[Siemens Financial Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 159 (Bombay)] The assessee was a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) and classified as an Asset Finance Company. In June 2021, it received a Section 148 notice stating that there was reason to believe that income chargeable to tax for AY 2016-2017 had escaped.

Later, the AO referred to the order of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (2022) 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC) and treated Section 148 notice as show cause notice in terms of Section 148A(b). Later, an order was passed under Section 148A(d).

The assessee contended that the Finance Act 2021 amended Section 151, which provides for sanction for the issue of notice. AY 2016-2017, three years elapsed on 31st March 2020; hence, the provisions of amended Section 151(i) and 151(ii) would have to be fulfilled, which have not been complied with. The matter reached before the Bombay High Court.

The Bombay High Court held that the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of certain provisions) Act, 2020 [TOLA] provided for a relaxation of certain provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Where any time limit for completion or compliance of an action, such as completion of any proceedings or passing of any order or issuance of any notice, fell between the period 20th March 2020, to 31st December 2020, the time limit for completion of such action stood extended to 31st March 2021.

Thus, TOLA only seeks to extend the limitation period and does not affect the scope of Section 151. AO cannot rely on the provisions of TOLA and the notifications issued thereunder as Finance Act, 2021, amended Section 151, and the provisions of the amended section would have to be complied with by AO, w.e.f., 01st April 2021.

Hence, the AO cannot take the shelter of TOLA as subordinate legislation cannot override any statute enacted by the Parliament. Further, the notification extending the dates from 31st March 2021 to 30th June 2021 cannot apply once the Finance Act 2021 is in existence.

The sanction of the specified authority has to be obtained in accordance with the law existing when the sanction is obtained. Therefore, the sanction must be obtained by applying the amended Section 151(ii). Since the sanction was obtained in Section 151(i), the impugned order and notice were bad in law and should be quashed and set aside.

'Time' and 'Value' are two ends of the same spectrum. Prudentially, a particular sum of money is considered to be more valuable now, than the same sum at a future point in time. This forms the conceptual base of the "Time value of money" and the underlying logic is the earning potential in the interim. Ignorance of the time value of money was a worrisome problem in the erstwhile Indian recovery laws. Revolutionarily, the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) was created with the core objectives of "time-bound resolution" and "value maximization", inter alia, in its long title. Nevertheless, there has been a constant tussle between these two objectives. This article analyzes the tussle by relating to the identically ongoing issue in Reliance Capital's resolution process. Thereafter, the article delves into likewise precedents emphasizing and elaborating on the dual objectives. Ultimately, the authors propose to create a decisive guide for such a dilemma in the form of a Code of Conduct for the Committee of Creditors (CoC).

The Curious Case of Reliance Capital:

Reliance Capital, a Financial Service Provider, was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), after an application for the same by the Reserve Bank of India. By the instance of four rounds of challenge mechanism and as on the date of the last day of auction (i.e., December 21, 2022), Torrent Investments submitted the highest bid of Rs. 8,640 crores, followed by Hinduja Group's offer of Rs.8,150 Crore. Pertinently, the liquidation value of Reliance Capital stood at Rs.12,500 crore as valued by Duff & Phelps and Rs.13,200 crore as valued by RBSA.1

Hinduja submitted a revised offer of Rs.9,500 Crore, including a Rs.8,800 Crore cash component. However, this revised offer was received a day after the conclusion of the auction.2 This revised offer of Hinduja left a chaotic confusion. Reportedly, on January 10, 2023, the committee of creditors took a decision to conduct another round of auction. Against this decision of the creditors, Torrent moved before the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai. The NCLT ruled in favour of the Torrent and remarked that the resolution process cannot be extended indefinitely under the pretext of "value maximization" and termed it as an "illegal mechanism" to circumvent the rules of India's bankruptcy code.3 Aggrieved by the NCLT's order, Hinduja appealed to the National Company Law Tribunal. The hearing in the appeal proceedings has concluded and is awaiting final orders.4

The reason behind the fierce competition to acquire Reliance Capital is the possibility of effortlessly venturing into business domains such as the insurance and financial services market without the hassle of getting new licenses, regulatory permits and other industrial permissions. The chain of events, in the creditors' eyes, is justified for the bidding value was drastically lower than that of the liquidation value. In the resolution applicant's eyes, it boils down to the arbitrary exercise of commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors. By and large, this fight exposes the constant tussle between 'value maximization' and 'time-bound process' under IBC.

A Tug of War:

In the case of Binani Industries Ltd. v. Bank of Baroda5 the NCLAT held that the objective of CIRP is to maximize the value in a time-bound manner for a distressed company's assets and that the resolution plan that maximizes the value should be preferred. Ultra Tech's revised bid provided a greater offer for the rehabilitation of Binani. The NCLAT cautioned that procedures cannot be rigidly applied in all circumstances and the delayed bids should not be rejected on the sole ground that it was filed late when there is a genuine reason for such delay. However, the bids submitted by fresh applicants after deadline should not be considered, even if they provide for a better revival solution. This ensures that the process remains fair and transparent. It was also added that the CoC should act responsibly and in the interest of all creditors. It was stated as follows:

"It is essential to note that the resolution process is not a sale or an auction, as no one is buying or selling the corporate debtor, if it was a sale the person offering the highest price would get the CD, but the object of the code is the resolution of the corporate debtor as a going concern with value maximization in a time-bound manner. Furthermore, it is not a recovery but a resolution process; whereas, a recovery bleeds a corporation to death, a resolution keeps it alive."

The concept of Time value of money essentially says that "money available at the present time is worth more than the identical sum in the future due to its potential earning capacity. This core principle of finance holds that provided money can earn interest, any amount of money is worth more the sooner it is received."5 Allottees/ homebuyers invest in real estate primarily because of two reasons; either they see it as an investment that could benefit them in future; or for residential needs; or both of these reasons. Case study 1: - Issue on application of 80-IA(8)

Facts:

Head office, a company having 3 different units;

Common services of the Group such as administration, HR, accounting are undertaken by the Head Office;

Issues:

Whether common overhead costs needs to be allocated to the qualifying unit?

Whether the actual expenditure can be allocated or whether the expenditure should be allocated based on FMV?

The issue of allocation of common expenses incurred by the head office has been discussed in the cases of Wipro Information Technology Ltd v. Dy. CIT [2004] 88 TTJ (Bang) 778 and Asstt. CIT v. Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. [2007] 14 SOT 18 (Mum.) (URO). The tax payer has argued that the expenditure which is directly attributable to the earning of profits of qualifying undertaking should only be considered for the purpose of computing tax holiday benefits. However, this argument was not accepted by the Tribunals. The Tribunal stated that non allocation of common costs may lead to inflation of profits of tax holiday units and reduction of income chargeable to tax of the head office which defeats the basic principle of taxation.

This issue is debatable. Unlike the international transaction covered by section 92(1) read with section 92B, the SDT provisions are not so broad based. Section 80-IA(8) of the Act provides as follows:

"Where any goods or services held for the purposes of the eligible business are transferred to any other business carried on by the assessee, or where any goods or services held for the purposes of any other business carried on by the assessee are transferred to the eligible business and, in either case, the consideration, if any, for such transfer as recorded in the accounts of the eligible business does not correspond to the market value of such goods or services as on the date of the transfer, then, for the purposes of the deduction under this section, the profits and gains of such eligible business shall be computed as if the transfer, in either case, had been made at the market value of such goods or services as on that date"

As seen from the above, section 80-IA(8) is applicable to a transaction relating to 'transfer of goods or services held for the purposes of' qualifying unit to or from any other 'business' carried on by the taxpayer for which a 'consideration' is charged by the transferor unit and paid by the recipient unit. Hence, it can be argued that section 80-IA(8) intends to cover services of 'marketable' nature. This view also finds support from the CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 which has explained the object of amendment of s. 80-IA(8) by FA 2001 to include reference to 'services' which reads as follows :-

"Under sub-section (8) of section 80-IA, where any goods are transferred for a consideration to any other business of the assessee, the consideration should correspond to the market value of such goods. As in certain cases, the transfer may relate to services, the provision has been accordingly amended to clarify that this would include services. Such services may include marketable services of operation and maintenance (O&M) in case of infrastructure facilities, marketable services for distribution of electricity and specified marketable services in telecom. Instead of the words "industrial undertaking" occurring in section 80IA, the word "undertaking" has also been substituted in the provision for the same reason."

In view of the above, though it can be argued that section 80A(6)/section 80-IA(8) is not be applicable to allocation of general Head Office expenses which may not be considered as marketable services, the issue may not be free from ligation.

The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

2. Accounting standards are crystallised accounting principles to meet different contingencies for recognition of income. Accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India are presently statutorily mandatory for companies under the company law. Even for others, they are bound to be observed in audit. They constitute Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). Even where they are not mandatory, there is no reason, why such principles embodied in the standards, should not have application in computation of taxable income. The Courts have had occasions to refer to accounting standards.

In the case of a chit company even in absence of any accounting standards specifically for such companies, the assessee, who spreadover the chit commission during the duration of chit on percentage of completion basis, relied upon Accounting Standard 22 for the spread over principle recognised both in Madras Industrial Investment Corpn.’s case (supra) and J.K. Industries v. Union of India [2008] 297 ITR 176 (SC). The Supreme Court in CIT v. Bilahari Investments (P.) Ltd. [2008] 298 ITR 1 / 68 Taxman 95 (SC) pointed out that accounting standards are of recent origin and that it is open to the department to consider these new accounting standards and concepts in future cases of chit transactions ‘without expressing any opinion in this regard’, but upholding assessee’s method with reference to method of accounting regularly adopted by the assessee. The Supreme Court did not decide the issue on merits as adoption of either method made little difference in the facts of the case. In J.K. Industries’ case (supra), the Supreme Court observed in the context of accounting for deferred tax, that accounting standards provide for discipline and harmonisation of concepts and accounting principles consistent with the objective of true and fair accounting.

Ascertainment of cost after deduction of commission paid for purchase, understood to be justified by Accounting Standard 2, was endorsed by the High Court in CIT v. George Oakes Ltd. [2008] 303 ITR 357 (Mad.). The Gujarat High Court in Amichand Investment (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (Asst.) [2008] 304 ITR 97 in the context of an issue relating to accounting of dividends for book profits tax found that the accounting treatment in Accounting Standard 13, could not be relied upon by revenue, since the assessment related to the year earlier to the effective date from which it became mandatory. There are a number of decisions of the Tribunal also, where accounting standards are relied upon by either party, whether assessee or revenue for their respective stand. Accounting standards 1 and 2 prescribed under section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 are not materially different from International Accounting Standards or those issued by the Institute.

On these facts, the issue for the consideration of the NCLT was whether the buyers advancing the money came within the category of financial creditors entitled to invoke IBC for the recovery of the sums advanced. The Petitioner's case before the NCLT was that it was clear that under the garb of allotting land to the public, the respondent had been borrowing/accepting deposits/loans from the public by showing it as investment against property, i.e., by showing the depositors to register for plots of specific measurements and also showing the projected value of the said investment/deposit/borrowing on the maturity date. S.5(7) defines 'financial creditor' to mean a person to whom a financial debt is owed. Financial debt is defined in s.5(8) to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes, inter alia, any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing [clause (f) of s.5(8).

According to the NCLT, receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot were for/time value of money and have the commercial effect of borrowing and, hence, sub-sections (7) & (8) of s.5 apply and, hence, the petitioner is to be taken as financial creditor. In coming to this view, the NCLT relied on the decision of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLTA) in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL - AT) where the following decision was taken by the NCLTA:-

"….From the provisions of law and discussion as made and quoted above, we find following essential criterias, to be fulfilled for a creditor to come within the meaning of financial creditor:-

(i)

A person to whom a financial debt is owned and includes a person, whom such debt has been legally assigned transferred to;

(ii)

The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and include any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of s.5".

The NCLT thus, pronounced its decision as under:-

"In the present case, the receipt-cum-acceptance letters (Annexure-A-1 to A-4 of the application) on the face of it state that they are for acquisition of plot and registration for plot booked. However, the maturity date of agreement is given as one year after the date of registration and the projected value is given, which is more than the consideration value given. Therefore, the time value of money has been built in and it has to be presumed that the receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot, have the commercial effect of borrowing. In view of sub-ss.(7) & (8) of s.5 of the Code (supra), the petitioners are to be treated as financial creditors".

It may be stated in the context of this decision that in reply, the respondent did not raise any objection that the petitioners before NCLT are not financial creditors. Rather it specifically stated saying that "there is some delay on the corporate debtor's part in returning the amount of the financial creditor [emphasis is provided].

Hence, this decision may not be a binding authority to claim that a homebuyer comes in the category of 'financial creditor'.

9. 'Sachin Tendulkar' entitled to vacancy allowance as he failed to find tenant for vacant flat

[Sachin R. Tendulkar v. DCIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 253 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The Assessee, Mr. Sachin Tendulkar, owned two properties in Pune - Flat S and Flat T. Flat T was let out, however, Flat S was vacant for the whole year as suitable tenant couldn't be found. He claimed that the said flat had remained vacant throughout the year despite his reasonable effort to let out the same. In this regard, he submitted three letters written to the builder. In first letter, he thanked the builder for identifying the tenant for the flat at Flat T and also requested to identify tenant for Flat S. Subsequently, the assessee had written second letter and after that third letter being reminders for identifying the tenant to let out Flat S.

Therefore, he claimed vacancy allowance under Section 23(1)(c) for Flat S and declared nil income. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer made additions for the notional rental income from Flat S, which was also upheld by the CIT(A).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee when same builder had helped the assessee to find tenant for another flat, it couldn't be said that these letters to the same builder to help him identify one more tenant, to be considered as fake, defied logic. Therefore, if a property was held with an intention to let out in the relevant year coupled with efforts made for letting it out, the same would fall within the purview of section 23(1)(c).

10. Sum received on relinquishment of 'right to sue' is non-taxable capital receipt: ITAT

[Bhojison Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 99 taxmann.com 26 (Ahmedabad - Trib.)]

The assessee-company entered into a development agreement by virtue of which a right in land was created in its favour by owner of land. Assessee's case was that despite development agreement entered into by landlord, the landlord had decided to sell said land to other parties. The assessee filed a suit in the Courts of law for specific performance of pre-emptive right to purchase the land. Later on, it received damages from the potential purchaser for relinquishment of 'right to sue' in the Courts of law for breach of development agreement. The assessee claimed that 'right to sue' was a personal right which would not fall within sweep of definition of 'capital asset' under section 2(14). Consequently, damages received from potential purchaser were treated as non-taxable capital receipts.

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

The essence of long list of judicial pronouncements cited by assessee was that section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act which uses the same expression 'property of any kind' in the context of transferability makes an exception in the case of a mere right to sue. The decisions thereunder make it abundantly clear that the 'right to sue' for damages is not an actionable claim. It cannot be assigned. Transfer of such a right is opposed to public policy as it tantamount to gambling in litigation.

Hence, such a 'right to sue' does not constitute a 'capital asset ' which, in turn, has to be 'an interest in property of any kind'. Despite the definition of expression 'capital asset ' in the widest possible terms in Section 2(14), a right to a capital asset must fall within the expression 'property of any kind' subject to certain exclusions.

Notwithstanding widest import assigned to the term 'property' which signifies every possible interest which a person can hold and enjoy, the ' right to sue' was a right in personam and such right could certainly not be transferred. In order to attract the charge of tax on capital gains, the sine qua non is that the receipt must have originated in a 'transfer ' within the meaning of section 45, read with section 2(47) of I-T Act. In the absence of its transferability, damages received by assessee couldn't be assessed as capital gains.

FORMER CHIEF JUSTICE OF THE SUPREME COURT OF INDIA

Ladies and gentlemen,

I have been quoted repeatedly by some of the valuable speakers that judges are not expected to know everything. I had said this in a different context. Unfortunately, today the context is different. There is so much misconception and misinformation in this world. The context was that in India, appeals lie directly from regulatory authorities to the Supreme Court. Regulatory bodies like SEBI – Stock Exchange, Electricity tariffs. Similarly in Telecoms, appeals lie to the Supreme Court. Now, do you expect the Judges to know, when matters come before them, engineering terms, like port charges? Do you expect judges to know accountancy when they have to decide appeals in tariffs matters?. Unless people tell us what are electricity port charges, you don't expect judges to answer or deliver justice. But on the flip side of the matter, I can tell you, is that today at the Indian Supreme Court and today I am going to discuss only about the Indian Supreme Court and the Indian Tax Administration problems that we have. As far as the Supreme Court today is concerned, these types of appeals coming before the Supreme Court is the result of convergence after globalization- convergence of law, economics, science, accountancy and if a judge may not know all the details, we may rightly say – but he must understand some of the concepts and that concept need to be told to him otherwise it would not be possible for him to render justice.

Many of us today have discussed tax abuse and tax avoidance. All these are concepts. But what I have learnt in the past 22 years in the primary function of all constitutions in the world, which is the basic law of the country, is that the rule of interpretation is the most important doctrine and most important law which every judge must understand and must apply. Now let me give you an example: If you are reading the Constitution of India, the words used are double textual like "complete justice" and "common good". These are open textual words and we judges are required to interpret those words in the widest possible terms. But if I have to decide or interpret a charging section under the Income-tax Act, certainly I will go by literary interpretation, particularly if it is the deeming provision. And particularly today in the context of laws like Transfer Pricing provisions, and that of the GAAR I would request each and every lawyer, like each professor who is sitting in this hall today to focus on the language (a) and (b) on the concepts and principles behind those provision. Today the main problem of Transfer Pricing for example or in GAAR is interpretation. An officer in the tax department can interpret in a way which would suit his purpose because he is faced with the target of revenue collection. He may not go in the principle, because he may not go on the rationale behind the provision and this is what is happening today. Unless lawyers, tax professors and tax policy makers concentrate on the language which is used, concentrate on the principles which are to be applied, things will not become clear.

Let me give you an another example: In the past we had to go strictly by form and not substance. But today with the introduction of the provisions of the Income-tax Act we are required to go into value. We are required to go into methodology of arriving at Arm Length Price. Are these not subject to concepts? Economic substance is one of the subjects of transfer pricing. So there is a paradigm shift which goes from form into substance and consequently and this is what I am trying to emphasise. Consequently there is a wide discretion which is coming into the hands of the tax department and that wide discretion needs to be controlled As Lord Bingham has said "all Constitutions in the democratic world proceed under the rule of law" and Lord Bingham has said repeatedly that "law is not discretion". If you want to control discretion, that discretion must be based on manageable data otherwise you have a situation where under Transfer Pricing the demand today runs up to 14 Billion according to the newspapers in India.
