For the assessment year 1984-85, the assessee filed return on 18-12-1987 declaring lottery income. The return was rejected as time-barred and the petition for condonation of delay was also rejected. However, while completing the assessment for the assessment year 1988-89, the Assessing Officer also included the income from lottery because the assessee had received the lottery amount during the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1988-89. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee did not main- tain any books of account and, therefore, the income from the lottery winning would be assessed in the assessment year 1988-89 on receipt basis.

The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the Assessing Officer himself had determined the tax to be deducted at source in respect of the lottery amount as early as in July 1983. From this fact, the Commissioner (Appeals) came to the conclusion that the Assessing Officer had recognized the assessee’s right to receive the amount during a period much earlier than the accounting period relevant for the assessment year 1988-89. The Commissioner (Appeals) considered that the assessee, in accordance with the method of accounting followed by him, accepted the right to receive the lottery amount as an accrual of income and accordingly filed a return of income for the assessment year 1984-85 and, hence, the same amount could not be assessed in a subsequent year.

The definition of gross amount charged was amended with effect from 10-5-2008 in order to provide that in case of transaction between 'associated enterprises', any amount debited or credited in the books of account of the person liable to pay service tax would also be included as 'gross amount charged'. Consequently, an amendment was also made to Rule 6 of the Service Tax Rules, 1994 whereby the Explanation was inserted with effect from 10-5-2008, declaring that in case of transactions between associated enterprises, payment received for taxable service would include any amount debited or credited in the books of account liable to pay service tax. Since on the date of amendment of section 67 and rule 6, such amounts were reflected under outstanding receipts, the appellant is liable to pay service tax on such amount under reverse charge mechanism as per section 66A. in ‘F’ at the same time again, it appeared that those shares were not actually transferred by the assessee in favour of IHCL. The Tribunal in its order also found out that all along the assessee contended that there was no income as capital gains as there was no transfer of the shares. The Tribunal noted that on this argument, no doubt, the assessee succeeded. This finding was not challenged by the department and, hence, the same could be considered to have become final. As regards the taxability of the receipts under the award, both the lower authorities had held that the receipt was connected with parting by the assessee of its intangible rights of possession and enjoyment of the property belonging to ‘F’. It appeared that both the lower authorities pierced the corporate veil and held that even without transfer of shares of ‘F’ to IHCL, its rights in the property was handed over by the shareholders of that company, one of such shareholders being the assessee company. A perusal of the award also supported this contention. Certainly, IHCL received certain benefits by way of transfer of certain rights in the property although the said property did not belong to ‘F’ or even its shareholders in the true legal sense. The payment of as high a sum as Rs. 25 lakhs was on that account alone. The finding of the Commissioner (Appeals) that in the process what was transferred was the goodwill of the business which was being run by the company ‘F’, could not be accepted. There was no doubt about the fact that ‘F’ was running a hotel on that property. IHCL, on acquisition of the property, however did not continue to run on that business. On the other hand, it dismantled that entire structure and built up a very big five star hotel under different name and style on the property. It was, therefore, clear that what IHCL did actually acquire was not the goodwill of the earlier hotel, but merely the uniteruppted right of possession and enjoyment of the property, coupled with the withdrawal by the assessee and its associate their rights to repossess the property at the end of the Director of Estates. The question would arise therefore, as to whether this intangible right of possession and enjoyment of the property had been acquired by the assessee and/its associate by incurring any cost or otherwise. The matter could not be answered simply by looking into the fact that the Assessing Officer in the assessment did not choose to tax the receipt either as business income or even as capital gains. Only by acquiring the shares of ‘F’ the assessee came into the joint possession and enjoyment of the property under consideration. The cost of acquisition of such intangible rights should therefore be equated with the cost of shares of ‘F’. Accordingly, the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and it must be held that inasmuch as the assessee had acquired the intangible rights which were ultimately parted with by it in favour of the IHCL, by purchasing the shares of ‘F’, capital gains tax would surely arise, the cost of acquisition of the capital asset being referable to the cost of the shares of ‘F’ in the hands of the assessee.

As regards the question of year of taxability of the capital gains, it could not be said that it was the award which ultimately led to the transfer of the capital asset under consideration. The award merely confirmed and vindicated the standpoint of the assessee and its associates about having intangible rights in the property. Such rights were however transferred in terms of the memorandum of agreement dated 13-3-1975. The facts of the case also showed that almost immediately after arriving at this memorandum, the assessee and its associates handed over the possession of the property in favour of IHCL, which started developing the same into a full- fledged five star hotel. Therefore, the transfer of the intangible rights belonging to the assessee did take place in assessment year 1976-77 and not in the assessment year 1980-81. Ultimately, therefore, the order of the Commissioner (Appeals) in deleting the capital gains from the assessment of the assessee for the assessment year 1980-81 was to be upheld on this ground alone.

The Commissioner (Appeals) practically accepted these estimates, but by making only certain marginal adjustments in expenses, fixed the cost at Rs. 63.74 lakhs. Further he approved the spread over of the additions to be made in three assessment years. However, he reduced the estimated cost of lift, medical equipments and furniture and fittings by Rs. 97,000, Rs. 30,000 and Rs. 1,20,000 respectively.

There are two other limitations upon this power, viz., that this reopening of the completed proceedings can be done, even for the aforesaid limited purpose, only with the concurrence of the assessee and secondly that this power cannot extend to a period beyond eight years from the end of the assessment year to which such proceeding relates. These two features make it abundantly clear that the section contemplates reopening of the completed proceedings not for the benefit of the assessee but in the interests of the Revenue. The exercise of the discretion by the Assessing Officer is required to be preceded by the formation of an opinion by the Assessing Officer of the necessity or expediency of making such a reference. However, the Court noted that provision does not make apparent the nature of such opinion. Is this a prima facie opinion or a considered opinion after examining all available materials? Court answered it thus: "A reading of section 92C and 92CA does not indicate that the Assessing Officer is required to form a prior considered opinion after considering all the available materials, even before making a reference to the TPO". The court noted that section 92CA (1) is in contrast with section 55A of the Act where the Assessing Officer is empowered to refer to the Valuation Officer (VO) the question of ascertaining the Fair Market Value (FMV) of a capital asset. The wording of section 55A is unambiguous that the Assessing Officer has to first form an opinion that the value declared is less than the FMV, before he can refer the question to the VO. If he does not, then the reference itself is bad. The question, in regard to section 92CA before the court: ‘Is reference to the TPO by the Assessing Officer to be made by the Assessing Officer only after he is satisfied by going through the steps enlisted in section 92C (1) to (3) that the price declared by the assessee is not to be accepted or can he make such a reference at an anterior stage? ’ The Court held that : "There is nothing in section 92CA itself that requires the Assessing Officer to first form a considered opinion in the manner indicated in section 92C(3) before he can make a reference to the TPO. It is not possible to read such a requirement into section 92CA(1). However, it will suffice if the Assessing Officer forms a prima facie opinion that it is necessary and expedient to make such a reference". The court’s reasoning was that the TPO is expected to perform the same exercise as envisaged under section 92C(1) to (3) while determining the ALP under section 92CA(3) by the Assessing Officer. The latter part of section 92CA(3) unambiguously states that the Assessing Officer shall by an order in writing, determine the ALP, in relation to the international transaction in accordance with sub-section (3) of section 92C. It will be pointless to have a duplication of this exercise at two stages one after the other. In the opinion of the court, the scheme of the provision is that after the TPO determines the ALP the matter revives before the Assessing Officer at the section 92C(4) stage where, in terms of section 92CA (4), the Assessing Officer will compute the total income "having regard to" the ALP determined by the TPO.

FACT: ■

The assessee-company was involved in the business of running a hotel. A search and seizure operation under section 132 was carried out at the hotel premises of the assessee.

■

The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee-company had shown certain amount spent on construction of hotel building in different years, whereas the value of the building was more. Accordingly, he referred the matter to the Departmental Valuation Officer (DVO) for calculating the investments made by the company in the hotel building and the DVO gave the report.

■

Thereafter, the Assessing Officer had made additions under section 69C on account of the difference in the value of investment on construction of hotel building shown by the assessee in the books of account as compared to the value of investment estimated by the DVO as unexplained investment.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the additions so made by the Assessing Officer.

■

On the assessee’s appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

The assessee was a private limited company, engaged in the business of running a Tourist Hotel. It filed its return of income admitting total income at Rs. 70.11 lakhs.

On scrutiny assessment, the Assessing Officer disallowed the claim of depreciation on the cost of windmill because the windmill had not been acquired during the relevant previous year.

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) allowed the appeal of the assessee and directed the Assessing Officer to delete the addition made on account of disallowance of depreciation.

On further appeal, the Tribunal confirmed the decision of the Commissioner (Appeals).

On appeal to the High Court:

■

The assessee-company was engaged in the business of developing resort and marketing of time share vacation credits in their own resorts.

■

During assessment, the Assessing Officer noted that the assessee had made addition under the head, 'Land & premises' and claimed depreciation on the same. He was of the view that the assessee had not acquired any building premises during the year and entire addition under the head 'office premises' was nothing but purchase of time share weeks which had been capitalised by treating the same as addition to fixed asset.

■

Accordingly, the Assessing Officer held that such transaction was hit by provisions of section 2(22)(e) and made addition on account of deemed dividend.

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) deleted the addition under section 2(22)(e) made by the Assessing Officer.

■

issued by the financial creditor to the corporate debtor and promoters, demanding the payment of amount due under the consent award. No payments having been made by the corporate debtor, an application under section 7 was filed by the financial creditors. [Para 19]

The instant Tribunal noticed the relevant clauses of share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement and consent terms, The issue was as to whether the amount invested by the financial creditors can be said to be 'financial debt' or not. [Para 22] The Supreme Court has emphasized the Judgment of Pioneer Urban Land and Infrastructure Ltd. v. Union of India [2019] 108 taxmann.com 747/155 SCL 622, that in the various categories under (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of section 5, the Legislature has only given instances, which could be included in the term 'financial debt'. However, the list is not exhaustive but inclusive. One may first consider as to whether the investment made by the financial creditors have commercial effect of borrowing or not. One would have noticed that raising of amount by the company through share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement was a commercial borrowing, since the said transaction has direct effect with the business, which was carried out by the corporate debtor, i.e. construction of building and township. The supplementary share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 12-7-2008, where the agreement clearly noted that 'the Company now requires further funding to the extent of Rs. 50 in order to carry out objectives of the Business Plan, i.e. approval of township, and actual execution of the township as per the designs prepared by the Company architects'. Thus, the raising of the amount through the said agreement has the commercial effect of borrowing, which is clearly demonstrated by the statements contained in the supplementary agreement. The use of expression 'further funding' indicates that transaction has commercial effect of borrowing. Now the question remains to be considered is as to whether the investment by the financial creditors can be said to be an investment by disbursal against consideration of time value of money. The expression 'time value of money' encompasses in itself the concept of time value of the disbursement. One would have already noticed the various clauses of amended and restated share subscription-cum-shareholders agreement dated 14-5-2008 and would have extracted the relevant clauses, where company and promoters were obliged to purchase all the shares held by the non-defaulting shareholders at a price that provides the non-defaulting shareholders at an internal rate of return of 15 per cent per annum compounded annually or the Fair Market Value, whichever is higher. Clauses 19.1(a) and 19.6(a) as extracted, contains clear indication that investment was with an eye to earn profits and the investment was for consideration for the time value of money. Binding term sheet, which one would have also noticed above also contains several clauses, which indicate that proposals were given by the promoters to develop the project and provide an exit to the investors and the exit consideration was carrying IRR of 17 per cent. [Para 30]

It is further relevant to notice that section 7 application filed by the financial creditor was not based only on the consent award passed by the arbitrator on 19-1-2021, but all previous transactions were also basis of the application. The application filed under section 7 cannot be said to be an application for execution of consent decree, rather section 7 application was filed on account of default committed by the company in not honouring its obligation under different agreements. [Para 31]

Certain judgments, have been relied by the appellant in support of his submission that in the application filed under section 7, there was no 'financial debt' and the application deserved to be rejected. The appellant has relied on judgment of the Supreme Court in Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. v. K.P. Jayaram [2020] 118 taxmann.com 560/[2021] 163 SCL 210 (SC). The case of Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), arose out of an application under section 7, which was admitted by the Adjudicating Authority. However, appeal against the same was allowed and the application filed under section 7 stood rejected as barred by limitation. In the Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra), the respondent had requested the company to convert a sum of Rs. 90 lakhs from out of the said outstanding loan as share application money for issuance of shares in the name of the respondent No. 2. [Para 32]

Section 5  of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual of - Assessment years 2004-05 and 2005-06 - Assessee-company was doing business in fields of hotel industries, resorts, clubs, etc. - It offered card facilities to its members, which included savings and discounts on purchases made by card members plus club facilities - It also offered holiday scheme to card members by way of advance sale of room nights to them at a discounted/special price - Members were entitled to utilize room nights as per terms of entitlement of scheme at any of hotels/clubs owned by assessee or its subsidiaries and also at other affiliated destinations - Further card members were entitled to surrender room nights in case they did not utilize them and might also opt for surrender value - In lieu of surrender value, members might also opt to buy or utilise products and services of assessee and its group companies - As per system of accounting adopted by assessee advance on sale of room nights was shown as an advance and thereafter income was apportioned based on happening of event of customer availing room nights - Assessing Officer passed assessment order accepting method of assessee - However, Commissioner, while exercising his powers under section 263 set aside assessment order on ground that entire advance received by assessee an account of sale of room night should have been taxed as income during year of receipt - Whether since amount received by assessee from its members on account of advance sale of room nights was a general amount wherein member had option of staying in many alternate properties as well as an option for refund of money with certain compensation called 'surrendered value' as well as an option to utilize/purchase products and services of assessee and its group companies, it could not be said that assessee had right to appropriate amount of advance on receipt, irrespective of rendering of service - Held, yes - Whether therefore, direction of Commissioner to tax entire amount received by assessee on account of advance sale of room nights as income during year was bad in law - Held, yes

Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

Liability of chit funds liable to pay service tax after 1-6-2015

Question - We understand that after enactment of Finance Act, 2015, chit funds are liable to pay service tax. Kindly advise.

Answer - In Delhi Chit Funds Association v. Union of India [2013] 32 taxmann.com 332/39 STT 955 (Delhi), the levy of service tax on chit funds has been held as invalid. It was (in effect) held that it is mere transaction in money and hence outside the definition of 'service' itself.

Departmental SLP against this decision has been dismissed by Supreme Court - Union of India v. Delhi Chit Fund Association [2014] 43 GST 524/42 taxmann.com 52.

In Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2008] 17 STT 491 (AP), the Board circular dated 23-8-2007 extending service tax to business chit funds has been held as invalid and has been squashed. - SLP against the order dismissed by SC - Union of India v. Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds [2015] 49 GST 274/53 taxmann.com 237 (SC).

However, in All Kerala Association of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2013] 40 STT 500/35 taxmann.com 620 (Ker.), validity of service tax on chit funds has been upheld.

Some changes were proposed in Finance Act, 2015 to get over these decisions. However, these changes have not been made effective so far, as explained below.

Proposed changes in definitions - Following definitions are proposed vide section 107 of Finance Act, 2015. However, these definitions have not been notified when other provisions of the Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, the following definitions are not effective.

'Transaction in money' shall not include any activity carried out for consideration by foreman of chit fund Service tax will be payable by foreman of chit fund on services provided by way of conducting a chit. - proposed Explanation 2(ii)(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 [which defines service] inserted by section 107(g) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this explanation is not effective.

Foreman of chit fund shall have the same meaning as is assigned to the term 'foreman' in section 2(j) of the Chit Funds Act - proposed section 65B(23A) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted by section 107(b) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this definition is not effective.

It was clarified that these amendments have been made as intention of law has always been to levy service tax on these activities. However, in view of contrary decisions of various High Courts, specific amendments are made in statutory provisions - para 5.1(ii) of MF(DR) letter DOF No. 334/5/2015-TRU dated 28-2-2015.

Interestingly, these amendments, though passed, have not been made effective when other provisions were made effective from 1-6-2015. Reason for this is not clear.

Conclusion - Since these changes, proposed in Finance Act, 2015 have not been notified and not made effective, in my view, the decisions of Delhi High Court and Andhra Pradesh High Court are valid and no service tax should be payable on chit funds.

On that basis, in assessment year 2018-19, the limitation period of 15 years in respect of the said assessment years, it cannot be said, has come to an end.

In this connection, a reference may be made to the following decisions:

(i)

RELIANCE JUTE AND INDUSTRIES LTD. v. CIT [1979] 2 Taxman 417 (SC)

"It is a cardinal principle of the tax law that the law to be applied is that in force in the assessment year unless otherwise provided expressly or by necessary implication - CIT v. Isthmian Steamship Lines [1951] 20 ITR 572 and Karimtharuvi Tea Estate Ltd. v. State of Kerala [1966] 60 ITR 262. On that principle, it is abundantly clear that when an assessment for the assessment year 1960-61 is to be made and section 24(2) is invoked, it is section 24(2) as in force in that assessment year which has to be applied. That is the provision as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. There is no question of the assessee possessing any vested right under the law as it stood before the amendment. The assessment for one assessment year cannot, in the absence of a contrary provision, be affected by the law in force in another assessment year. A right claimed by an assessee under the law in force in a particular assessment year is ordinarily available only in relation to a proceeding pertaining to that year. Therefore, inasmuch as the provisions of section 24(2), as amended in 1957, govern the assessment for the assessment year 1960-61, the High Court is right in affirming that the unabsorbed loss of Rs. 15,50,189 of the assessment year 1950-51 cannot be carried forward for more than eight years, and consequently cannot be set off against the business income of the assessment year 1960-61." (Emphasis supplied)

Section 65(105)(zzze) - Club or association service - Club membership 4.9 The appellants were running holiday resorts in various parts of the country. They collected amount from individuals/partnership firms/companies who were admitted as ‘time sharers’, otherwise called ‘members’. A part of the gross amount collected by the appellants from the so-called ‘members’ was collected prior to 16-6-2005 and the remainder was collected on/after 16-6-2005. These amounts were determined on a pro rata basis out of large amounts which were collected by the appellants from the members on long-term basis. The service recipients had a variety of schemes provided by the appellants. Some of them could avail of the facilities in the resorts for a short period, say, 5 years, some others could avail of the same for a longer period, say, 25 years, and so on. The resort could be used, in this manner, even up to 99 years. The appellants collected various amounts from these time-sharers depending on the length of the time period. The gross amount for the purposes of levy of service tax was determined on pro rata basis for the relevant period (16-6-2005 to 30-9-2006). The authorities below taking view that the appellants were covered under the category of ‘club or association service’ under section 65(25a) confirmed demand of service tax of over Rs. 2.5 crores against them under proviso to section 73(1). Against said order, the instant appeal was filed wherein it was submitted that, on the terms and conditions of the agreement entered into between the appellants and a time-sharer, the latter received a right to stay in the former’s holiday resorts and avail of various facilities, amenities and advantages for the prescribed period. It could enjoy the benefit under a ‘Certificate of Membership’ issued by the company known as Trump Certificate. It was contended that as the Trump Certificate was freely transferable for a determinate value by a member to any other person at any stage, it qualified to be ‘goods’ within the meaning of this word defined under the Sale of Goods Act. An alternate argument was that the Trump Certificate should be regarded as a deed of conveyance of a right to reside in immovable property; that a major part of the amounts paid by the certificate-holder to the appellants was in the nature of rental for such right to reside in the resort; that such amount was not exigible to levy of service tax prior to 1-7-2007; and that, for the period of dispute, the appellants were not liable to pay any service tax in respect of the aforesaid amount. The appellants also pleaded limitation against the impugned demand. It was submitted that the taxable service in question was introduced only with effect from 16-6-2005 and, therefore, the appellants could not be held to have suppressed any fact material to that service before the department prior to that said date; it was, accordingly, argued that the extended period of limitation was not invocable in the instant case.

The Tribunal held that what had been referred to by the appellants as a saleable product appeared to be a ‘Certificate of Membership’, which signified the so-called time-sharer having been admitted to ‘membership’ for a specified period to enjoy a specified number of ‘Trump Units’ in the holiday resort. This document was issued upon an application for ‘membership’ having been filed by the person concerned. Expressions such as ‘number’, ‘membership’, ‘associate member’, etc., were seen oft-repeated in these records. Prima facie, it appeared that it could not be gainsaid that the time-sharers were members of the body into which they were admitted as members. The statutory definition would rule out the common parlance meaning of ‘club’ or ‘association’. What the statute lays down is the law. Prima facie, each holiday resort run by the appellants answered the definition of ‘club’ or ‘association’ given under section 65(25a) ibid. In this view of the matter, the appellants could not be said to have made out a prima facie case against the impugned demand of service tax on merits. In the same view of the matter, the plea of ‘goods’ and the alternate plea of ‘immovable property’ would not be sustainable.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

CHAPTER 4

CLARIFICATION REGARDING WHAT TYPE OF TRANSACTION/COMPONENTS CAN COME UNDER THE UMBRELLA OF "FINANCIAL DEBT"?

The interest was not charged at the time of the original assessment because there was no taxable income at the time of original assessment. Had there been a taxable income at the time of original assessment, the assessees would not have challenged the levy. In other words, in terms of the Supreme Court decision in the case of Central Provinces Manganese Ore Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1986] 160 ITR 961/ 27 Taxman 275 the jurisdictional fact attracting the levy was not disputed. As per the decision of the Supreme Court in Modi Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1995] 216 ITR 759/ 82 Taxman 377 it is true that regular assessment would mean only the first/original assessment and interest would be levied only up to the date of such assessment. But the Supreme Court has further held that interest so levied will be increased or reduced on account of the variations in income brought about by orders passed as a result of various proceedings that may take place subsequent to the original assessment. The orders mentioned therein include the one passed under section 155. Thus, once when order under section 155 was passed to include the share income in the partner’s income, clause (b ) of section 139(8) would be pressed into operation, provided the jurisdictional fact of levy was not denied. Simultaneously, interest shall be levied only up to the date of the original assessment and not up to the date of the order made under section 155. Therefore, the levy of interest under section 139(8) and under section 215 should be calculated up to the date of original assessment in the case of the assessee.

Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) (supra): The NCLAT in the present case elaborately dealt with the question as to who is an FC and consequently upheld the decision of the AA on the said point which provides that the FC is a person to whom a financial debt is owed. The tribunal while understanding financial debt stated that as per the definition given under section 5(8), the financial debt has to have a disbursement which was against the consideration for the time value of money. It further went on to elaborate the phrase "time value of money" and referred to the Black's Law Dictionary which provides that it is the "price which is associated with the length of time that an investor has to wait until an investment matures or related income is earned". Hence, the investment and outcome are separated by time and the compensation for such time is the time value of money.

Time Value of Money Includes Interest

1.

Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 549 of 2020, dated 19-1-2021]: The Appellate Tribunal was faced with the question of whether the inter-corporate loan which was given to the CD by the FC which was to be repaid in 90 days with 15% interest will come under the definition of financial debt or not. The NCLAT admits the contention of the FC who stated that even if an inter-corporate deposit was to be repaid within a certain period with interest then such transaction will fall within the definition of financial debt. The Appellate Tribunal further went on to say that the interest component in the present transaction is the time value of money. Hence, the decision was given in favour of the FC.

2.

Monica Ramesh Shah v. Al Fara'A Properties (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 1047 of 2019]: The question before the Appellant Tribunal was that whether the allottee who had purchased an existing flat or agreed to purchase a flat in an existing building will come under the definition of FC or not. The NCLAT relied upon the judgment of AA which stated that neither there was any evidence to prove that premise purchased was against the time value of money nor the agreement constitutes of any interest component. Hence, there was no financial debt in the present matter. The Tribunal further held that at the most, the default will create a debt that can be recovered but not the financial debt and thus, the petition was dismissed.

3.

Divyansh Pratham Infracon (P.) Ltd. v. Dwarika Infocom (P.) Ltd. [2019] 110 taxmann.com 381 (NCLT-New Delhi): The AA in the above-mentioned case observed that the debt will not be termed as financial debt as there was no agreement which evidences the fact that there was the consideration of interest against time value of money.

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required.

Section 32(2) pursuant to the amendment in Finance Act, 1996 curtailed the benefit of carry forward of unabsorbed depreciation loss to a period of 8 years and brought the said provision at par with the unabsorbed business losses. This provision was in force till assessment year 2001-02. Again the Finance Act, 2001 with effect from assessment year 2002-03 amended section 32(2) and restored back to the original version of the section as it stood prior to amendment by Finance Act, 1996, allowing the benefit of carry forward of losses to an infinite period and treating the same different from that of unabsorbed business losses. The explanatory memorandum to Finance Act, 2001 clearly spells out the intention of the legislature to provide the benefit of brought forward unabsorbed depreciation to be allowed to be eternally carried forward for an infinite period irrespective of the years to which it pertains. Though it is stated that the proposed amendment will take effect from 1-4-2002, going by the intention behind the amendment to this section vide Finance Act, 2001 restoring back to the same old provisions as it was then existing prior to 1-4-1997, it could only be logical to conclude that the legislature in its wisdom thought it fit not to disturb any of the unabsorbed depreciation losses to be made available for set off for an infinite period. In other words, the same has to be understood as the legislature only intended that any unabsorbed depreciation available to an assessee as on 1-4-2002 will be dealt with in accordance with the provisions of section 32(2) as amended by Finance Act, 2001 and not by the provisions of section 32(2) as it stood before the said amendment.

No specific provision has been incorporated by the Finance Act, 2001 in section 32(2) restricting the allowability of carry forward of unabsorbed depreciation loss upto assessment year 1996-97 as available to be set off only for a period of 8 years. Hence the purposive and harmonious interpretation has to be taken keeping in view the intention of the amendment of section 32(2) by Finance Act 2001. While construing taxing statutes, rule of strict interpretation has to be applied, giving fair and reasonable construction to the language of the section without leaning to the side of the assessee or the revenue. But if the legislature fails to express clearly and the assessee becomes entitled for a benefit within the ambit of the section by the clear words used in the section, the benefit accruing to the assessee cannot be denied. [Para 7]

Act, 1922, as it stood before its amendment with effect from April 1,1957, the assessee had acquired a vested right to have the unabsorbed loss carried forward from year to year until it was completely set off, and the subsequent amendment limiting the period for carrying forward the loss to eight years could not divest the assessee of the vested right which has thus accrued to him. It was pointed out that the amendment effected in 1957 is not retrospective in operation.

The Supreme Court rejected the plea of the assessee and held, as follows :

"The assessee claims a vested right under sec. 24(2)(iii), as it stood before its amendment in 1957, to have the unabsorbed loss of 1950-51 carried forward from year to year until the loss is completely absorbed. The claim is based on a misconception of the fundamental basis underlying every income-tax assessment. It is a cardinal principle of the tax law that the law to be applied is that in force in the assessment year unless otherwise provided expressly or by necessary implication: CIT v Isthmian Steamship lines [1951] 20 ITR 572 (SC) and Karimtharuvi Tea Estate Ltd. v. State of Kerala [1966] 60 ITR 262 (SC). On that principle, it is abundantly clear that when an assessment for the assessment year 1960-61 is to be made and section 24(2) is invoked, it is section 24(2) as in force in that assessment year which has to be applied. That is the provision as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, there is no question of the assessee possessing any vested right under the law as it stood before the amendment. The assessment for one assessment year cannot, in the absence of a contrary provision, be affected by the law in force in another assessment year. A right claimed by an assessee under the law in force in a particular assessment year is ordinarily available only in relation to a proceeding pertaining to that year. Therefore, inasmuch as the provisions of section 24(2), as amended in 1957, govern the assessment for the assessment year 1960-61, the High Court is right in affirming that the unabsorbed loss of Rs. 15,50,189 of the assessment year 1950-51 cannot be carried forward for more than eight years, and consequently, cannot be set off against the business income of the assessment year 1960-61."

But the Income-tax Act does not provide for all expenditures which are allowable or not. So, if the Act does not provide for any expenses, then the accounting treatment plays a very important role. It is true that accounting practice does not override provisions of the Act, but it is also true that they have wide implication regarding allowability of expenses. Many court cases also provide that if accounting practice is recognized and it does not violate the provisions of the Act, then that will be valid for allowability. 3.2 Relevance of accounting for allowability of expenditure - The next question is, how far accounting is relevant for claiming expenditure under the Act? Income under the head ‘Business and profession’ is calculated as per method of accounting generally followed as per section 145. Also the assessee has to maintain accounts and records as per section 44AA. So, the assessee has to make the accounting entries in books maintained under section 44AA as per method of accounting followed under section 145. But the question is whether the accounting entries affect the allowability of expenditures? For example, if we do not make any entry in the accounts, whether the expenditure can be claimed under the Act? Generally, the accounting entries are relevant but not conclusive. Except where there is specific provision under the Act (for example in case of bad debts), the allowability is dependent on the provisions of law and accounting entries are not relevant. So, even if there are no accounting entries in the accounts then also the assessee can claim the expenditure if otherwise allowable under the Act.

3.3 In which year expenditure is allowable - If one comes to know that a particular expenditure is allowable, then the next thing is in which year it is allowable? Because if not claimed in right year, then that will not be allowable in the other year. Though generally the income is calculated as per method of accounting, yet there are special provisions which override this general proposition just as section 43B, etc. Then also there are certain circumstances in which it is very difficult to know the time of accrual as in the case of disputes or contingencies. So, it is very important to know the accrual of liability, so that it can be claimed in that year only. The next question is when the deduction can be claimed? It simply means, that whether the deduction can be claimed in the year different from the year of accrual? For example, as per agreement you have to pay rent for three years at the time of agreement, so the accrual is at that time. But the question is whether the total amount is allowable in one year or has to be allowed in three different years, though in other two years there will be not any accrual. Simply it means, whether the matching principle is applicable or not?

3.4 How to claim - The next point is how the deduction can be claimed? What is the method of making claim for deductions? It means whether the deduction can be claimed in the return of income only or it can be claimed during assessment or appeal, etc.? For example, if you come to know of a liability relating to the year at the time of its assessment or appeal, whether you can claim the same at that time even if you have not claimed it in the return? The answer is simply, yes. You can also claim it during assessment in certain cases. Due to ignorance of this fact, the assessee does not claim the same and in other years it is not allowed by the Assessing Officer. So, the assessee loses the claim for ever.

3.5 Allowable amount - Every other aspect that has found place in tax literature and standard books, may be a little or more, but one aspect which has hardly got attention is the amount of allowance. If you ask any Chief Finance Officer of any Company the time value of money, then you come to know that amount of allowance is a very important aspect, always ignored under the Income-tax Act. Let’s have some examples:—

If you have purchased your stock-in-trade for Rs. 50,000/- and the amount is payable:

u At the time of delivery

u In five equal instalments of Rs. 10000/- P.A.

u At the end of 5 years Rs. 50000/ only.

Though the total amount allowable in all these cases will be Rs. 50,000 only, yet the effective amount in all these three cases will be different. Let us see the present value of this amount in all the three cases :

Approx. Present value @ 8%

u At the time of delivery50,000.00

u In five equal instalments of Rs. 10,000/ P.A. 39,900.00

u At the end of 5 years Rs. 50,000/- only.34,000.00

So, the effective amount in present time is different, but for allowability the amount is the same. So this can be used for the purpose of manipulation also. Simple purpose of my discussion is that if there is time difference between payment and allowability, then there should be provision to take cognizance of time factor also in allowability. This proposition is also supported by the following provisions and case law.

As per provisions of section 55(2)(b )(ii), the indexing has to be allowed if transferred capital asset became property of the assessee or of the previous owner before the first day of April, 1981. In the instant case, it was an admitted position that construction of flat was completed in about 1988 as per valuation report submitted by the assessee. The most important point was that building was not even in existence as on 1-4-1981 because admittedly, construction of the building was completed in about 1988 and, hence, till construction of the building was completed and possession was handed over to the previous owner, i.e., the HUF, what was held by HUF, was the right to obtain title and possession of the flat and it could not be said that the flat itself became property of the HUF prior to that date and, hence, the Commissioner (Appeals) was not justified in holding that the assessee was entitled to adopt market value of the flat as on 1-4- 1981. For the purpose of section 255(2)(b)(ii ), the capital asset, i.e., flat in the instant case, should have become the property of the previous owner before 1-4-1981 to make the assessee entitled to this benefit, i.e., adopting market value as on 1-4-1981, but since in instant case, the flat was not even in existence till 1988, the assessee could not be given this benefit. Till 1988, the previous owner, i.e., HUF was not owner of the flat but was owner of right to get possession and title of the flat. In view of the above, the assessee could not be given benefit to adopt market value of the flat as on 1-4-1981 and order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and that of the Assessing Officer was to be restored to that extent. Regarding indexation, cost inflation index for the first year in which the asset was held by the assessee had to be considered. In the instant case, there was no dispute that the asset in question, i.e., flat was held by the assessee only from the financial year 1991-92, i.e., when the partition of the HUF took place. As per provisions of section 2(42A ), read with Explanation 1(i)(b ), the period for which the asset was held by the previous owner has to be added to decide as to whether the asset was short-term capital asset or long-term capital asset and since, admittedly, construction of the house was completed in 1988, the asset was a long-term capital asset in view of the Explanation to section 2(42A), but in view of the specific provisions of Explanation (iii) to section 48, indexing had to be allowed from financial year 1991-92, i.e., the year from which flat was held by the assessees on partition of the HUF and, hence, on that issue also, order of the Commissioner (Appeals) was to be reversed and that of the Assessing Officer was to be restored. On conjoint reading of section 153(3)(ii ) of the Act and section 199 of the Act, as well as the relevant case laws, it becomes clear that the bar of limitation automatically stands lifted if there is an order of the Court and in consequence thereof, AO makes assessment, reassessment or recomputation of the assessee. It further becomes clear that as per section 199, the assessee can only claim a tax credit from the tax deducted at source in case he offers his income for assessment. In the instant case, the assessee for the assessment years 1987-88 to 1991-92, had not offered his income for assessment but had claimed credit from the tax deducted at source which meant that in the light of the aforesaid provisions, the assessee was not entitled to claim the same. [Para 8.5]

From the provisions of section 153(3)(ii ), it appears that the bar of limitation automatically stands lifted if there is an order of the Court, but contrary to the same, the assessee had not given any contention as regards any provision of law under which beyond a period of 10 years, he was not liable to show any tax payable by him nor he was able to show that it was not within the purview of the Act to consider the credit for the tax deducted at source by the Assessing Officer beyond a period of ten years. [Para 8.6]

From the ratio of the decision rendered by the Apex Court in the case of K. S. Krishna Rao v. CIT [1990] 181 ITR 408/[1991] 54 Taxman 339 , it was clear that interest on enhanced compensation received by the assessee, of course, could not be taxed in lumpsum but the same had to be charged by spreading the same on an annual basis, which meant that even the abovesaid decision (supra) did not create bar of limitation for levying tax of the interest received by the assessee only for a period of ten years and not beyond that. [Para 8.8]

Hence, the plea taken by the assessee that neither he was liable to show tax payable beyond a period of ten years nor the same could be deduced by the ITO beyond a period of ten years, had no merit and, accordingly the same was rejected. [Para 8.9]

The applicant financial creditor provided unsecured loan to the respondent company. The respondent-company failed to repay loan amount. A similar issue had arisen before the Supreme Court in Reliance Jute & Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 921 (SC) in case of unabsorbed losses.

In 1957 there was an amendment to section 24(2)(iii)of the 1922 Act (corresponding to section 72). The assessee, in this case contended that by virtue of section 24(2)(iii) of the Indian I.T. Act, 1922, as it stood before its amendment with effect from April 1,1957, the assessee had acquired a vested right to have the unabsorbed loss carried forward from year to year until it was completely set off, and the subsequent amendment limiting the period for carrying forward the loss to eight years could not divest the assessee of the vested right which has thus accrued to him. It was pointed out that the amendment effected in 1957 is not retrospective in operation.

The Supreme Court rejected the plea of the assessee and held, as follows :

"The assessee claims a vested right under sec. 24(2)(iii), as it stood before its amendment in 1957, to have the unabsorbed loss of 1950-51 carried forward from year to year until the loss is completely absorbed. The claim is based on a misconception of the fundamental basis underlying every income-tax assessment. It is a cardinal principle of the tax law that the law to be applied is that in force in the assessment year unless otherwise provided expressly or by necessary implication: CIT v Isthmian Steamship lines [1951] 20 ITR 572 (SC) and Karimtharuvi Tea Estate Ltd. v. State of Kerala [1966] 60 ITR 262 (SC). On that principle, it is abundantly clear that when an assessment for the assessment year 1960-61 is to be made and section 24(2) is invoked, it is section 24(2) as in force in that assessment year which has to be applied. That is the provision as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957, there is no question of the assessee possessing any vested right under the law as it stood before the amendment. The assessment for one assessment year cannot, in the absence of a contrary provision, be affected by the law in force in another assessment year. A right claimed by an assessee under the law in force in a particular assessment year is ordinarily available only in relation to a proceeding pertaining to that year. Therefore, inasmuch as the provisions of section 24(2), as amended in 1957, govern the assessment for the assessment year 1960-61, the High Court is right in affirming that the unabsorbed loss of Rs. 15,50,189 of the assessment year 1950-51 cannot be carried forward for more than eight years, and consequently, cannot be set off against the business income of the assessment year 1960-61."

The Supreme Court has held that interest on enhanced compensation cannot be taxed all in a lump sum as having accrued on the date on which the Court passes the order for enhanced compensation : the interest has to be spread over on an annual basis right from the date of delivery of possession till the date of the order of the Court on a time basis . Obviously, the intention in using the expression 'spread over on an annual basis' in the judgment emphasises that the income becomes taxable in the relevant year. The said intention cannot be stretched to an extent to hold that the assessee is under an obligation to show the component of income relevant for the assessment year under consideration as income having accrued 'pending the judgment' and thereby fastening a liability on the assessee to comply with the provisions of sections 208 to 210 and also charge interest under sections 234B and 234C for such stipulated failure to pay advance tax. It was obvious that the assessee could not have foreseen the amount of enhanced compensation as also the interest awardable in relation thereto during the years under consideration at the time of filing returns, which were ultimately processed under section 143(1). Thus, there was no failure on the part of the assessee so as to attract the provisions of sections 234B and 234C.

In Madras Industrial Development Corpn. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802 / 91 Taxman 340 the liability of the company with reference to the debentures existed for a span of 12 years. It was in the light of the subsistence of the corresponding liability for the 12 year period that the Supreme Court had held that the discount paid for selling those debentures had to be divided proportionately for the entire span of 12 years and the per year deduction should be on that pro rata basis. It was on the basis of the principle of ‘matching liability’ that the Supreme Court had held in that case that the assessee was entitled to claim a pro rata deduction of the discount element suffered by the company in issuing the debentures. The above ratio declared by the Supreme Court would not help the case of the assessee here. By exercising the option to receive the interest in lumpsum at a discounted rate, the assessee had foregone its right to receive the interest for the remaining two years. The assessee had no right at all for any interest for the remaining two years. When no such right to receive the interest existed for those two years, correspondingly there was no question of interest accruing or being received for those two years. Here, it was not a case of ‘interest received in advance’. It was a case of interest received at discounted rate. The right of the assessee to receive the interest for the future years was liquidated. Therefore, it was not possible for the assessee to divide the interest in three parts and offer only one part for assessment in the first year.

Hence, the Assessing Officer’s action was to be upheld, and the revenue’s appeal to be allowed.

HEADNOTE: Section 5 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Income - Accrual of - Assessment years 1998-99 to 2002-03 - Whether where assessee was engaged in business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts, entire amount of timeshare membership fee receivable by it at time of enrolment of member was not income chargeable to tax in initial year on account of contractual obligation that was fastened to receipt i.e., to provide services in future over term of contract - Held, yes

FACT: The assessee-company was in the business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts. During relevant assessment years, the assessee collected revenue from timeshare members but same was not recognised as revenue for the current year. The explanation of the assessee was that it had considered only 40 per cent of the membership fees collected as income and the balance 60 per cent was treated as deferred income. It was stated that the balance amount was to be spread over the next 33 years during which the assessee was expected to provide timeshare facilities to the members. It was also stated that in order to provide various facilities during the next 33 years, it had to incur many costs. Further explanation of the assessee was that the AMC was exclusively meant to cover the maintenance of various facilities which were an integral part of the timeshare property. These charges were for the maintenance of various electronic gadgets made available in the accommodation, furniture, kitchen equipments, central air-conditioning etc. On the other hand, the consideration for future obligations received in the initial stages was towards transfer facility from one resort to another, split, accumulation and advancing facility, domestic and international exchange, transmission, upgradation etc. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and, hence, income had to be accounted for on accrual basis. He was of the view that the receipt was undisputedly income as the assessee itself had shown it as deferred income. However, the Act does not recognise the concept of deferred income and, hence, the assessee’s explanation could not be accepted. Considering all these aspects, the Assessing Officer added certain amount being 60 per cent of the receipts shown by the assessee as advance subscription. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee had to construct holiday resorts and provide timeshare facilities over a period of time. Further, the annual subscription fee collected met only the maintenance of the resorts. The utility charges collected ‘were as per actual consumption of things like electricity, water etc. It did not cover major renovation and repairs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also took note of the fact that over a period of 24 years, the assessee had to incur about 171 per cent of the original investment for major renovation and replacement of assets. Accordingly, he upheld the contentions of the assessee and deleted the addition in all the years.

Section 43(1) of the Act defines actual cost. The definition does not specify the criteria as to what expenditures should be included in actual cost (i.e. components of actual cost). The definition merely specifies that portion of actual cost met by any other person or authority must be excluded from 'actual cost'. There are 15 existing Explanations in section 43(1) which specify how actual cost is to be worked out in various situations as per the Table below: 7.6A-1 New proviso inserted by Finance Act, 2017 to exclude from actual cost any expenditure involving cash payment above the threshold of Rs. 10,000

In order to discourage cash transactions even for capital expenditure, the Finance Act, 2017 has amended the provisions of section 43(1) of the Act by inserting a new proviso. The new proviso provides that where an assessee incurs any expenditure for acquisition of any asset in respect which a payment or aggregate of payments made to a person in a day, otherwise than by an account payee cheque drawn on a bank or account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account, exceeds ten thousand rupees, such expenditure shall be ignored for the purposes of determination of actual cost of such asset.

These amendments will take effect from 1st April, 2018 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2018-19 and subsequent years.

7.6A-2 New proviso inserted in Explanation 13 to section 43(1) as regards situation where deduction allowed u/s 35AD is deemed income

Clause (1) of section 43 defines "actual cost" for the purposes of claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Act in certain situations. However, there is no clarity on determination of actual cost for the purposes of allowance of depreciation of such assets in respect of which the deduction which is already allowed in a pre-vious year under section 35AD of the Act, is withdrawn in terms of sub-section (7B) of the said section.

In light of the recommendations of Income-tax simplification committee and to bring clarity, provisions of the section 43 of the Act have been amended to provide that where any capital asset in respect of which deduction allowed under section 35AD is deemed to be the income of the assessee in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (7B) of the said section, the actual cost to the assessee shall be the actual cost to the assessee, as reduced by an amount equal to the amount of depreciation calculated at the rate in force that would have been allowable had the asset been used for the purposes of business since the date of its acquisition.

This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2018 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2018-19 and subsequent years.

7.6A-3 In case of conflict between ICDS-V (new) and section 43(1), section 43(1) shall prevail

ICDS-V (new) requires inclusion of all expenditure that meets the criteria in Para 5 of ICDS-V (new). This is irrespective of mode of payment of expenditure involved. However, the new proviso in section 43(1) (See Para 7.6A-1 above) provides for exclusion from actual cost of cash expenditure above threshold of Rs. 10000. The new proviso to section 43(1) shall prevail over Para 5 of ICDS-V (New) and the expenditure involving cash payment above Rs. 10000 shall be excluded from actual cost even if it meets the criteria of Para 5 of ICDS-V (New)

"Tangible fixed asset" is an asset being land, building, machinery, plant or furniture held with the intention of being used for the purpose of producing or providing goods or services and is not held for sale in the normal course of business. [Para 2(1)(a) of ICDS-V (New)]

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

On the revenues appeal to the Tribunal :

HELD: There is a distinction between "receive of property being the shares of the amalgamating companies" and "underlying assets and transfer of said assets to the amalgamated company. For the purpose of attracting the rigours of section 56(2)(viia), the crucial date is the date of receive of any property being the shares of the amalgamated companies. The Assessing Officer was not certain about the year of chargeability i.e., whether it is to be charged on the year of receipt of property or it is to be charged in the year of the transfer of property pursuant to the scheme of amalgamation. [Para 20]

The year of chargeability would be the year in which the assessee received the properties i.e., the assessment year under consideration and therefore, the Assessing Officer had rightly charged the income under section 56(2)(viia). [Para 20.1]

In this regard, the above said principle is not universally applicable and is required to be applied with caution and on case to case basis. In the instant case, the Assessing Officer was wrongly harboring the view that the additions were required to be made on substantive basis in the year of transfer i.e., assessment year, 2012-13. Admittedly no proceedings were pending at the time of passing of assessment order dated 31-12-2016, therefore it is not possible to make the addition on substantive basis for Assessment year 2012-13. If the same is held then the Bench would be asking the Assessing Officer to do the impossible. Further, there is a time limit provided under the Act for the completion of assessment under section 143(3) for assessment year 2014-15 and the assessment proceedings for assessment year 2014-15, on the basis of protective addition, cannot be put in abeyance till the additions are made on substantive basis for assessment year 2012-13. In view of the above, the contention of the assessee that the substantive addition should precede the protective addition could not be accepted. [Para 21]

Further, though the assessee had made the plea on the submission that section 148 proceedings initiated against the assessee for assessment year 2012-13 had been dropped, which were initiated on substantive basis, but the said contention was not dealt by the CIT(A) while passing the impugned order. [Para 21.1]

It is clear that the assessee did not exist in the assessment year 2012-13. Therefore, no addition can be made in the hands of a non-est entity i.e., assessee for the assessment year 2012-13 as it was not in existence in that assessment year. Moreover if the contention of the assessee is accepted that the substantive additions were dropped for the assessment year 2012-13, then the protective addition made in the assessment year 2014-15 are required to be converted into substantive addition. [Para 21.2]
