Merely because some other High Courts have taken a different view, it is not correct to say that the issue, which has been subjected to rectification, is a debatable one in so far as that particular State is concerned. It is permissible for the income-tax authorities to resort to the provisions of section 154 for bringing a matter in consonance with the judicial pronouncements of the High Court of the State where such authorities are working. However, in the instant case, the unabsorbed depreciation was held to be eligible for being carried forward in the hands of the assessee in the assessment orders for the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78. It was, therefore, clear that the error existed in the assessment orders passed by the ITO for the assessment year 1975- 76 on 18-1-1977 and for the assessment year 1977-78 on 19-11-1989. The said error or mistake apparent from record could be rectified by passing appropriate orders under section 154 for the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78, provided such rectification orders had been passed within the time-limit of four years prescribed under section 154(7). Once a right had been extinguished under the provisions of law and once a matter had become barred by limitation of time, it could not be revived by such an indirect route of passing an order under section 154 for a subsequent year, namely, the assessment year 1980-81. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in holding that the proceedings of rectification pertaining to the assessment years 1975-76 and 1977-78, which had already became barred by limitation of time, could not be revived by allowing the ITO to pass an order under section 154 for the assessment year 1980-81.

As regards the interest under section 215, the provisions of section 215(3) as it existed prior to its amendment with effect from 1-4-1985 did not provide for any enhancement or increase in the amount of interest charged under section 215 where the amount payable increased as a result of an order of rectification or an order on appeal or revision, etc. The provisions providing for consequent increase or enhancement in the amount of interest charged under section 215 had for the first time been introduced by the Taxation Laws (Amendment) Act, 1984 with effect from 1-4-1985. The very fact that the aforesaid amendment has not been made with any retrospective effect clearly showed that prior to the assessment year 1985-86, interest charged under section 215 could not be increased where as a result of an order under section 154 or 147 or 250 or 254, etc., such amount had been increased. Therefore, the Commissioner (Appeals) was justified in directing the ITO to remit the interest charged under section 215.

In the case of Sushil Ansal v. CIT [1986] 160 ITR 308 (Delhi), jurisdictional High Court held that the execution of an agreement of sale coupled with the handing over of possession was not sufficient to confer on the assessee the right of ownership in the flats. The High Court further held that rentals from a flat in a multistoreyed building were assessable under the head ‘Income from other sources’.

Admittedly, in the instant case, the flat had never been conveyed in favour of the assessee by the builder by execution of a conveyance deed registrable under the provisions of the Indian Registration Act, 1908. Thus, the assessee had an imperfect title to the property. Therefore, capitalisation of the rental was not an objective method for the valuation of the flat. The orders of the lower authorities were, therfore, set aside and the matter was sent back to the WTO with the direction that the valuation of the flat be made afresh in accordance with law and in tune with the decision in case of Sushil Ansal (supra) as well as the decision of the Supreme Court in the case of Nawab Sir Mir Osman Ali Khan v. CWT [1986] 162 ITR 888, since what was assessable as an asset in the hands of the assessee was his right to enjoyment and rentals minus legal ownership.

Executive Summary

In Asstt. CIT (International Taxation) v. Shelf Drilling Ron Tappmeyer Ltd. [2025] 177 taxmann.com 262 (SC), decision dated 8 August 2025, the Supreme Court of India (SC) delivered a split verdict in a batch of appeals concerning the interplay between Section 144C and Section 153 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 (IT Act). The dispute centered on whether the time consumed

carried forward and adjusted against the total income of the assessee up to 8 assessment years from the immediately succeeding previ-ous year of the year in which the ship or aircraft was acquired or the plant was installed, as the case may be. Further, sub-section (6) of section 32A deals with the situation of carry forward and adjustment of the unabsorbed investment allowance of the amalgamating company in case of amalgamation. [Paras 15 and 16] On going through the provisions of sections 72A and 32A, it is evident that section 72A deals with carry forward and set-off of accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation allowance in case of amalgamation. According to this section, accumulated business loss and unabsorbed depreciation allowance of the amalgamating company shall be deemed to be the loss, or as the case may be, of the amalgamated company for the previous year in which amalgamation was affected and other provisions of this Act relating to set-off of any carry forward of loss allowance for depreciation shall apply accordingly. Hence, the amalgamated company would get the original period for its carry forward and set-off. But in case of investment allowance, the unabsorbed/balance of investment allowance of the amalgamating company shall be deemed to be the unabsorbed investment allowance of the amalgamated company and it shall be entitled to claim its carry forward and adjustment against the total income subject to fulfilment of other conditions for the remaining period of 8 years. In any case, the total period of its carry forward would not exceed the period of 8 years specified in sub-section (3) of section 32A. Therefore, if the amalgamating company has availed the benefit of carry forward of three assessment years, the amalgamated company can claim the carry forward only up to 5 years and not full 8 years, as in the case of carry forward of accumulated loss and unabsorbed depreciation. In the instant case, nowhere either under the rehabilitation-cum-amalgamation scheme sanctioned by the BIFR or the BIFR order, it had been mentioned that investment allowance shall be carried forward up to the full period of 8 years, contrary to the provisions of section 32A(6). Therefore, there was no force in the argument of the assessee that it had been specifically specified in the BIFR order or the scheme that amalgamated company would be entitled to carry forward of the unabsorbed investment allowance up to 8 years. Therefore, the amalgamated company would only be entitled to the carry forward of unabsorbed investment subject to fulfilment of other conditions upto the remaining period of eight years. [Para 18]

Therefore, the revenue’s stand was correct and the assessee was not entitled to set-off of unabsorbed investment allowance for the impugned assessment year as it fell beyond the period of 8 years. [Para 19]

The cheque discounting charges are different from interest payments and are not attracted by the provisions of section 201(1A).

Even if the same is to be considered as interest, the case is not attracted by the provisions of section 201(1A). Two dates are crucial for arriving at the amount of interest chargeable under section 201(1A), that is, the date of deduction of tax and the date of actual payment of such tax to the credit of the Government. In the instant case, the date on which such tax was actually paid was not available for the Assessing Officer to work out interest. In such circumstances, machinery section failed in the instant case. The Assessing Officer was not right in substituting ‘the date of assessment order’ in place of ‘the date on which such tax was actually paid’ for computing the impugned interest as it is not permissible to read into a taxing provision any words which are not there or exclude any which are there. The words found in the provisions must be given their natural meaning. [Para 5]

Further, the Assessing Officer could not charge interest under section 201(1A) in stages, i.e., one up to the date of the assessment order and the other from the date of assessment order to the date of actual payment of tax. In all, the application of section 201(1A) in the instant case, was impracticable inasmuch as one of the components required for the computation of interest, namely, ‘the date of payment of tax to the Government’ was not available on record. Therefore, no interest under section 201(1A) could be charged not only in respect of cheque discounting cheques, but also in case of TVK. [Para 6]

As regards interest credited to TVK, a concern, and interest credited to interest payable account in the previous years relevant to the assessment years 1986-87 and 1987-88, even though the interest was credited to the interest payable account, the assessee was liable to deduct tax the moment the same was credited to such account. The fact that the assessee had paid the amount into treasury on 27-2-1990 could drive to the inference that the assessee had impliedly accepted the theory that even though the interest was credited to interest payable account, he was liable to deduct tax at source as per section 194(A). Hence, the Assessing Officer was to be directed to levy interest under section 201(1A) for the assessment years 1986-87 and 1987-88, respectively, on the amounts of tax deposited on 27-2-1990 from the date of credit to the interest payable account till 27-2-1990, the date of payment of tax deducted at source into the bank. [Para 8]

In the result, the appeal for the assessment year 1985-86 was to be dismissed and the appeals for the assessment years 1986-87 and 1987-88 were to be partly allowed. [Para 9]

7.3 Liberalisation in capital gains taxation arising from transfer of immovable property (Section 50C)

Section 50C(1), prior to its amendment by Finance Act, 2018, provided, inter alia, that if a person transfers land or building or both for a consideration where the stamp duty value of the property exceeds the declared consideration, then, the stamp duty value of the property shall be deemed to be the consideration for the purpose of computation of capital gains under section 48. 12.4 Change in the time limit to pass the order by the Transfer Pricing Officer [Section 166 of ITA 2025 (corresponding to section 92CA of ITA 1961)]

12.4-1 Position under the ITA 1961

Section 92CA of the ITA 1961 deals with the case where the assessee has entered into an international transaction or specified domestic transaction in any previous year, and the AO may refer the computation of the Arm's Length Price (ALP) in relation to the said international transaction or specified domestic transaction under section 92C to the Transfer Pricing Officer (TPO).

Sub-section (3A) to section 92CA states that TPO is required to pass an order before sixty days prior to the date on which the period of limitation under section 153, or as the case may be, in section 153B for making the order of assessment, reassessment or recomputation or fresh assessment, as the case may be, expires.

12.4-1a Exclusion of the last day of assessment limitation - The interpretation of the phrase 'before sixty days prior to the date' has been a consistent point of contention between taxpayers and the revenue, leading to significant litigation.

The Madras High Court, in the case of Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), which affirmed the Single Judge's decision in Jt. CIT v. Pfizer Healthcare India (P.) Ltd. [2021] 124 taxmann.com 536 (Madras), held that the word 'date' in section 92CA(3A) refers to the last date for the AO to pass the assessment order under section 153 (e.g., December 31st). The crucial words 'prior to' indicate that, for the purpose of calculating the 60 days, this last date must be excluded. Therefore, if the assessment limitation expires on December 31st, the TPO order ought to have been passed on or before October 31st.

This interpretation was consistently followed across numerous ITAT benches, including in the following cases:

Teleperformance Global Services (P.) Ltd. [2023] 155 taxmann.com 658 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Zydus Lifesciences Ltd. [2024] 163 taxmann.com 349 (Ahmedabad-Trib.)

Frost & Sullivan (India) (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 739 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Shell India Markets (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 366 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Siemens Technology and Services (P.) Ltd. [2024] 162 taxmann.com 357 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Huhtamaki India Ltd. [2024] 164 taxmann.com 194 (Mumbai-Trib.)

Atos India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 152 taxmann.com 217 (Mumbai-Trib.)

CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore-Trib.)

Pioneer India Electronics (P.) Ltd. [2025] 178 taxmann.com 553 (Delhi-Trib.)

Sigma Aldrich Chemicals (P.) Ltd. [2022] 141 taxmann.com 431 (Bangalore-Trib.)

12.4-1b Mandatory nature of the time limit - Another critical aspect clarified by the judiciary is whether the time limit prescribed in section 92CA(3A) is mandatory or merely directory. The revenue often argued that the use of the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) implies a directory nature.

However, the Madras High Court in Dy. CIT v. Saint Gobain India (P.) Ltd. [2022] 137 taxmann.com 215 (Madras), after a detailed analysis of the scheme of the Act and the consequences of non-compliance, unequivocally held that the word 'may' in section 92CA(3A) has to be construed as 'shall' and the time period fixed therein has to be scrupulously followed.'

The court reasoned that the overall scheme of transfer pricing assessments, with various interlinked time limits (including extensions under the proviso to section 92CA(3A) and section 153), indicates a legislative intent to ensure timely completion. If the TPO's time limit were merely directory, it would undermine the entire assessment process. This principle has been reiterated in the case of Asstt. CIT v. CAE India (P.) Ltd. [2023] 153 taxmann.com 691 (Bangalore - Trib.).

The provisions are explained in the table given below: 4.2-1 Constitutional validity - The aforesaid amendment seeks to tax income which might have never been received. Hence doubts have arisen as to the constitutional validity of the amendment.

In K.P. Varghese v. ITO [1981] 131 ITR 597, the Supreme Court had to interpret section 52(2) of the Act which provided that if in the opinion of the AO, the fair market value of a capital asset transferred by an assessee exceeds the consideration declared by the assessee by at least 15% of the consideration so declared, then such fair market value shall be deemed to be the full value of the consideration for such capital asset. Thus, section 52(2), on literal interpretation permitted substitution of the declared consideration by fair market value. The Supreme Court did not accept the literal interpretation on various grounds based on the language, the context, the Finance Minister's speech, etc., and also on certain general principles of law.

The Supreme Court observed as follows:

"section 52 is not a charging section but is a computation section. It has to be read along with section 48 which provides the mode of computation and under which the starting point of computation is "the full value of the consideration received or accruing". What in fact never accrued or was never received cannot be computed as capital gains under section 48. Therefore, sub-section (2) cannot be considered as bringing within the computation of capital gains an amount which, by no stretch of imagination, can be said to have accrued to the assessee or been received by him".

". . . .It is a well settled rule of interpretation that the Court should as far as possible avoid that construction which attributes irrationality to the Legislature. Besides, under entry 82 in List I of the Seventh Schedule to the Constitution, which deals with "Taxes on income other than agricultural income" and under which the Income-tax Act, 1961, has been enacted, Parliament cannot "choose to tax as income an item which in no rational sense can be regarded as a citizen's income or even receipt. Sub-section (2) would, therefore, on the construction of the revenue, go outside the legislative power of Parliament and it would not be possible to justify it even as an incidental or ancillary provision or a provision intended to prevent evasion of tax".

". . . .Sub-section (2) would also be violative of the fundamental right of the assessee under article 19(1)(f) - which fundamental right was in existence at the time when sub-section (2) came to be enacted - since on the construction canvassed on behalf of the revenue, the effect of sub-section (2) would be to penalize the assessee for transferring his capital asset for a consideration lesser by 15% or more than the fair market value and that would constitute unreasonable restriction on the fundamental right of the assessee to dispose of his capital asset at the price of his choice".

". . . .Sub-section (2) has no application in the case of an honest and bona fide transaction where the consideration received by the assessee has been correctly declared or disclosed by him and there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration".

All the aforesaid arguments are applicable in relation to section 50C :

(a)

It attempts to tax what may have never accrued or received.

(b)

It goes outside the legislative power of the Parliament since such fair value cannot in a rational manner be regarded as income/receipt.

(c)

It would hit a bona fide transaction, where there is no concealment or suppression of the consideration.

Having regard to the above it appears that there are strong arguments against the constitutional validity of section 50C.

Further, different stamp duty statutes have different basis or valuation. To illustrate, in Andhra Pradesh, the stamp duty is payable on the market value of the property. In Punjab, the stamp duty is payable on the value or amount of consideration (Article 23). In Delhi, it is payable on the consideration amount set forth in the instrument (Article 23). In Maharashtra, it is payable on the 'true market value' of the property (Article 25). Thus, the section puts different entities in different States in different position vis-a-vis section 50C.

It may be noted that the section refers to stamp duty valuation by a State Government and is silent about a property in a Union Territory.

The sum of Rs.37 lakhs retained under section 132 exceed the amount required to meet the liability under section 132B(1)(i) and the department is, therefore, liable to make payment of interest at the rate applicable from the date of expiry of 120 days under section 132(4) to the date of regular assessment/re-assessment or last such assessment or re-assessment, as the case may be. [Para 14]

Although section 132B(5) has been deleted by the Finance Act No. 2 of 2002 with effect from 1-6-2002 and on the same date section 132B(4) has been introduced. The principal of law as laid down in the case of Chironjilal Sharma (HUF) v. Union of India [2014] 360 ITR 237/222 Taxman 352/41 taxmann.com 274 (SC) is not diluted in any manner because of the said amendment. Therefore, the assessee is entitled to interest at the rates applicable on the sum of Rs. 37 lakhs for the pre-assessment period in accordance with section 132B(4)(b) at the rates applicable from time to time after expiry of 120 days from the date of the seizure till the date of the assessment. [Para 14]

So far as the prayer for interest under section 243/244A is concerned, two division benches of this Court in the case of Vijay Prakash Agrawal v. CIT (Central) [2013] 355 ITR 114 and in the case of Prayag Udyog (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2012] 348 ITR 217/[2013] 33 taxmann.com 599 (All.) have laid down that the assessee would be entitled to interest at the rates which were applicable from time to time on the amount due from the date of block assessment till the date of actual payment which aspect of the matter has been ignored by the authorities while making payment of interest at the flat rate of .5 per cent per month to the assessee. In view of the above, the assessee is held entitled to interest at the rates applicable from time to time under section 243A on this sum of Rs. 37 lakhs from the date the money became refundable till the date of actual refund. [Paras 16, 17]

So far as issue of payment of compensation for the inordinate delay in the payment of interest under section 132(B)(4) and section 244A is concerned, it has to be examined as to whether there has been unexplained inordinate delay in the matter of payment of interest within the statutory period by the department or not. [Para 17]

From the facts it is apparent that the assessee became entitled to payment of interest at least for the pre-assessment period from the date his appeal by the Commissioner was allowed. This payment of interest has been denied to the assessee without any justifiable cause even after expiry of 9 years from the date interest was payable. Similarly, for the post-assessment period, the assessee should have been paid interest on the sum of Rs. 37 lakhs refunded to him on 2-2-2007 from the date of the appellate order till the date money was so returned. It has taken nearly 8 years from the department to make the payment of the interest and that too on wrong conclusion. [Para 19]

The assessee must be compensated for retention of money, i.e., interest due under section 132B(4) and section 244A by the department for long duration, namely, 9 and 8 years. Such payment of compensation has been recognized and accepted in the case of Sandvik Asia Ltd. (supra), as also in the subsequent judgment of the Apex Court in the case of CIT v. Gujarat Flouro Chemicals [2012] 348 ITR 319/210 Taxman 583/24 taxmann.com 338. [Para 20]

The department was legally not justified in retention of the amount of interest which was payable to the assessee both under section 134B(4) as well as under section 243A for the period of nearly 9 and 8 years respectively. The case of the assessee falls within the category of cases where there has been inordinate delay on the part of the department to pay the statutory interest and, therefore, the assessee is entitled to be compensated for such wrongful retention of the money by the department. In the facts of the case the assessee is entitled to be compensated at the same rates, i.e. 9 per cent as was provided for by the Apex Court in the case of Sandvik Asia Ltd. (supra). [Para 21]

It is not in dispute that seized Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, etc., continued to be retained by the Income-tax department even after conclusion of the assessment proceedings in the year 1996 unreasonably for long duration. There is absolutely no explanation from the side of the department as to why these Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, Fixed Deposit Receipts, etc., were retained by the department even after the assessment proceedings had been completed in the year 1996 and as to why the same were not encashed/renewed. [Para 14].

The money invested in the shape of Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, etc., continued to be the money available with the Union of India all along. This money was utilized by the Government for its own purposes, which fact can be inferred as the Vikas Patras, etc. were never encashed. [Para 22]

In the case of Sandvik Asia Ltd. v. CIT [2006] 280 ITR 643/150 Taxman 591, the Apex Court held that where there had been inordinate delay on the part of the revenue in returning the money, which will include statutory interest, revenue must compensate and the same is not payment of interest on interest. [Para 30]

It is not in dispute that because of non-return of Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, Fixed Deposit Receipts, etc., and because of non-extension of the period of their validity by the revenue for all the said period these investments lay in the control of the revenue, although illegally, after assessment proceedings had been finalized. The same should have been returned to the assessee after assessment. This act of the department has resulted in uncalled loss of interest on the aforesaid investment, in the shape of Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, Fixed Deposit receipts, etc. The loss has been caused to the assessee for no fault of his. [Para 32]

The Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, Fixed Deposit Receipts, etc., would have earned interest in normal course of things, if they had been revalidated/encashed as per the option available to the revenue. If the revenue has failed to do so and the money all along continued to remain deposited with the Union of India and available for utilization by the revenue itself, the revenue should pay interest on the aforesaid Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikash Patras, Fixed Deposit Receipts, etc., at par with the interest, which money would have earned, on the face value of the aforesaid documents, under the provisions of the Income-tax Act, had the investments revalidated/renewed been encashed by the department. [Para 33].

In the facts and circumstances of the case, the order of the Assistant Commissioner, insofar as it refuses to make payment of interest under section 132B on the ground that Kishan Vikas Patras, Indira Vikas Patras, Fixed Deposit Receipts, etc., had not been encashed, cannot be legally sustained and is quashed. [Para 34]

Union of India [2014] 360 ITR 237/222 Taxman 352/91 taxmann.com 274 (SC), Sandvik Asia Ltd. (supra) strictly in accordance with the provisions of the Income-tax Act. [Para 35]

There was a significant change in the amended section 7 with effect from 1-4-1989 where in the words ‘if sold in the open market on the valuation date’ were omitted and valuation is to be determined only in the manner laid down in Schedule III. This clearly shows that the rent capitalisation method in the manner laid down in schedule III is to be preferred to that of a value which the property would fetch in the open market. The interpretation of Commissioner (Appeals) in the instant case was apparently based upon rule 8(a) of Schedule III according to which if, in the opinion of Assessing Officer, it is not practicable to apply the provision rule of then the property shall be valued in the manner laid down in rule 20, that is, the value which could be fetched if sold in the open market on the valuation date. The word ‘practicable’ means and specifies that which is feasible or practicable of being put to practice within the available means and resources. In other words, when the Assessing Officer is of the opinion that there is insurmountable difficulty in computing the value as per rent capitalisation method as per rule 3 such situation can be considered as not ‘practicable’ and even under such circumstances, the Assessing Officer has to take the prior approval of Dy. Commissioner so as to apply the procedure under rule 20. Merely because the value as per the agreement of sale is higher than the value worked out under rule 3, the valuation as arrived at under rule 3 cannot be considered as impracticable. In the instant case, nothing had been brought on record to show that the Assessing Officer could not have computed the rental value as per rule 3. In fact Assessing Officer had never applied rule 3 which clearly indicated that there was no insurmountable difficulty in applying rule 3. Under such circumstances, Commissioner (Appeals) was wrong in holding that it was not practicable to apply rule 3 and, therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to adopt the value of property as shown which was in consonance with the procedure prescribed in rule 3.

Section 43(1) defines 'actual cost' as the actual cost of the assets to the assessee. Explanation 8 to section 43(1) was inserted by section 9 of the Finance Act, 1986, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1974. It declares that where any amount is paid or is payable as interest in connection with the acquisition of an asset, so much of such amount as is relatable to any period after such asset is first put to use shall not be included, and shall be deemed never to have been included, in the actual cost of such asset.

Therefore, the amount of interest could not be included in the actual cost for the purpose of depreciation and investment allowance applying Explanation 8 to section 43(1).

Accordingly, the Tribunal was not right in law in holding that the interest payable by the assessee on deferred payment liability for purchases of machinery was liable to be capitalized and entitled to depreciation and investment allowance.

18. Extended time limit provided by TOLA is not applicable for sanction of notice under Section 151: HC

[Siemens Financial Services (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT [2023] 154 taxmann.com 159 (Bombay)] The assessee was a Non-Banking Finance Company (NBFC) and classified as an Asset Finance Company. In June 2021, it received a Section 148 notice stating that there was reason to believe that income chargeable to tax for AY 2016-2017 had escaped.

Later, the AO referred to the order of the Supreme Court in the case of Union of India v. Ashish Agarwal (2022) 138 taxmann.com 64 (SC) and treated Section 148 notice as show cause notice in terms of Section 148A(b). Later, an order was passed under Section 148A(d).

The assessee contended that the Finance Act 2021 amended Section 151, which provides for sanction for the issue of notice. AY 2016-2017, three years elapsed on 31st March 2020; hence, the provisions of amended Section 151(i) and 151(ii) would have to be fulfilled, which have not been complied with. The matter reached before the Bombay High Court.

The Bombay High Court held that the Taxation and Other Laws (Relaxation and Amendment of certain provisions) Act, 2020 [TOLA] provided for a relaxation of certain provisions of the Income-tax Act, 1961. Where any time limit for completion or compliance of an action, such as completion of any proceedings or passing of any order or issuance of any notice, fell between the period 20th March 2020, to 31st December 2020, the time limit for completion of such action stood extended to 31st March 2021.

Thus, TOLA only seeks to extend the limitation period and does not affect the scope of Section 151. AO cannot rely on the provisions of TOLA and the notifications issued thereunder as Finance Act, 2021, amended Section 151, and the provisions of the amended section would have to be complied with by AO, w.e.f., 01st April 2021.

Hence, the AO cannot take the shelter of TOLA as subordinate legislation cannot override any statute enacted by the Parliament. Further, the notification extending the dates from 31st March 2021 to 30th June 2021 cannot apply once the Finance Act 2021 is in existence.

The sanction of the specified authority has to be obtained in accordance with the law existing when the sanction is obtained. Therefore, the sanction must be obtained by applying the amended Section 151(ii). Since the sanction was obtained in Section 151(i), the impugned order and notice were bad in law and should be quashed and set aside.

The issue before the Delhi High Court was:

"Whether Explanations 6 and 7 appended to Section 9(1)(i), which was inserted by the Finance Act 2015 with effect from 01.04.2016, can operate retrospectively?"

The Delhi High Court held that Section 9(1)(i) inter-alia seeks to impose tax albeit via a deeming fiction qua all income accruing or arising, whether directly or indirectly, through or from any property in India or through or from any asset or through transfer of asset situated in India, or the transfer of a capital asset situated in India.

The judgment of the Supreme Court rendered in the case of Vodafone International Holdings BV v. Union of India excluded from the scope and ambit of Section 9(1)(i) gain or income arising from the transfer of shares of a company located outside India. However, the value of the shares was dependent on assets situated in India. To cure this gap in the legislation, Explanations 4 and 5 were introduced by the Finance Act 2012, which was effected from 1-4-1962.

Explanations 4 and 5 presented difficulties in that the expressions' share and interest' and 'substantially' found in the explanations were vague, resulting in undue hardship for transferors where the percentage of share or interest transferred was insignificant. Explanations 6 and 7 alone would have no meaning if they were not read along with Explanation 5. Therefore, if Explanations 6 and 7 have to be read along with Explanation 5, which concededly operates from 1-4-1962, they would have to be construed as clarificatory and curative.

To propose under one head of income and in scrutiny or a reassessment to finalise under another head is perfectly permissible. [Para 9]

The further question is whether there was any possibility of it being recovered. If the recovery had been barred by limitation,necessarily, it has to be treated as an income from the business and the same had to be assessed under the Act. Even if the deviation from the proposal is found to be improper, the assessment has to be sustained, as an income from business; which was the original proposal. If the other company had occupied the premises the amounts would definitely be shown as income from business. [Para 10]

With respect to the contention of limitation having not expired in the relevant previous year, it is to be noticed that the assessment itself was finalised after three years, which was normal period of limitation for recovery of money, even calculated from the date on which the last refund was made. The assessment order itself was passed, after three years from the date of commencement of limitation and there was no claim made by the assessee, who participated in the assessment proceedings, as to any recovery proceedings having been commenced by the other company or a repayment having been effected.

‘Actual cost’ has both a time dimension and a price dimension. Section 43A(1), which governs the price dimension, has this effect, namely, that the incremental cost gets added to the actual cost.

When it is said that actual cost has a time dimension, it means that, conceptually speaking, actual cost is necessarily related to the point of time at which an asset is purchased. When one is dealing with the Act, the time dimension assumes special significance.

Now the incremental cost occasioned by fluctuation in rate of exchange comes into being after depreciation/investment allowance is allowed to the assessee. Consequently, the augmenting of the actual cost by the incremental cost contemplated by section 43A(1) must necessarily relate back to the assessment year in which the allowance was granted to the assessee. Investment allowance is allowed either in the year of the installation or in the first year of user of the plant and machinery. Thus, investment allowance is a one-time allowance. Now, having regard to this special feature the question arises as to how one should go about while giving effect to section 43A(1). Here, section 154 readily suggests itself. But considering the fact that a bar of limitation by time is incorporated into it, that section provides, only to a limited extent, the procedural modalities for adding the incremental cost to the actual cost. Stated differently, that section cannot be invoked to add to the actual cost the incremental cost that arises after the expiry of the limitation period incorporated into that section. Section 155 is silent on the issue.

Again, the granting of investment allowance is, inter alia, subject to the creation by the assessee of investment allowance reserve. The most practical solution would allow the assessee the benefit of investment allowance in respect of the incremental cost in the year in which the incremental cost arises provided, of course, that the assessee created a suitable reserve for this purpose.

Conclusion 10. There is a little doubt with regard to the fact that service tax is value addition tax. This tax is levied on the value added to the property. But in case of immovable property on rent, there is no value being added to the property by either tenant or the landlord. So, there should not be any service tax on renting of the immovable property. If renting of immovable property itself is made subject to the service tax, then the tax which is being collected by the Central Government would be tax on the property. And the tax on the property can be levied only by the State Government according to List II of 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India. So, levying service tax on renting of immovable property falls outside the legislative competence of the Parliament. Based on the above discussion, only one logical conclusion follows that the renting of immovable property per se should not be made taxable.

Disposal of applications for rectification under section 154

9.5 Hitherto, section 154(7) provided that rectification order (order making an amendment) cannot be passed after the expiry of four years from the end of the financial year in which the order sought to be rectified was passed. The said time-limit was uniformly applicable irrespective of whether the rectification order was passed by the Income-tax Authority

(i) on its own motion; or

(ii) on an application by the assessee; or

(iii) in case of the Income-tax Authority being the CIT(A) on an application by the Assessing Officer.

Section 154(8) has been inserted to provide that ‘Without prejudice to the provisions of section 154(7), anything containing in section 154(7), where an application for amendment under this sub-section is made by an assessee on or after 1-6-2001 to an income-tax authority referred to in the said section, the authority shall pass an order within six months from the end of the month in which the application is received by it, either making the amendment or refusing to allow the claim.

However consequences of failure to pass such an order within the said time-limit have not been enacted.

Block assessment

9.6 Hitherto, as per section 158B(a) of the Act relating to assessment in cases of search or requisition, ‘block period’ meant the previous years relevant to ten assessment years preceding the previous year in which the search was conducted under section 132 or requisition was made under section 132A, and included, in the year in which the search was conducted or requisition was made, the period up to the date of commencement of such search or, as the case may be, the date of such requisition.

The definition of ‘block period’ is amended to mean the period comprising the previous years relevant to six assessment years preceding the previous year in which the search was conducted under section 132 or requisition was made under section 132A, and including the period up to the date of commencement of such search, or as the case may be, the date of such requisition, in the year of search or requisition. The reduction to six years (from the earlier ten years) seems to be in line with the amendment brought about in section 149(1) of the Act.

The aforesaid amendment will take effect from 1-6-2001 and will apply in relation to searches initiated or requisitions made on or after that date.

Interest under sections 234A, 234B and 234C

9.7 Under sections 234A and 234B of the Act, interest is levied for defaults in furnishing return of income and in payment of advance tax. There was a dispute as to whether these interests are to be levied on returned income or on assessed income. Recently, in CIT v. Ranchi Club Ltd. [2001] 114 Taxman 414 the Supreme Court held that interest under sections 234A and 234B could be levied only on the tax on returned income and not on the tax on assessed income.

9.7-1 Amended provisions - With a view to nullify the effect of the aforesaid Supreme Court judgment, the Finance Act, 2001 has made retrospective amendments in all these sections with effect from assessment year 1989-90. The amendments made are as follows :

(i) Explanation 4 to section 234A defining the words ‘tax on total income’ for the purposes of section 140A has been deleted.

(ii) Explanation 1 to section 234B defining the words ‘assessed tax’ has been substituted. The amended Explanation runs on the similar lines that of old Explanation except that it has deleted Explanation 1(a).

(iii) Section 140(1A) and 140(1B) have been inserted and it provides for the calculation of interest chargeable under sections 234A and 234B for the purpose of filing the return of income.

The effect of above amendment is that interest under sections 234A and 234B has to be charged on the basis of tax on assessed income and not on the tax on returned income.

To overcome the judicial rulings conflicting with the provisions of ICDSs I, II, III, IV, VI, VII, VIII, IX the Finance Act, 2018 had made various amendments with retrospective effect from Assessment Year 2017-18 as under:

| ICDS | Provisions of ICDS struck down by Delhi HC with reasons i.e. reasons of conflict with judicial precedents | Validating provisions enacted by Finance Act, 2018 to restore legitimacy of struck down provisions of ICDS |
| --- | --- | --- |
| ICDS I | ICDS-I doing away with concept of 'prudence', as the same is contrary to the Act and binding judicial precedents and is therefore unsustainable in law. | Clause (xviii) inserted in section 36(1) of the Act to provide that marked to market loss or other expected loss as computed in the manner provided in ICDSs shall be allowed deduction. |
|  | Clause (13) inserted in section 40A of the Act to provide that no deduction or allowance in respect of marked to market loss or other expected loss shall be allowed except as allowable under newly inserted clause (xviii) of sub-section(1) of section 36. |  |
| ICDS II | ICDS-II pertaining to valuation of inventories and eliminates the distinction between a continuing partnership business after dissolution from one which is discontinued upon dissolution is contrary to the decision of the Supreme Court in Shakti Trading Co. v. CIT [2001] 250 ITR 871 (SC). It fails to acknowledge that the valuation of inventory at market value upon settlement of accounts of the outgoing partner is distinct from valuation of the inventory in the books of the business which is continuing. ICDS-II is held to be ultra vires the Act and struck down as such. | Section 145A of the Act amended to provide that, for the purpose of determining the income chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession, the valuation of inventory shall be made at lower of actual cost or net realizable value computed in the manner provided in the ICDSs. |
| ICDS III | The treatment to retention money under Paragraph 10(a) in ICDS-III will have to be determined on a case to case basis by applying settled principles of accrual of income. By deploying ICDS-III in a manner that seeks to bring to tax the retention money, the receipt of which is uncertain/conditional, at the earliest possible stage, irrespective of the facts, the Respondents would be acting contrary to the settled position in law as explained in the decisions CIT v. Simplex Concrete Piles India (P) Ltd. [1988] 179 ITR 8 (ii) CIT v. P & C Constructions (P.) Ltd. [2009] 318 ITR 113 (iii) Amarshiv Construction (P.) Ltd. v. DCIT [2014] 367 ITR 659 and (iv) DIT v. Ballast Nedam International [2013] 355 ITR 300 which followed the decision in Anup Engineering Limited v. CIT [2000] 247 ITR 114 and to that extent para 10 (a) of ICDS-III would be rendered ultra vires. | Section 43CB inserted in the Act to provide that the contract revenue shall include retention money. |
| ICDS III | Para 12 of ICDS-III read with para 5 of ICDS-IX, dealing with borrowing costs, makes it clear that no incidental income can be reduced from borrowing cost. This is contrary to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Bokaro Steel Limited [1999] 236 ITR 315 and is therefore struck down. | Section 43CB inserted in the Act to provide that contract cost shall not be reduced by incidental interest, dividend and capital gains. |
| ICDS IV | Para 5 of ICDS-IV requires an Assessee to recognize income from export incentive in the year of making of the claim if there is 'reasonable certainty' of its ultimate collection. This is contrary to the decision of the Supreme Court in CIT v. Excel Industries Limited [2015] 358 ITR 295 (SC) and is, therefore, ultra vires the Act and struck down as such. | Section 145B inserted to provide that the claim for escalation of price in a contract or export incentives shall be deemed to be the income of the previous year in which reasonable certainty of its realisation is achieved. |
| ICDS IV | The proportionate completion method as well as the contract completion method have been recognized as valid method of accounting under the mercantile system of accounting by the Supreme Court in CIT v. Bilhari Investment Pvt. Ltd. [2008] 299 ITR 1 (SC). This Court too has done likewise in CIT v. Manish Buildwell Pvt. Ltd. [2011] 245 CTR 397 (Delhi) and Paras Buildtech India Pvt. Ltd. v. CIT [2016] 382 ITR 630 (Delhi). Therefore, to the extent that para 6 of ICDS-IV permits only one of the methods, i.e., proportionate completion method, it is contrary to the above decisions, held to be ultra vires the Act and struck down as such. | Section 43CB inserted in the Act to provide that profits arising from a construction contract or a contract for providing services shall be determined on the basis of percentage of completion method except for certain service contracts, and that the contract revenue shall include retention money, and contract cost shall not be reduced by incidental interest, dividend and capital gains. |

The Assessing Officer invoked the provisions of section 56(2)(vii)(b) and held that the stamp value of the property purchased as on the date of registration of sale deed and the actual purchase consideration was liable to be considered as income under the said section. He, accordingly, made an addition.

The Commissioner (Appeals) affirmed the said addition.

On the assessee's appeal before the Tribunal: HELD: First proviso to section 56(2)(vii)(b) categorically provides that where the date of agreement fixing the amount of consideration for the transfer of immovable property and the date of registration are not the same, the stamp duty value on the date of the agreement maybe taken for the purpose of this provision. Admittedly, the irrevocable Power of Attorney was registered in the year 2008 fixing the price of the property at Rs. 21 lakhs, even though the actual transfer took place in the year 2015. Prescription of the second proviso is admittedly fulfilled in the instant case inasmuch as the assessee paid a sum of Rs. 1 lakh as part payment prior to the date of the agreement in the year 2008 through banking channel. In view of the foregoing discussion, it is to be held that the mandate of the main part of section 56(2)(vii)(b) does not apply to the facts of the instant case as it is covered by the first and second provisos inasmuch as the assessee entered into an agreement fixing the amount of consideration for the purchase of the immovable property in the year 2008 but the actual registration took place in 2015 and, further, the assessee paid a part of the consideration by cheque in the year 2008 before the date of the agreement. In such circumstances, it is the stamp value on the date of agreement in the year 2008, which should be applied for the purpose of the sub-clause and not the stamp value as in the year 2015. Stamp value of the property as on the date of the agreement in 2008 was Rs. 23.75 lakhs. As such stamp value is obviously less than the actual consideration at Rs. 31 lakhs. Thus, it is to be held that the mandate of section 56(2)(vii)(b) is not attracted so as to warrant any addition on this score. Therefore, addition of Rs. 26.07 lakhs is to be deleted. [Para 7]

■ It is found that the Assessing Officer has adopted "look through approach" holding that the transaction is not for "sale of shares" but for "sale of underlying assets", and disregarded the substance of the transaction which is transfer of shares of UEM held by assessee and not the assets of the company without having any evidence or cogent material or information on record. In fact, the Assessing Officer determination of the full value of consideration at Rs. 484.13 crore, which is actually the value of the company in perpetuity on the basis of projected cash flow (not the underlying assets) as in financial year 2020-21, has no basis in law. Therefore, the Assessing Officer has wrongly adopted the total capitalised value of the company for perpetuity of 484.13 crore as in financial year 2020-21 as against value per share worked out for the financial year 2015-16. [Para 41]

■

Further, for determining the full value of sale consideration in cases of transfer of unquoted shares of a company, the Assessing Officer could have invoked the enabling provisions of section 50CA read with rule 11UA for determining the fair market value (FMV) of the shares and substitute the same with the sales consideration adopted by the assessee. Section 50CA provides that where consideration received or accruing as a result of transfer of a capital assets being unquoted shares of a company, is less than the fair market value determined in the manner as prescribed in rule 11 UA, then the value so determined shall, for the purpose of section 48, be deemed to be full value of consideration received or accrued as a result of such transfer. There is however legal difficulties in invoking the deeming fiction of section 50CA in the present proceedings, as the unquoted equity shares of UEM, were transferred in financial year 2015-16 prior to 1-4-2018. The provisions of section 50CA cannot be invoked for period before 1-4-2018 to determine the FMV for taking it as full value of consideration for the computation of capital gains under section 48. It is therefore opined that the full value of consideration received on transfer of shares cannot be substituted either by fair market value or by any other manner, at least in the concerned assessment year 2015-16. On the basis of discussion above, it is therefore held that the Assessing Officer’s invocation of section 50 to consider the 'sale of shares' as 'sale of asset' for calculating short-term capita gain, is invalid and not supported by any legal provisions. Therefore, the Assessing Officer is directed to delete the additions made as short-term capital gain. [Para 42]

There can be no quarrel to the proposition laid by the Supreme Court in the Radha Exports (India) (P.) Ltd. (supra). When shares are duly issued to a third party, on the basis of which amount, filing of an application under section 7 by the respondent was rightly rejected, which was affirmed by the Supreme Court. The Supreme Court has again reiterated that 'financial debt' means debt along with interest, if any disbursed against the consideration for time value of money. The instant is not a case regarding allocation of shares by payment of money on the basis of which money, section 7 application is filed. The transactions, which have come up for consideration contains several clauses which makes it clear that it is not a case of simple allotment of shares against payment of money. The judgment of Supreme Court in Kotak Mahindra Bank Ltd. v. A Balakrishnan [2022] 138 taxmann.com 567/172 SCL 696, where the Supreme Court has clearly held that Legislature could never have intended to keep a debt, which is crystallized in the form of a decree, outside the ambit of section 5, sub-section (8). Section 7 application filed by the financial creditor was admitted by Adjudicating Authority, which was challenged by Raj Singh Gehlot. The appeal was allowed by, thus, Tribunal, on which heavy reliance has been placed by the appellant. It is to be noticed that in the said case, there was arbitral award in favour of the financial creditor. The Tribunal in the Raj Singh Gehlot's judgment (supra), placed reliance on judgment of the Supreme Court in Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. When one looks into the judgment of this Tribunal in the above case, the basis of the judgment of this Tribunal is that section 7 application was filed on the basis of breach of settlement agreement, which is not permissible under section 7. [Para 38]

In Anuj Jain (supra), it was held that there has to be disbursal of fund by the financial creditor. The Tribunal held that award received under Arbitration and Conciliation Act or amount emerged from the settlement agreement will not come within the purview of section 7 application. [Para 40]

The ratio of the judgment Anuj Jain (supra) on the Tribunal, as noted above was that since section 7 application was filed alleging breach of settlement agreement, the application was not maintainable. The basis of judgment is that settlement agreement, which resulted into decree cannot be made basis for section 7 application. The judgment of the Supreme Court in Kotak Mahindra Bank (supra), which clearly says that mere fact that a decree had been obtained by the financial creditor, shall not take him out of section 7 proceedings and if ingredients of 'financial debt' are in existence, section 7 application is maintainable. The Tribunal in Raj Singh Gehlot's case (supra), has noticed the amendment made in the shareholder agreement. As per the judgment of the instant Tribunal, there was no consideration for time value of the debentures. [Para 41]

[Para 13] Every receipt is not an income; only those receipts which partake the character of the income of the current year will only be taxable during the current year, whereas the portion of receipt which is though in the nature of income but not the income of the current year, cannot be brought to tax during the current year. Section 2(45) defines ‘total income’ as ‘the total amount of income referred to in section 5, computed in the manner laid down in this Act. The principal charging section 4 makes the "total income of the previous year" subject to the charge of the income-tax. Thus the assessee’s income, which could be subject to tax, was the income of previous year and not the income which pertained to future 99 years. In the instant case, there was no dispute to the fact that the assessee had to render services to the holder of time share unit in the next 99 years; therefore, there was no reason for taxing the receipt relatable to further 99 years in the year of receipt itself. No material had been brought on record by the department to the effect that the assessee was not required to render any services to the holder of the time share unit in further 99 years. In the above connection, the observations of the Supreme Court in K. P. Varghese (supra) are apposite. But the question then arises why has Parliament introduced the first condition as a prerequisite for the applicability of sub-section (2)? Why has Parliament provided that in order to attract the applicability of sub-section (2), the fair market value of the capital asset as on the date of the transfer should exceed by 15 per cent or more the full of the consideration for the transfer declared by the assessee? The answer is obvious. The object of imposing the condition of difference of 15 per cent or more between the fair market value of the capital asset and the consideration declared in respect of the transfer clearly is to save the assessee from the rigour of sub-section (2) in marginal cases where difference in subjective valuation by different individuals may result in an apparent disparity between the fair market value and the declared consideration. It is a well-known fact borne out by practical experience that the determination of fair market value of a capital asset is generally a matter of estimate based to some extent on guess work and despite the utmost bona fides, the estimate of the fair market value is bound to vary from individual to individual. It is obvious that if the restrictive condition of difference of 15 per cent or more between the fair market value of the capital asset as on the date of the transfer and the consideration declared in respect of the transfer were not provided in sub-section (2), many marginal cases would, having regard to the possibility of difference of opinion in subjective assessment of the fair market value, fall within the mischief of that sub-section and the statutory measure enacted in that sub-section for determining the consideration actually received by the assessee would be applicable in all its rigour in such cases. This condition of 15 per cent or more difference is merely intended to be a safeguard against undue hardship which would be occasioned to the assessee if the inflexible rule of the thumb enacted in sub-section (2) were applied in marginal cases and it has nothing to do with the question of burden of proof, for the burden of establishing that there is understatement of the consideration in respect of the transfer always rests on the revenue. The postulate underlying sub-section (2) is that the difference between one honest valuation and another may range up to 15 per cent and that constitutes the class of marginal cases which are taken out of the purview of sub-section (2) in order to avoid hardship to the assessee.

It is a moot point as to whether section 50CA can be automatically invoked in all cases of difference or it cannot apply in the cases mentioned by the Supreme Court. Further, if the rules prescribe an artificial method, it is unclear as to whether it would be valid in all circumstances. Again, different methods of valuation are applicable to different types of companies. If different types of methods for different types of companies are not prescribed, it is unclear as to whether the Rules would be valid in all circumstances.

7.13 Exemption under section 54EC [Section 54EC]

Section 54EC provides that capital gain to the extent of Rs. 50 lakhs arising from the transfer of a long-term capital asset shall be exempt if the assessee invests the whole or any part of capital gains in certain specified bonds, within the specified time. Investment in bonds issued by the National Highways Authority of India or by the Rural Electrification Corporation Limited are eligible for exemption under this section.

Section 54EC has been amended with effect from assessment year 2018-19 to provide that investment in any other bond notified by the Central Government in this behalf shall also be eligible for exemption.

7.14 Shifting base year from 1981 to 2001 for computation of capital gains [Section 55/48]

Section 48 provides that for computation of capital gains, an assessee shall be allowed deduction for cost of acquisition of the asset and also cost of improvement, if any. Hitherto, section 55 provided that for computing capital gains in respect of an asset acquired before 1-4-1981, the assessee was allowed an option to take either the fair market value of the asset as on 1-4-1981 or the actual cost of the asset as cost of acquisition. The assessee was also allowed to claim deduction for cost of improvement, if any, incurred after 1-4-1981.

Section 55 has been amended with effect from assessment year 2018-19 to provide that the cost of acquisition of an asset acquired before 1-4-2001 shall be allowed to be taken as fair market value as on 1-4-2001 and the cost of improvement shall include only those capital expenses which are incurred after 1-4-2001.

Consequential amendment is also made in section 48 so as to align the provisions relating to cost inflation index to the said base year of 1-4-2001 instead of 1-4-1981.

'Time' and 'Value' are two ends of the same spectrum. Prudentially, a particular sum of money is considered to be more valuable now, than the same sum at a future point in time. This forms the conceptual base of the "Time value of money" and the underlying logic is the earning potential in the interim. Ignorance of the time value of money was a worrisome problem in the erstwhile Indian recovery laws. Revolutionarily, the Insolvency & Bankruptcy Code, 2016 (IBC) was created with the core objectives of "time-bound resolution" and "value maximization", inter alia, in its long title. Nevertheless, there has been a constant tussle between these two objectives. This article analyzes the tussle by relating to the identically ongoing issue in Reliance Capital's resolution process. Thereafter, the article delves into likewise precedents emphasizing and elaborating on the dual objectives. Ultimately, the authors propose to create a decisive guide for such a dilemma in the form of a Code of Conduct for the Committee of Creditors (CoC).

The Curious Case of Reliance Capital:

Reliance Capital, a Financial Service Provider, was admitted into Corporate Insolvency Resolution Process (CIRP), after an application for the same by the Reserve Bank of India. By the instance of four rounds of challenge mechanism and as on the date of the last day of auction (i.e., December 21, 2022), Torrent Investments submitted the highest bid of Rs. 8,640 crores, followed by Hinduja Group's offer of Rs.8,150 Crore. Pertinently, the liquidation value of Reliance Capital stood at Rs.12,500 crore as valued by Duff & Phelps and Rs.13,200 crore as valued by RBSA.1

Hinduja submitted a revised offer of Rs.9,500 Crore, including a Rs.8,800 Crore cash component. However, this revised offer was received a day after the conclusion of the auction.2 This revised offer of Hinduja left a chaotic confusion. Reportedly, on January 10, 2023, the committee of creditors took a decision to conduct another round of auction. Against this decision of the creditors, Torrent moved before the National Company Law Tribunal, Mumbai. The NCLT ruled in favour of the Torrent and remarked that the resolution process cannot be extended indefinitely under the pretext of "value maximization" and termed it as an "illegal mechanism" to circumvent the rules of India's bankruptcy code.3 Aggrieved by the NCLT's order, Hinduja appealed to the National Company Law Tribunal. The hearing in the appeal proceedings has concluded and is awaiting final orders.4

The reason behind the fierce competition to acquire Reliance Capital is the possibility of effortlessly venturing into business domains such as the insurance and financial services market without the hassle of getting new licenses, regulatory permits and other industrial permissions. The chain of events, in the creditors' eyes, is justified for the bidding value was drastically lower than that of the liquidation value. In the resolution applicant's eyes, it boils down to the arbitrary exercise of commercial wisdom of the committee of creditors. By and large, this fight exposes the constant tussle between 'value maximization' and 'time-bound process' under IBC.

A Tug of War:

In the case of Binani Industries Ltd. v. Bank of Baroda5 the NCLAT held that the objective of CIRP is to maximize the value in a time-bound manner for a distressed company's assets and that the resolution plan that maximizes the value should be preferred. Ultra Tech's revised bid provided a greater offer for the rehabilitation of Binani. The NCLAT cautioned that procedures cannot be rigidly applied in all circumstances and the delayed bids should not be rejected on the sole ground that it was filed late when there is a genuine reason for such delay. However, the bids submitted by fresh applicants after deadline should not be considered, even if they provide for a better revival solution. This ensures that the process remains fair and transparent. It was also added that the CoC should act responsibly and in the interest of all creditors. It was stated as follows:

"It is essential to note that the resolution process is not a sale or an auction, as no one is buying or selling the corporate debtor, if it was a sale the person offering the highest price would get the CD, but the object of the code is the resolution of the corporate debtor as a going concern with value maximization in a time-bound manner. Furthermore, it is not a recovery but a resolution process; whereas, a recovery bleeds a corporation to death, a resolution keeps it alive."

LD: Although the TRO had proceeded with the recovery proceeding by way of sale of the land, yet it transpired that necessary permission had been sought from the competent authority with regard to the reopening of the assessment proceedings but as it was apparent from the record, the assessee or her legal heirs had not been involved in the auction proceeding properly. Of course, in all fairness, the assessee could have agitated this issue before some civil court as it was a matter of administrative improprieties. In the instant case, one was not aware whether the concerned authority entrusted with the recovery proceeding, attachment and auction sale of the property of the assessee, was also entrusted with the payment of capital gains tax, if any, on the sale value so received by the auction seller. However, the contention of the assessee that capital gains tax would not be chargeable in his hands could not be accepted. The assessee’s contention that capital gains tax would not be chargeable in her hands because of the law laid down in case of J. Narayana Murthy (Supra) could not be simply accepted. It was because the facts of the cited case and the impugned case were totally different. The assessee had not been declared as insolvent rather, for recovery of the tax dues or resultant effect leading to attachment and auction sale, action was taken by the revenue. But there was serious infirmity in computing the capital gains tax because the Assessing Officer determined the cost of acquisition as on 1-4-1964 as per the balance sheet filed by the assessee and not the value as had to be determined on the basis of indexed cost of acquisition as has been envisaged under the Explanation (iii) to the proviso to section 48, i.e., the section related to mode of computation. However, the Assessing Officer did not enquire into the indexed cost of improvement, if any, made in between the period from 1-4-1964 to 1-4-1981 as per the provision of Explanation (iv) of the proviso to section 48. Therefore, in all fairness, the cost of acquisition had to be determined and adopted by the Assessing Officer on the basis of fair market value as on 1-4-1981. Therefore, the Assessing Officer was directed to collect the value so adopted in a case of sale in the nearby vicinity as on 1-4-1981 or any nearby date next to 1-4-1981 or prior to 1-4-1981. In this connection, both the assessee and the revenue were directed to collect the requisite information from the DSR in order to arrive at the rate of computation of indexed cost as on 1-4-1981.

Finance Act, 1996

Modification of the provisions relating to deduction from profits derived from the business of providing long-term finance [Sec. 36(1)(viii)]

10.5 Under section 36(l)(viii), in case of a financial corporation, engaged in providing long-term finance for industrial or agricultural development or development of infrastructure facility in India or in case of a public company formed and registered in India, with the main object of carrying on the business of providing long-term finance for construction of purchase of house in India for residential purposes, an amount not exceeding 40% of the profits derived from such business and carried to a special reserve, is allowed as a deduction subject to certain conditions. An amendment carried out by the Finance Act, 1995, has resulted in allowing the deduction from total income computed before making any deduction under this 'section' and not before making deduction under this 'clause'. As this was not the intention this error has been rectified by providing with effect from assessment year 1996-97 that the deduction shall be allowed on total income before making deduction under section 36(1)(viii).

The expression long-term finance' was not earlier defined. Section 36 has now been amended with effect from assessment year 1996-97 to define the expression long-term finance' to mean any loan or advance, where the terms under which monies are loaned or advanced provide for repayment along with interest thereof during a period of not less than five years.

A loan would be reckoned as long-term finance even if, substantial amount of the loan is repayable before 5 years (say 90%) and only the balance is repayble in the 5th year. The proviso to rule 1(v) of the Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 reads as follows:

"Provided that such moneys are borrowed for the creation of a capital asset in India and the agreement under which such moneys are borrowed provides for the repayment thereof during a period of not less than seven years."

Courts have interpreted this proviso as follows:

If the moneys had been borrowed under an agreement whereby the moneys were to be repaid during a period of not less than seven years, then the fact that the assessee had been able to repay the amount before the expiry of seven years was not relevant. [CIT v. Zenith Steel Pipes Ltd. 181 ITR 291 (Bom.)]

If the agreement originally provides for repayment of the loan within 7 years and subsequently it is modified for repayment within 8 years and the loan is repaid within 8 years, the loan cannot be set to be repayable within the period of 7 years. [CIT v. New India Industries Ltd. 212 ITR 653 (SC)]

The aforesaid decisions would be relevant for interpreting the term long-term finance in section 36(1)(viii).

10.5-1 Amendment regarding computation of deduction - Section 36(1)(viii) has been amended still further. Under the second proviso to the said section as it stood prior to the amendment, the allowance in respect of special reserve was allowable only till such period upto which the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve from time to time did not exceed twice the amount of share capital. Further, in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves were to be excluded.

The said second proviso is now amended with effect from assessment year 1997-98 so as to provide that:

the allowance will be allowed till such period upto which the aggregate of special reserve does not exceed the aggregate of share capital and general reserves; and

Thus, in case of corporations making profits consistently and ploughing back the profits regularly by increasing the general reserves, the deduction in respect of special reserve could be allowed year after year almost perpetually.

16.9 Time limit for sale of attached immovable property

Rule 68B of the Second Schedule provides for time limit for sale of attached immovable property.

Rule 68B(1), prior to its amendment, provided that no sale of immovable property attached towards the recovery of tax, penalty, etc., shall be made after the expiry of 3 years from the end of the financial year in which the order giving rise to a demand of any sum, for the recovery of which the immovable property had been attached,

(a)

had become conclusive under section 245-I; or

(b)

final in terms of Chapter XX.

The said sub-rule has been amended with effect from 1-9-2019 to extend the said period from 3 years to 7 years.

Further, a proviso to the said sub-rule has been inserted to provide that the CBDT may, for reasons recorded in writing, extend the aforesaid period by a further period not exceeding 3 years. Thus, the total time period for sale of attached immovable property could now extend to 10 years from the end of the financial year in which the order is conclusive/final.

The purpose of the amendment as explained in the Memorandum is as follows:

"In order to protect the interest of the revenue, especially in those cases where demand has been crystallised on conclusion of the proceedings, it is proposed to amend the aforesaid sub-rule so as to extend the period of limitation from three years to seven years.

In order to ensure that the limitation of time period for sale of attached property may not be an impediment in recovery of tax dues and may not lead to permanent loss of revenue to the exchequer, it is further proposed to insert a new proviso in the said sub-rule so as to provide that the Board may, for reasons to be recorded in writing, extend the aforesaid period of limitation by a further period of three years."

The amendment is not retrospective in operation. For the purpose of section 149 prescribing time limit for issue of notice for reassessment it has been held that the assessment orders issued for the period where liability was extinguished cannot be reopened invoking the extended limitation period in the amended provision [Varkey Jacob v. CIT [2005] 146 Taxman 665 (Ker.)/Principal CIT v. Vernan (P.) Trust [Income Tax Appeal No. 692 of 2016, dated 18-12-2018] (Bom.) (SLP dismissed in Principal CIT v. Vernan (P.) Trust [Special Leave Petition (Civil) Diary No. 18762 of 2019, dated 4-7-2019] (SC)]. Similarly, it appears that the amendment cannot revive the time limit for an order in respect of which the period of 3 years has expired. However, it appears that the amendment can extend the time limit for an order already passed but in respect of which the period of 3 years has not expired.

It will of course apply only in respect of orders passed on or after 1-9-2019.
