The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted three new sub-sections (7A), (7B) and (7C) in section 35AD which provide as under:

New sub-section (7A) provides that any asset in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under this section shall be used only for the specified business, for a period of eight years beginning with the previous year in which such asset is acquired or constructed. New sub-section (7B) deals with a situation where any asset, in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under this section is used for a purpose other than the specified business during the period specified in sub-section (7A) otherwise than by way of a mode referred to in clause (vii) of section 28. In such a case, the total amount of deduction so claimed and allowed in one or more previous years, as reduced by the amount of depreciation allowable in accordance with the provisions of section 32 as if no deduction under said section 35AD was allowed, shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" of the previous year in which the asset is so used.

New sub-section (7C) provides that nothing contained in sub-section (7B) shall apply to a company which has become a sick industrial company under sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, during the period specified in sub-section (7A).

These amendments will take effect from 1st April, 2015 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2015-16 and subsequent assessment years.

The Explanatory Memorandum explains these amendments as under :

II. The existing provisions of section 35AD do not provide for a specific time period for which capital assets on which the deduction has been claimed and allowed, are to be used for the specified business. With a view to ensure that the capital asset on which investment linked deduction has been claimed is used for the purposes of the specified business, it is proposed to insert sub-section (7A) in section 35AD to provide that any asset in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under section 35AD, shall be used only for the specified business for a period of eight years beginning with the previous year in which such asset is acquired or constructed.

If any asset on which a deduction under section 35AD has been allowed, is demolished, destroyed, discarded or transferred, the sum received or receivable for the same is chargeable to tax under clause (vii) of section 28. This does not take into account a case where asset on which deduction under section 35AD has been claimed is used for any purpose other than the specified business by way of a mode other than that specified above. Accordingly, it is proposed to insert sub-section (7B) to provide that if such asset is used for any purpose other than the specified business, the total amount of deduction so claimed and allowed in any previous year in respect of such asset, as reduced by the amount of depreciation allowable in accordance with the provisions of section 32 as if no deduction had been allowed under section 35AD, shall be deemed to be income of the assessee chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" of the previous year in which the asset is so used.

HEADNOTE: Section 67 of the Finance Act, 1994 - Valuation of taxable services for charging service tax - Assessee was in business of operating hotels under its various brands - Any entrepreneur interested in running a hotel under assessee's banner signed an operating agreement with assessee to operate hotel under one of brands of assessee - Thereupon assessee sent its employees to such hotel for working therein and to ensure that proper standards were maintained in actual operation of hotel - Assessee directly paid salary to its above employees and same was reimbursed by hotel on actual basis without any markup to assessee - Adjudicating Authority levied service tax on expenses reimbursed by hotel to assessee under section 67 - Whether in terms of law declared by Delhi High Court in case of Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2012] 38 STT 75/28 taxmann.com 213, such reimbursable expenses collected by services provider (assessee) from service recipient (hotel) could not be held to be a part of value of services being provided by assessee and same could not be subjected to service tax - Held, yes [Para 4] [In favour of assessee]Service Tax : Reimbursable expenses collected by services provider from service recipient could not be held to be a part of value of services being provided by services provider and same could not be subjected to service tax

FACT: The assessee was in the business of operating hotels under its various brands. Any entrepreneur interested in running a hotel under the assessee's banner signed an operating agreement with the assessee to operate the hotel under one of the brands of the assessee.

Thereupon the assessee sent its employees on secondment (deputation) to such hotel. Such employees were not employed by the hotel and they continued to be in the employment of the assessee. Though they continued to be on the rolls of the assessee, but in fact worked for the hotel in the actual day-to-day operation and running of the hotel. They also ensured that proper standards were maintained in the actual operation of the hotel so as to protect the valuable brand of the assessee. The salaries and expenses of such employees were continued to be paid by the assessee, but the same was reimbursed by the hotel on actual basis without any markup.

The Adjudicating Authority levied service tax on the expenses reimbursed by the hotel to the assessee under section 67.

On appeal to Tribunal:

HELD: The Delhi High Court in the case of Intercontinental Consultants and Technocrats (P.) Ltd. v. UOI [2012] 38 STT 75/28 taxmann.com 213 has held that reimbursable expenses cannot form part of the gross value of the services being provided by the service provider. In the instant case, the salary of the employees being sent by the assessee to the hotel is being paid by the assessee directly to the employees and the same is being reimbursed by the hotel without any markup. As such, in terms of the law declared by the High Court such reimbursable expenses collected by the services provider from the service recipient cannot be held to be a part of the value of the services being provided by the assessee and the same could not be subjected to service tax under section 67. [Para 4].

Apart from the fact that the issue is covered by the earlier decision of the Delhi High Court, the demand is barred by limitation having been raised by invoking longer period of limitation. The issue involved is a bona fide issue of interpretation of legal points which were the subject matter of various decisions. As such, it cannot be said that there was any suppression or misstatement with any mala fide intention to evade tax on the part of the assessee, thus justifying invocation of longer period of limitation. [Para 5]

In view of the aforesaid, the demand of service tax upon the assessee was liable to be set aside. [Para 6]

FACT: The assessee entered into a contract with a German firm for purchase of machinery. The delivery was not within the time stipulated nor was it according to specifications. The assessee, therefore, instituted a suit against the said firm in 1935 for recovery of a sum of Rs. 2,05,000. The suit was ultimately decreed in December, 1953, for the said sum plus interest pendente lite. The assessee could however, recover only Rs. 2,20,192 from the Custodian of Enemy Properties. This amount was received by the assessee in the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1961-62. The assessee claimed that it was a capital receipt and hence not taxable. The ITO accepted the said claim only in respect of a small portion of the said amount and included the rest in the income of the assessee. On appeal, the amount to be included in the income was reduced substantially. Even so, the assessee filed a further appeal to the Tribunal. The Tribunal allowed the appeal on the only ground that the said amount could not be included in the assessment year 1961-62 for the reason that the assessee was maintaining its accounts on the mercantile basis and that the said amount must be deemed to have accrued on the date of the decree.

On the basis of the Tribunal's judgment, the ITO reopened the assessment for the relevant assessment year. However, on appeal, the Tribunal set aside the reassessment proceedings.

On reference:

HELD: Admittedly, the action was under section 147(a ) and could not have been under section 147(b). The action was being taken after the expiry of eight years. Action under clause (a) of section 147, could, therefore, be taken only in cases where the income that escaped assessment was in the sum of Rs. 50,000 or above. In this case, the proposal submitted by the ITO to the Board clearly said that the assessee received Rs. 2,05,000 as compensation and Rs. 12,500 towards interest thereon. The Tribunal had held that the sum of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt and only the interest of Rs. 12,500 constituted income (revenue receipt). Even in the earlier assessment proceedings, there was a controversy as to whether the whole or any part of the compensation amount constituted revenue receipt. The AAC had opined that out of the amount received, only an amount of Rs. 91,004 constituted revenue receipt. Evidently, the ITO had not applied his mind to the relevant facts. He seemed to have proceeded on the assumption that the entire compensation amount constituted a revenue receipt. In this, he was evidently wrong.

The Tribunal had subsequently found that only the sum of Rs. 12,500 representing the interest was includible in the income and that the remaining amount of Rs. 2,05,000 constituted a capital receipt. If so, the reopening of the assessment after eight years was clearly unsustainable under section 149 as it then stood.

Note : The case was decided in favour of the assessee.

Section 5 (8)4 of the Code, defines "financial debt" as a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and include any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing. The bench observed that the allottees/ homebuyers were already included in the provision, thus the amendment was a merely an elucidation. In response to an argument from the petitioner that at the best, real estate developers were operational debtors and not financial debtors, the Court made many points of distinction; first one being that in case a real estate developer takes money in advance from allottees/ homebuyers for the construction of the building. Additionally, operational creditors do not concern themselves with the financial health of the Corporate Debtor. Whereas, a home allottees/ homebuyers is extremely concerned with the fact that whether the Corporate Debtor is financially sound or not, as it plays an imperative role in the final product of a real estate project, namely a house. The bench further remarked that payments that are made in advance for goods and services are not utilized in manufacture or production of such goods or services. Goods or Services provided to the Debtor contain no consideration for time value of money; the consideration being the goods or services themselves. In case of allottees/ homebuyers in a real estate project, the money raised from allottee/ homebuyer for the time value of money. The concept of Time value of money essentially says that "money available at the present time is worth more than the identical sum in the future due to its potential earning capacity. This core principle of finance holds that provided money can earn interest, any amount of money is worth more the sooner it is received."5 Allottees/ homebuyers invest in real estate primarily because of two reasons; either they see it as an investment that could benefit them in future; or for residential needs; or both of these reasons. Just because payment in case of a real estate project is made in instalments does not render it as operational debt. The Court made a reference to a previous NCLAT judgement Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructures Ltd. [2018] 94 taxmann.com 131/148 SCL 221 (NCLT - New Delhi) wherein it was held that amounts raised by developers under assured return schemes had the "commercial effect of a borrowing". A major reason for concern of the Real Estate Developer was raised, that the Code be misused to blackmail and divert funds that are to be used for real estate development. This could result in winding up of a perfectly solvent company or worse dormancy of the project in case of non-approval of Resolution plan, at the instance of one allottees/ homebuyers. It was one of the contentions that the developer had obtained foreign funding and wasn't utilizing the funds paid by allottees/ homebuyers and so the money advance was not debt as there was no "borrowing". The Court also relied upon the Insolvency Committee Report to come to the conclusion that "amounts raised under the contracts of home buyers are in effect for the purposes of raising finance, and are a means of raising finance. Thus, the Committee deemed it prudent to clarify that such amounts raised under a real estate project from a home buyer fall within entry (f) of Section 5(8)."6 Further, it may be noted that the amount of money given by home buyers as advances for their purchase is usually very high, and frequent delays in delivery of possession may thus, have a huge impact. For instance, in Chitra Sharma v. Union of India [2017] 85 taxmann.com 209/144 SCL 1 (SC).the amount of debts owed to home buyers, which was paid by them as advances, was claimed to be Fifteen Thousand Crore, more than what was due to banks. Despite this, banks were in a more favourable position under the Code since they were financial creditors.

■ The basic dispute in the instant case is whether the valuation of shares at a premium of Rs. 90 per share is representative of the fair market value. According to the appellant the valuation of fair market value of the shares has been made on the basis of the DCF method which had been introduced as an alternative to the valuation based on Net Asset Value method during the assessment year under consideration. However, according to the Assessing Officer, the same could not have been adopted for valuation purpose because the shares in question had been subscribed and allotted on 29-9-2012 which was before the date of the coming into effect of the DCF method, in the Rules. The assessee, however, contends that the option to the assessee to adopt DCF method was available because the assessment in this case was pending on that date which was completed later on 29-3-2016. The DCF method could be applied for valuation purposes for the assessments pending at that time. Besides, the Circular stated that rule would apply from the date of its publication. This assessment was pending on that date. The benefit of the DCF method of valuation was thus even otherwise available to the assessee as per the Circular. Further rule 11UA(2)(b) provides for the acceptance of the valuation made by Chartered Accountant as an acceptable mode for determining the fair market value of shares. The assessee has filed a report of CA, which certifies the fair market value, higher than Rs. 100 at Rs. 106 per share. The attempt of the Assessing Officer to locate and establish discrepancies or errors in that report of the Chartered Accountant is not based on any acceptable principle or approved standards. The discrepancies as pointed out by the Assessing Officer are not relevant in the context of capital restructuring in the case of group companies. Valuation by itself is a specialized exercise which can be disputed only on the basis of the findings of another expert as recognized in law for that purpose. The valuation as proposed by the DCF method cannot, therefore, be faulted. There is no overvaluation of shares over the fair market value. Accordingly the invocation of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) by the Assessing Officer being erroneous cannot be upheld. Thus, the addition made by the Assessing Officer under section 56(2)(viib) is directed to be deleted. [Para 6.1]

■

As to the other objection of the assessee, to the action of the Assessing Officer to add the share capital amount as collected by way of premium from the subscribing companies by invoking the proviso to section 68, it is viewed that the proviso provides for the scrutiny and assessment of the funds of the immediate subscribing company. The proviso does not extend that power to scrutinise the financial capacity of the secondary source which has provided funds to the subscribing companies. It is also noticed that in the case of some of the secondary sources, there are scrutiny assessment orders on record. Further the fact that the investments as made by the subscribing companies were out of funds which they possessed at the beginning of the year and no fresh infusion of funds by the subscribing companies during the assessment year under consideration and the source of funds are all proceeds of investments made in earlier years in the course of business and have been recalled/encashed was corroborated by the director of the subscribing companies in his statement recorded on oath. Therefore with these facts remaining uncontroverted no addition could have been even otherwise validly made under section 68 by the Assessing Officer. It is also noticed from the assessment orders placed on record that the Assessing Officers of the respective subscribing companies have not raised any objection to their returns of income relating to this year. As noticed earlier, in the case of BGS Credit Pvt. Ltd. there is a scrutiny assessment order on record for the assessment year 2012-13. Considered holistically, it is viewed that invocation of the proviso to section 68 by the Assessing Officer was, therefore, erroneous and not justified. The basic ingredients of section 68 of identity, creditworthiness and genuineness of the transactions are, in the circumstances of the case, apparently beyond doubt. There is no undisclosed income which could be charged under section 68. The addition as made by the Assessing Officer under section 68 is also, therefore, directed to be deleted. [Para 6.2]

That is the reason why sub-section (2) of section 150 provides that the enlargement of time provided in sub-section (1) would not be available where, even on the date when the assessment was completed, an assessment or reassessment of the income for the assessment year 1998-99 would have been barred by time. [Para 5] In the instant case, the assessment order for the assessment year 1978-79 was passed on 23-3-1990 under section 144. It was in this assessment order that the capital gain was first brought to assessment. There was an appeal against the assessment order and the Commissioner(Appeals) upheld the assessment to capital gain by order dated 15-5-1991. It was this order of the Commissioner(Appeals) that was carried in further appeal to the Tribunal, which passed the order on 14-6-2000 holding that the capital gain was assessable in the assessment year 1980-81. Now the question for consideration arose as to whether on 22-3-1990, the date on which the assessment for the assessment year 1978-79 was framed, the Assessing Officer could have taken action by issue of notice under section 148 to reopen the assessment for the assessment year 1980-81. According to section 149(1)(b)(iii ), as it stood with effect from 1-4-1989 but before being amended by the Finance Act, 2001, with effect from 1-6-2001, if seven years had elapsed from the end of the assessment year 1980-81, but not more than ten years had elapsed, the notice under section 148 could be issued for the assessment year 1980-81, provided the escaped income was likely to be Rs. 50,000 or more. Seven years from the end of the assessment year 1980-81 would have elapsed on 31-3-1988. Ten years would have elapsed on 31-3-1991. On 22-3-1990, seven years had elapsed but not ten years. Further, the income chargeable to tax was more than Rs. 3 lakhs. Therefore, the Assessing Officer could have validly issued notice under section 148 on 28-3-2003 in respect of the assessment year 1980-81 taking advantage of the direction issued by the Tribunal in the appeal for the assessment year 1978-79. Such a notice was saved by sub-section (1) of section 150 and the provisions of sub-section (2) of the section 150 were not applicable. The contention of the assessee was that the law as on 28-3-2003 would govern the issue of notice under section 149(1)(b), according to which, the maximum period of six years would have elapsed from the assessment year 1980-81 on 31-3-1987 and, therefore, the Assessing Officer could not have issued the notice under section 148 on 22-3-1990. There was no merit in the contention of the assessee, because under section 150(2), the time-limit within which notice under section 148 could be issued by the Assessing Officer had to be reckoned, in the very nature of things, under the provisions of section 149 as they stood as on 22-3- 1990, as is clear from the words 'assessment year in respect of which an assessment, reassessment or recomputation could not have been made at the time the order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision, as the case may be, was made by reason of any other provision limiting the time within which any action for assessment, reassessment or recomputation may be taken'. In the very nature of things, such other provision limiting the time for issue of notice under section 149 had to be reckoned with only on the date on which the assessment order for the assessment year 1978-79 was passed, which was on 22-3-1990. On this date, the Assessing Officer could have issued notice under section 148 within the time-limit provided by section 149(1)(b)(iii ) as it stood on that date. [Para 6]

5.1-2 Carry forward and set off in subsequent years under section 74 5.1-3 Impact of the amendment on loss up to assessment year 2002-03 - The amendment in section 74 comes into force from assessment year 2003-04. A question that arises is whether long-term capital loss up to assessment year 2002-03 can be set off against any gains or will it be set off only by application of the amended section 74 against long-term gains.

There are apparently two conflicting judgments of the Supreme Court which are relevant for resolving this issue :

(i) Reliance Jute & Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1979] 120 ITR 921 (SC)

(ii) CIT v. Shah Sadiq & Sons [1987] 166 ITR 102 (SC) which dealt with speculation loss.

Reliance’s case (supra) was concerning an amendment in 1957 to section 24(2)(iii) of the Income-tax Act, 1922 (hereinafter referred to as ‘1922 Act’) (corresponding to section 72 of the 1961 Act). Before the amendment, carried forward losses were allowed to be carried forward indefinitely. Thereafter with effect from assessment year 1957-58, losses were allowed to be carried forward for 8 years only. For assessment year 1960-61, the assessee contended that by virtue of section 24(2)(iii) of the 1922 Act, as it stood before its amendment with effect from 1-4-1957, the assessee had acquired a vested right to have the unabsorbed loss of assessment year 1950-51 carried forward from year to year indefinitely until it was completely set off, and the subsequent amendment limiting the period for carrying forward the loss to eight years could not divest the assessee of the vested right which has thus accrued to him. It was pointed out that the amendment effected in 1957 was not retrospective in operation.

The Supreme Court rejected the plea of the assessee and held, as follows :

“It is a cardinal principle of the tax law that the law to be applied is that in force in the assessment year unless otherwise provided expressly or by necessary implication : CIT v. Isthmian Steamship Lines [1951] 20 ITR 572 (SC)and Karimtharuvi Tea Estate Ltd. v. State of Kerala [1966] 60 ITR 262 (SC). On that principle, it is abundantly clear that when an assessment for the assessment year 1960-61 is to be made and section 24(2) is invoked, it is section 24(2) as in force in that assessment year which has to be applied. That is, the provision as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. There is no question of the assessee possessing any vested right under the law as it stood before the amendment. The assessment for one assessment year cannot, in the absence of a contrary provision, be affected by the law in force in another assessment year. A right claimed by an assessee under the law in force in a particular assessment year is ordinarily available only in relation to a proceeding pertaining to that year. Therefore, inasmuch as the provisions of section 24(2) as amended in 1957, govern the assessment for the assessment year 1960-61, the High Court is right in affirming that the unabsorbed loss of Rs. 15,50,189 of the assessment year 1950-51 cannot be carried forward for more than eight years, and consequently, cannot be set off against the business income of the assessment year 1960-61” (p. 923)

In Shah Sadiq & Sons (supra), the Court was concerned with carry forward and set off of speculation losses. In the 1922 Act speculation losses of a firm were allowed to be carried forward and set off by the firm. However, in the 1961 Act, section 75(2) was introduced which allowed the losses to be set off only by the partners and not by the firm. The assessee firm had incurred losses in speculation business for the assessment years 1960-61 and 1961-62 (that is, under the 1922 Act) and claimed that they should be set off against the speculation profit for the assessment year 1962-63 (under the 1961 Act).

Option for claiming deduction

4.4-5 The section provides that the deduction shall be ‘allowed to the assessee.’ In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/ 109 Taxman 225, the Supreme Court has held that the word ‘allowed’ in section 32(1) suggests that the depreciation claim is optional and it cannot be thrust upon the assessee: a thing is allowed when it is claimed. Having regard to this and the same expression allowed being used in section 35AD, it could be argued that the deduction under section 35AD is optional and it cannot be thrust upon the assessee. In such a situation the special provisions of section 28(vii), section 50B and section 73A should not become applicable to the assessee.

Allowability of discount on ZCB

4.5 Explanation to section 36(1)(iiia) provides for the definition of the expression ‘discount’ as the difference between the amount received or receivable by an issuer upon issue of a ZCB and the amount payable by such issuer upon maturity or redemption of such bond.

The said Explanation has been amended with effect from assessment year 2009-10 to include scheduled banks in the category of issuers. The amendment is consequent upon change in the definition of ZCB.

Extension of special deduction under section 36(1)(viii)

4.6 Section 36(1)(viii) provides special deduction to financial corporations and banking companies of an amount not exceeding 20% of the profits subject to creation of a reserve.

Hitherto, the benefit of section 36(1)(viii) was available, inter alia, to entities engaged in long-term financing for construction or purchase of houses in India for residential purpose. The definition of eligible business has now been amended with effect from assessment year 2010-11 to provide that eligible business will include provision of long-term finance for development of housing in India. In other words, corporations engaged in providing long-term finance (including re-financing) for development of housing in India will now be eligible for the benefit under section 36(1)(viii).

The amendment, however, deletes the expression ‘construction or purchase of houses in India’. Now, purchase of existing house may not result in development of housing and hence, it appears that an entity engaged in long term financing for purchase of house may not qualify for the deduction.

The contention of the assessee that basement had no value was also rejected because car parking area was as much a saleable space as any other space. It could either be sold along with the flats or separately or might be retained for being leased to the flat-owners. The rates at which the flats were booked on various dates were to be considered for valuation of those flats. In case of any space earmarked for the appellant which had not been so agreed to be sold, but was intended to be retained by the appellant himself it had to be valued at the rate at which initial booking was started, because it was based on the initial understanding with the builder. However, upon the assessee deciding not to sell some flats at a later point of time, the rate that was prevalent then had to be adopted for those flats. The Tribunal being concerned with the market value of the flats and not their cost of construction, these need to be valued at the same rate at which it would be available to the public.

The adoption or estimate by the Commissioner (Appeals) of the rates at which some space could be made available to the buyers of the basements, upper ground floor, etc., was improper, because he did not consider the rates at which public was invited to buy the flat space. The rates were revised upwards more than once, which suggested that the public was slow in responding to the invitation but, all the same, it was those rates with which the flats were to be related and not any imaginery rate. If, as on 31- 3-1983, some flats in the ground floor, upper ground floor first, second and other floors were not booked, then the most proximate rate at which invitation was advertised should be adopted as the value for those flats. White adopting the rates, care must be exercised to ensure that the rates adopted were for those respective floors, i.e., the rates of second floor could not be adopted for valuing the third floor, unless both the floors had the same rate.

The rates at which the flat space was sold were similar to recoverable debt and since the flat price was payable in instalments spread over a few years, the instalments that became due after the valuation date needed to be discounted to arrive at the present worth of the space involved. Further, since the building in which the space was allotted to the several buyers required the sanction of the L & DO on payment of commercialisation charges, it was very much a charge on the present value of the flat space. Similarly, the settlement with the tenant, who had carried the matter to the High Court that was ultimately settled in 1986, was also a charge on the present value of the flats. Since the property was under construction as on the relevant valuation dates, and some more cost had to be incurred, as the construction got completed in 1987, i.e., almost four and three years from 31-3-1983 and 31-3-1984, respectively this element equated as interest also required to be allowed deduction of for arriving at the present value of the flat space.

The Assessing Officer was, accordingly, directed to recalculate the value of the space on the two valuation dates separately, as above.

The appeals were, accordingly, partly allowed.

It is noteworthy that there is no change in the benchmarking approach of the assessee, as it has been consistently following the same benchmarking approach year after year. [Para 15]

■ Undisputedly, the issue is fully covered by the orders of coordinate bench in the assessee's own case for preceding years viz. assessment year 2014-15, assessment year 2015-16, assessment year 2018-19, assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22, where the addition made in respect of transfer of electricity was deleted and the assessee's benchmarking approach of using the purchase price of electricity from SEB was upheld. It is also clear that the case of the assessee for assessment year 2014-15 travelled upto Delhi High Court and the Revenue's appeal on the issue of transfer of electricity was dismissed by the Court dealing with the issue fully on merits and by observing as follows: "Thus, the market for supply of electricity is regulated. To apply the CUP method, it is necessary to ascertain comparable transactions similar in material aspects and without differences that bear on price. IEX is a platform for short-term surplus power and not a source for uninterrupted supply. There is wide fluctuation in IEX rates, and rates quoted there are for power supplied and not the power consumed. These material differences between electricity supplied by SEBs or distribution companies and that secured by bidding on IEX have a significant bearing on price. The CUP method cannot be applied where there is significant dissimilarity between the comparable transactions. In Commissioner of Income Tax v. Jindal Steel and Power Limited [2023] 157 taxmann.com 207/297 Taxman 253/460 ITR 162 (SC), the Supreme Court held that 'market value' under Section 80IA(8) means the price determined in an open market in an environment of free competition and that, for captive power supplies, the rate at which the State Electricity Board supplied power to industrial consumers has to be taken as the market value for computing deduction under Section 80IA. As is apparent, the Supreme Court accepted the rates at which electricity was supplied by the SEBs to industrial consumers as being the market value for the purposes of Section 80IA(8)." [Para 16]

■

The limited issue is whether the assessee's benchmarking approach of adopting the purchase price of electricity from respective SEB for determination of transfer price of captive power adheres with the arm's length principle or not. As stated above, this question has been answered by the High Court in the assessee's own case forassessment year 2014-15 relying upon the judgement of Supreme Court in the case of CIT v. Jindal Steel & Power Ltd. [2023] 157 taxmann.com 207/297 Taxman 253/460 ITR 162 (SC). Therefore, respectfully following the same, the assessee's benchmarking approach is accepted and the methodology suggested by the TPO is rejected. TPO/AO have also erred in not following the directions unreservedly which is against the statutory mandate as contained in Section 144C(10) of the Income Tax Act, 1961. In terms of their own submissions, no appeal was filed by the Revenue against the order of High Court inassessment year 2014-15 till the date of giving effect to the DRP directions, therefore, they should have followed the DRP directions and deleted the addition. The TPO/AO on the other hand sustained the addition on the ground that department is in the process of filing SLP against the High Court's order. ■ The judgments cited above clearly show that, Deferred income, the matching principle and the proportionate completion method are not alien to the Income-tax Act, 1961. On this score, the view taken by the ITAT is fundamentally erroneous. [Para 16]

■

In a batch of appeals in respect of Mahindra Holidays and Resorts India Ltd (supra)., carrying on similar business, the Court had the advantage of considering all these aspects and held in favour of assessee. Therefore, the reasoning to arrive at the said conclusion, in the Court’s opinion, needs no repetition, except to point out that though there are few differences in the terms of agreements regarding how the facilities and amenities promised to be met, the collection of Annual Maintenance or utility charges collected for actual usage by members while staying at resort not to be matched or equated with the facilities/Amenities assured to the members on payment of the fees. The recurring expenses till the expiry of the agreement period are certain and not contingent. For the sake of completion, the judgments which have recognised the accounting method of deferring part of the income to meet future expenditure are capsulised. (i) Treasure Island Resorts (supra). (ii) Madras Industrial Investment Corpn. Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 91 Taxman 340 (SC)/[1997] 225 ITR 802 (SC). (iii) Metal Box Company of India Ltd v. Their Workmen [1969] 1968 taxmann.com 162 (SC)/1968 SCC OnLine SC 83. [Para 17]

■

This is in tune with the earlier judgment of the Supreme Court in Calcutta Co. Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 37 ITR 1 (SC), wherein, the Supreme Court has held that the liability on the assessee having been imported, the liability would be an accrued liability and would not convert into a conditional one merely because the liability was to be discharged at a future date. There may be some difficulty in the estimation thereof but that would not convert the accrued liability into a conditional one; it was always open to the tax authorities concerned to arrive at a proper estimate of the liability having regard to all the circumstances of the case. [Para 18]

■

The above proposition has been consistently followed by other High Courts, such as the Delhi High Court in CIT v. Shyam Telelink Ltd. [2019] 101 taxmann.com 218 (Delhi)/[2019] 260 Taxman 402 (Delhi)/[2019] 410 ITR 31 (Delhi), and in CIT v. Dinesh Kumar Goel [2011] 9 taxmann.com 188 (Delhi)/[2011] 197 Taxman 375 (Delhi)/[2011] 331 ITR 10 (Delhi) and the Gujarat High Court in Winner Business Link (P) Ltd (supra). It is also to be noted that the Supreme Court dismissed the appeal filed by the revenue in Winner Business Link (supra) which has followed the principles laid down in Treasure Island (supra) and Dinesh Kumar Goel (supra). Therefore, the law being settled, the substantial questions of law are in favour of the assessee. [Para 19]

Prima facie, each holiday resort run by the appellants answered the definition of ‘club’ or ‘association’ given under section 65(25a) ibid. In this view of the matter, the appellants could not be said to have made out a prima facie case against the impugned demand of service tax on merits. In the same view of the matter, the plea of ‘goods’ and the alternate plea of ‘immovable property’ would not be sustainable. The Tribunal further held that the period of limitation for a demand notice for service tax has to be reckoned with reference to the dates of filing of the service tax returns for the material period. In the instant case, for the first half year of a fiscal, a return had to be filed on or before 24th October and, for the second half year, it had to be filed on or before the 24th April of the next fiscal. The revenue submitted that, on this basis, the demand of service tax covered by the Annexure-I to the impugned order was within the normal period, amounting to over Rs. 1.34 crores. It was not claimed that the demand covered by the Annexure-II to the order was within the normal period. In this frame of the case, prima facie it was viewed that the demand covered by the Annexure-II to the order was beyond the normal period and the same might not be sustainable on the ground of suppression of facts inasmuch as the party could not have suppressed before 16-6-2005 any fact relevant to levy of service tax on ‘club’ or ‘association’ defined under section 65(25a). The appellants argued that nothing contained in section 67 could be invoked to levy service tax on any amount collected by them from their time-sharers prior to 16-6-2005. The Tribunal came across a circular of the Board which governed this area of dispute, which circular had been referred to in the impugned order as well. This circular clarified that, in respect of a taxable service, any amount collected prior to the date of introduction of that service, for a period after that date would also form part of the taxable value under section 67. It was on record that the amounts collected by the appellants from their members for the period 16-6-2005 to 30-9-2006 included amounts collected in advance prior to 16-6-2005 also. Such amounts collected prior to 16-6-2005 had been apportioned pro rata so as to cover the period of dispute. It was this apportionment which stood supported by the Board’s circular. The appellant’s contention that this had no legal sanction could not be accepted after perusal of the full text of section 67. Nevertheless, a case was found for the appellants on the ground of limitation insofar as the demand covered by Annexure-II to the impugned order was concerned. The plea of financial hardships was also taken into account.

On an overall assessment of the case, including the plea of limitation, put forth by the appellants, the Tribunal opined that the appellants should pre-deposit only a part of the amount of service tax covered by Annexure-I to the impugned order. Accordingly, the appellants were directed to pre-deposit an amount of Rs. 30 lakhs.

CIT 180 Taxman 422 (SC), the Supreme Court has observed that a provision is recognised when: (a ) an enterprise has a present obligation as a result of a past event; (b) it is probable that an outflow of resources will be required to settle the obligation; and (c ) a reliable estimate can be made of the amount of the obligation. If these conditions are not met, no provision can be recognised. In the instant case, as already observed that the assessee had a present obligation as a result of a past event. Thus, the first condition was satisfied. It was also observed that outflow of resources was probable to settle the obligation. The second condition was also satisfied. However, considering the nature of activity, it was the third condition which was difficult to satisfy. The demand for accommodation by the members was essentially tourism oriented. Tourism, in turn, depends on several factors. They may be social, political, climatic and so on. If wedding season is in full swing, tourism can get affected. If there is some commotion around a particular resort or if the law and order situation is not conducive, tourism can be affected. Sudden change in weather can also affect tourism. Further, availability of rail or air reservation can also affect tourism. The possibility of Leave Travel concession (LTC) getting lapsed can see sudden spurt in tourism. These are only a few illustrations which can affect the demand for accommodation either way. There may be many possibilities which may not come to mind but may put the assessee into tremendous pressure. All these factors are such which are twined with the normal human life and, hence, are not only certain to occur but also make it difficult to reasonably estimate the probable outflow of resources. Moreover, as mentioned earlier, most of the grievances are settled by consumer forum and it can be anybody’s guess as to what damages the forum will award. Therefore, recognising the entire receipt as income in the year of receipt could lead to distortion. [Para 31]

As a result the proposition of the assessee that it was not justifiable to tax the entire income in a single year was to be accepted. [Para 31]

Accordingly, the entire amount of time share membership fee receivable by the assessee up front at the time of enrolment of a member was not the income chargeable to tax in the initial year on account of contractual obligation that was fastened to the receipt to provide services in future over the term of contract. [Para 32]

In the result, the appeal filed by the revenue was to be dismissed. [Para 33]

Case study 1: - Issue on application of 80-IA(8)

Facts:

Head office, a company having 3 different units;

Common services of the Group such as administration, HR, accounting are undertaken by the Head Office;

Issues:

Whether common overhead costs needs to be allocated to the qualifying unit?

Whether the actual expenditure can be allocated or whether the expenditure should be allocated based on FMV?

The issue of allocation of common expenses incurred by the head office has been discussed in the cases of Wipro Information Technology Ltd v. Dy. CIT [2004] 88 TTJ (Bang) 778 and Asstt. CIT v. Asea Brown Boveri Ltd. [2007] 14 SOT 18 (Mum.) (URO). The tax payer has argued that the expenditure which is directly attributable to the earning of profits of qualifying undertaking should only be considered for the purpose of computing tax holiday benefits. However, this argument was not accepted by the Tribunals. The Tribunal stated that non allocation of common costs may lead to inflation of profits of tax holiday units and reduction of income chargeable to tax of the head office which defeats the basic principle of taxation.

This issue is debatable. Unlike the international transaction covered by section 92(1) read with section 92B, the SDT provisions are not so broad based. Section 80-IA(8) of the Act provides as follows:

"Where any goods or services held for the purposes of the eligible business are transferred to any other business carried on by the assessee, or where any goods or services held for the purposes of any other business carried on by the assessee are transferred to the eligible business and, in either case, the consideration, if any, for such transfer as recorded in the accounts of the eligible business does not correspond to the market value of such goods or services as on the date of the transfer, then, for the purposes of the deduction under this section, the profits and gains of such eligible business shall be computed as if the transfer, in either case, had been made at the market value of such goods or services as on that date"

As seen from the above, section 80-IA(8) is applicable to a transaction relating to 'transfer of goods or services held for the purposes of' qualifying unit to or from any other 'business' carried on by the taxpayer for which a 'consideration' is charged by the transferor unit and paid by the recipient unit. Hence, it can be argued that section 80-IA(8) intends to cover services of 'marketable' nature. This view also finds support from the CBDT Circular No. 14 of 2001 which has explained the object of amendment of s. 80-IA(8) by FA 2001 to include reference to 'services' which reads as follows :-

"Under sub-section (8) of section 80-IA, where any goods are transferred for a consideration to any other business of the assessee, the consideration should correspond to the market value of such goods. As in certain cases, the transfer may relate to services, the provision has been accordingly amended to clarify that this would include services. Such services may include marketable services of operation and maintenance (O&M) in case of infrastructure facilities, marketable services for distribution of electricity and specified marketable services in telecom. Instead of the words "industrial undertaking" occurring in section 80IA, the word "undertaking" has also been substituted in the provision for the same reason."

In view of the above, though it can be argued that section 80A(6)/section 80-IA(8) is not be applicable to allocation of general Head Office expenses which may not be considered as marketable services, the issue may not be free from ligation.

Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

The general approach is that: the opinion of the profession is entitled to respect but is not binding on the Courts. ACCOUNTING STANDARDS AS A BRIDGE

2. Accounting standards are crystallised accounting principles to meet different contingencies for recognition of income. Accounting standards issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India are presently statutorily mandatory for companies under the company law. Even for others, they are bound to be observed in audit. They constitute Generally Accepted Accounting Principles (GAAP). Even where they are not mandatory, there is no reason, why such principles embodied in the standards, should not have application in computation of taxable income. The Courts have had occasions to refer to accounting standards.

In the case of a chit company even in absence of any accounting standards specifically for such companies, the assessee, who spreadover the chit commission during the duration of chit on percentage of completion basis, relied upon Accounting Standard 22 for the spread over principle recognised both in Madras Industrial Investment Corpn.’s case (supra) and J.K. Industries v. Union of India [2008] 297 ITR 176 (SC). The Supreme Court in CIT v. Bilahari Investments (P.) Ltd. [2008] 298 ITR 1 / 68 Taxman 95 (SC) pointed out that accounting standards are of recent origin and that it is open to the department to consider these new accounting standards and concepts in future cases of chit transactions ‘without expressing any opinion in this regard’, but upholding assessee’s method with reference to method of accounting regularly adopted by the assessee. The Supreme Court did not decide the issue on merits as adoption of either method made little difference in the facts of the case. In J.K. Industries’ case (supra), the Supreme Court observed in the context of accounting for deferred tax, that accounting standards provide for discipline and harmonisation of concepts and accounting principles consistent with the objective of true and fair accounting.

Ascertainment of cost after deduction of commission paid for purchase, understood to be justified by Accounting Standard 2, was endorsed by the High Court in CIT v. George Oakes Ltd. [2008] 303 ITR 357 (Mad.). The Gujarat High Court in Amichand Investment (P.) Ltd. v. Dy. CIT (Asst.) [2008] 304 ITR 97 in the context of an issue relating to accounting of dividends for book profits tax found that the accounting treatment in Accounting Standard 13, could not be relied upon by revenue, since the assessment related to the year earlier to the effective date from which it became mandatory. There are a number of decisions of the Tribunal also, where accounting standards are relied upon by either party, whether assessee or revenue for their respective stand. Accounting standards 1 and 2 prescribed under section 145 of the Income-tax Act, 1961 are not materially different from International Accounting Standards or those issued by the Institute.

Corporate debtor failed to allot any plot to financial creditors. When financial creditors approached corporate debtor for payment of maturity value of investment, same was not paid. Corporate debtor submitted that there was delay in repayment as promised, since real estate market was in bad shape. However, debt was duly acknowledged by corporate debtor. Further, it did not raise any objection. In the receipt-cum-acceptance letter, it was stated on face of it, that these were for acquisitions and registrations of plots booked and maturity date of agreement was given as one year after date of registration and projected value was more than consideration value.

On these facts, the issue for the consideration of the NCLT was whether the buyers advancing the money came within the category of financial creditors entitled to invoke IBC for the recovery of the sums advanced. The Petitioner's case before the NCLT was that it was clear that under the garb of allotting land to the public, the respondent had been borrowing/accepting deposits/loans from the public by showing it as investment against property, i.e., by showing the depositors to register for plots of specific measurements and also showing the projected value of the said investment/deposit/borrowing on the maturity date. S.5(7) defines 'financial creditor' to mean a person to whom a financial debt is owed. Financial debt is defined in s.5(8) to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes, inter alia, any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing [clause (f) of s.5(8).

According to the NCLT, receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot were for/time value of money and have the commercial effect of borrowing and, hence, sub-sections (7) & (8) of s.5 apply and, hence, the petitioner is to be taken as financial creditor. In coming to this view, the NCLT relied on the decision of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLTA) in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL - AT) where the following decision was taken by the NCLTA:-

"….From the provisions of law and discussion as made and quoted above, we find following essential criterias, to be fulfilled for a creditor to come within the meaning of financial creditor:-

(i)

A person to whom a financial debt is owned and includes a person, whom such debt has been legally assigned transferred to;

(ii)

The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and include any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of s.5".

The NCLT thus, pronounced its decision as under:-

"In the present case, the receipt-cum-acceptance letters (Annexure-A-1 to A-4 of the application) on the face of it state that they are for acquisition of plot and registration for plot booked. However, the maturity date of agreement is given as one year after the date of registration and the projected value is given, which is more than the consideration value given. Therefore, the time value of money has been built in and it has to be presumed that the receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot, have the commercial effect of borrowing. In view of sub-ss.(7) & (8) of s.5 of the Code (supra), the petitioners are to be treated as financial creditors".

It may be stated in the context of this decision that in reply, the respondent did not raise any objection that the petitioners before NCLT are not financial creditors. Rather it specifically stated saying that "there is some delay on the corporate debtor's part in returning the amount of the financial creditor [emphasis is provided].

Hence, this decision may not be a binding authority to claim that a homebuyer comes in the category of 'financial creditor'.

9. 'Sachin Tendulkar' entitled to vacancy allowance as he failed to find tenant for vacant flat

[Sachin R. Tendulkar v. DCIT [2018] 96 taxmann.com 253 (Mumbai - Trib.)]

The Assessee, Mr. Sachin Tendulkar, owned two properties in Pune - Flat S and Flat T. Flat T was let out, however, Flat S was vacant for the whole year as suitable tenant couldn't be found. He claimed that the said flat had remained vacant throughout the year despite his reasonable effort to let out the same. In this regard, he submitted three letters written to the builder. In first letter, he thanked the builder for identifying the tenant for the flat at Flat T and also requested to identify tenant for Flat S. Subsequently, the assessee had written second letter and after that third letter being reminders for identifying the tenant to let out Flat S.

Therefore, he claimed vacancy allowance under Section 23(1)(c) for Flat S and declared nil income. During the course of assessment proceedings, the Assessing Officer made additions for the notional rental income from Flat S, which was also upheld by the CIT(A).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee when same builder had helped the assessee to find tenant for another flat, it couldn't be said that these letters to the same builder to help him identify one more tenant, to be considered as fake, defied logic. Therefore, if a property was held with an intention to let out in the relevant year coupled with efforts made for letting it out, the same would fall within the purview of section 23(1)(c).

10. Sum received on relinquishment of 'right to sue' is non-taxable capital receipt: ITAT

[Bhojison Infrastructure (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 99 taxmann.com 26 (Ahmedabad - Trib.)]

The assessee-company entered into a development agreement by virtue of which a right in land was created in its favour by owner of land. Assessee's case was that despite development agreement entered into by landlord, the landlord had decided to sell said land to other parties. The assessee filed a suit in the Courts of law for specific performance of pre-emptive right to purchase the land. Later on, it received damages from the potential purchaser for relinquishment of 'right to sue' in the Courts of law for breach of development agreement. The assessee claimed that 'right to sue' was a personal right which would not fall within sweep of definition of 'capital asset' under section 2(14). Consequently, damages received from potential purchaser were treated as non-taxable capital receipts.

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

The essence of long list of judicial pronouncements cited by assessee was that section 6 of the Transfer of Property Act which uses the same expression 'property of any kind' in the context of transferability makes an exception in the case of a mere right to sue. The decisions thereunder make it abundantly clear that the 'right to sue' for damages is not an actionable claim. It cannot be assigned. Transfer of such a right is opposed to public policy as it tantamount to gambling in litigation.

Hence, such a 'right to sue' does not constitute a 'capital asset ' which, in turn, has to be 'an interest in property of any kind'. Despite the definition of expression 'capital asset ' in the widest possible terms in Section 2(14), a right to a capital asset must fall within the expression 'property of any kind' subject to certain exclusions.

Notwithstanding widest import assigned to the term 'property' which signifies every possible interest which a person can hold and enjoy, the ' right to sue' was a right in personam and such right could certainly not be transferred. In order to attract the charge of tax on capital gains, the sine qua non is that the receipt must have originated in a 'transfer ' within the meaning of section 45, read with section 2(47) of I-T Act. In the absence of its transferability, damages received by assessee couldn't be assessed as capital gains.

I have been quoted repeatedly by some of the valuable speakers that judges are not expected to know everything. I had said this in a different context. Unfortunately, today the context is different. Many of us today have discussed tax abuse and tax avoidance. All these are concepts. But what I have learnt in the past 22 years in the primary function of all constitutions in the world, which is the basic law of the country, is that the rule of interpretation is the most important doctrine and most important law which every judge must understand and must apply. Now let me give you an example: If you are reading the Constitution of India, the words used are double textual like "complete justice" and "common good". These are open textual words and we judges are required to interpret those words in the widest possible terms. Let me give you an another example: In the past we had to go strictly by form and not substance. 19. Excess share premium not taxable in hands of closely held co. if its shareholders are relatives: ITAT

[Vaani Estates (P.) Ltd. v. ITO [2018] 98 taxmann.com 92 (Chennai - Trib.)] The assessee-company had only two shareholders 'S' and her husband. On passing away of husband, his shares devolved on their daughter 'V'. The assessee proposed to acquire an immovable property at approximately Rs. 23.09 crores. 'S' brought in money into the company in lieu of allotment of fresh 10,100 shares with a share premium of Rs. 23.31 crores.

The Assessing Officer opined that company had received excess price/share premium for the shares allotted to 'S' over and above the face value of shares. Accordingly, he brought Rs. 23.31 crores to tax in the hands of the company under Section 56(2)(viib).

The ITAT held in favour of assessee as under:

When 'S' introduced money into the company for allotment of shares at an exorbitant premium in contrast to its intrinsic value of just Rs. 10 per share, the benefit of such investment had only passed on to her daughter because there were only two shareholders in the company at that point of time. Had 'S' gifted the money to her daughter 'V' and thereafter if daughter had brought the same into the company for allotment of equity shares at face value, question of invoking of the provisions of section 56(2)(viib) would not have arisen.

Provisions of section 56(2)(viib) couldn't be invoked in the case of the assessee-co. because by virtue of introducing cash in the company by 'S' for allotment of equity shares with unrealistic premium the benefit had only passed on to her daughter 'V' and there was no scope in the Act to tax when cash or asset was transferred by a mother to her daughter.

During the course of assessment proceedings, assessee claimed that Article 6 of India-UAE tax treaty doesn't expressly recognize the right of the resident State to tax the income from immovable property situated in the source State. 21. Australia has taxing rights under Australia-India DTAA even if there is no provision in its domestic law: Australian Court

[Satyam Computer Services Ltd. (Now Tech Mahindra Limited) v. Commissioner of Taxation [2018] 98 taxmann.com 358 (FC-Australia)]

The Applicant, Tech Mahindra, had offices in Sydney and Melbourne through which it provided software products and information technology services to entities in Australia. Payments received by applicant for the services provided in Australia by the employees located in India were treated as 'Royalties' as per Article 12(3)(g) of the Australia-India DTAA .

Applicant argued that, though Australia was allocated the right to tax the 'Royalties' by the Indian Agreement but it could only exercise that right if it had the right to impose tax on those amounts under Australia's domestic law. As of now, the domestic law does not give any right to Australia to tax such income.

The Federal Court of Australia held as under:

The language of Article 23 should be given effect to according to its terms and the context. Article 23 provides that that income derived by a resident of one contracting States may be deemed to be income from sources in other contracting state for purpose of law of that other State. Therefore, royalty income was to be included in the applicant's assessable income because it was income from an Australian source by reason of Article 23 of the Australia-India DTAA. The Court rejected the argument that the tax treaties can only be used as shields not swords. It held that the tax treaties also provide standalone taxing power and independent imposing of tax to a particular income.

(2) The TPO, not an expert on valuation, is bound to refer the valuation report to Departmental Valuation Officer as per the procedure laid down in the statute

During the assessment proceedings for Assessment Year (AY) 2006-07, the TPO observed that taxpayer has incurred certain expenditure towards purchase of fixed assets (including two second hand machineries). The taxpayer submitted a report from the approved valuer in U.S. to justify the ALP of these two machineries. TPO was of the view that the valuer has not provided the basis for arriving at the valuation and proceeded to make an adjustment to the extent of 50 per cent of the value of the second hand machinery. Further, the taxpayer paid certain amounts on account of a cost sharing arrangement wherein the AE was reimbursed the actual cost incurred. The TPO determined the ALP of the transaction at 'nil' stating that the information submitted by the taxpayer is incomplete. The DRP upheld the aforesaid disallowances.

Tribunal ruling

Purchase of second hand machineries

TPO was duty bound to refer the valuation of the machineries to the DVO as per the procedure laid down under the statutory provisions, before rejecting the valuation report from the approved valuer indicating the fair market value of machineries purchased. TPO, not being an expert to determine the value of machineries, could not have quantified the value of the machineries at 50 per cent of the value shown by the taxpayer in the absence of any enquiry made by him to ascertain the fair market value of such machineries.

TPO is bound to determine the ALP by applying any of the methods prescribed under section 92C of the Act. However, the TPO has determined the ALP on ad hoc basis.

TPO failed to refer the valuation to the DVO and proceeded to quantify the value of the machineries at 50 per cent in violation of the statutory provisions of the Act. Therefore, the matter could not be restored back to the TPO. Tribunal deleted the adjustment on account of disallowance of 50 per cent of purchase value of second hand machineries.

Cost sharing arrangement

TPO failed to demonstrate what information was required from the taxpayer to establish that the payments made were for availing of services from the AE. The determination of ALP at 'nil' without applying the method prescribed under the statutory provisions is legally unsustainable.

The Tribunal observed that the TPO in the AY 2007-08, disallowed 20 per cent of the total cost incurred by the taxpayer towards such services which demonstrated that the TPO had accepted that the AE has provided certain services to the taxpayer and the taxpayer has availed such services in the subsequent year. Thus, Tribunal deleted the adjustment.

This ruling reiterates the fundamental principle that the TPO can proceed to make an adjustment only based on substantive evidence or material on record and not on ad hoc basis. The TPO is not allowed to reject the valuation report of an approved valuer as he is not an expert and as provided under the statute, needs to refer the valuation to the DVO. This decision is expected to go a long way in providing relief to those taxpayers who obtain and furnish genuine valuation reports issued by experts to determine the ALP.

into account. It is a well-accepted proposition that for the purpose of ascertaining profits and gains, the ordinary principles of commercial accounting should be applied so long as they do not conflict with any express provision of the relevant statutes. The above rule will apply only where there is no definition or other provision to the contrary in the statute - CIT v. U.P. State Industrial Development Corpn. [1997] 225 ITR 703 / 92 Taxman 45 (SC). On the other hand, in another case a company had deposited its surplus funds during its pre-production period and earned interest thereon. The company claimed that such receipts must go to reduce the cost of the project. In its stand the assessee relied on the guidance notes issued by the Institute of Chartered Accountants of India explaining the accounting practice to be followed in respect of pre-production receipts and expenses. There is no specific provision in the statute dealing which such receipts or expenditure. One would have expected that the principle enunciated in the Challapalli Sugar Mills Ltd.’s case (supra) referred to above should have been applied. However, the Supreme Court held that the interest income on surplus funds invested prior to commencement of production is taxable under the head ‘Other sources’. The Court observed that the accountants might have taken some other view, but accounting practice was not necessarily good law - Tuticorin Alkali Chemicals & Fertilizers Ltd. v. CIT [1997] 227 ITR 172/ 93 Taxman 502 (SC). In fact the observation of the Apex Court is not without a parallel. In the case of B.S.C. Footwear Ltd. v. Ridgway (Inspector of Taxes) [1970] 77 ITR 857 (CA) (which was later upheld by the House of Lords in B.S.C. Footwear Ltd. v. Ridgway (Inspector of Taxes) [1972] 83 ITR 269) Russel, LJ. of the Court of Appeal observed while rejecting the argument based on well-settled accounting practice that the income-tax law does not march step by step in the divergent foot step of the accounting profession. Lord Morris of the House of Lords held that ‘whatever merits there may be in the company’s accounting methods for the purpose of its internal affairs, I am not persuaded that Cross, J. and the Court of Appeal were wrong in finding these unacceptable for tax purposes’. Here accounting practice received a severe jolt as it were and the revenue view was upheld.

State Bank of Travancore v. CIT [1986] 158 ITR 102 / 24 Taxman 337 (SC) is a case where the Bank credited the interest accrued on sticky loans to an ‘Interest Suspense Account’ and claimed it as not taxable. The Supreme Court held that where an income has accrued and in a given circumstance the amount had been taken to a suspense account for accounting purposes, that would not affect its taxability as such. Similarly, an auctioneer collected sales-tax in addition to commission on auctioned goods and credited the sales-tax received to a separate account. It was neither refunded to the customers nor paid over to the Government. The Supreme Court held that it is the true nature and quality of the receipt and not the head under which it is entered in the account books as would prove decisive. If a receipt were a trading receipt, the fact that it is not so shown in the account books of the assessee would not prevent the assessing authority from treating it as a trading receipt - Chowringhee Sales Bureau (P.) Ltd. v. CIT [1973] 87 ITR 542 (SC). A similar view was expressed in Punjab Distilling Industries Ltd. v. CIT [1959] 35 ITR 519 (SC).

In yet another case, an assessee entered into an agreement for purchase of a property. The vendor sold the property to a third party. The assessee filed a suit for specific performance. The High Court upheld the verdict of the trial court to grant mesne profits. The trial court ordered compensation in the account year 1962-63. The amount was actually received in the account year 1963-64. The ITO assessed it in the assessment year 1964-65. The first appellate authority held that it was assessable in the 1963-64 assessment year. The Tribunal held that it was assessable in the year of agreement for sale, viz., 1959-60. The High Court upheld the view that it was assessable in 1963-64 assessment year when the compensation was quantified and the assessee got the right to receive the same. In this judgment, the High Court observed that the question of accrual or non-accrual of income and the subsidiary question of time of accrual of income have to be decided only on fiscal principles and not on the basis of any given accounting method which is in vogue or which might be practised by the assessee - CIT v. P. Mariappa Gounder [1984] 147 ITR 676/ 17 Taxman 292 (Mad.).

Attribution of income taxable under section 67(10)87 to capital assets remaining with the specified entity, under section 7288.

[R. 8AB of the 1962 Rules]

50. (1) For the purposes of section 72(5)89, the amount chargeable to income-tax as income of specified entity under section 67(10)87, shall be attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in the manner provided in this rule.

(2) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, chargeable to tax under section 67(10)87 relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90 shall be—

A= B×(C/D).

Where,—

A= the amount attributable to the capital asset remaining with the specified entity for purpose of section 72(5)90;

B= amount charged under section 67(10)91;

C= increase in, or recognition of, value of the asset remaining with the specified entity, because of revaluation or valuation; and

D= aggregate of increase in, or recognition of, value of all assets because of the revaluation or valuation.

(3) Where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, is in excess of the balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 does not relates to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(4) Irrespective of anything contained in sub-rule (2) or sub-rule (3), where the aggregate of the value of money and the fair market value of the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, in excess of balance in his capital account, charged to tax under section 67(10)91 relate only to the capital asset received by the specified person from the specified entity, the amount charged to tax under section 67(10)91 shall not be attributed to any capital asset for the purposes of section 72(5)90.

(5) The specified entity shall furnish the details of amount attributed to capital asset remaining with the specified entity in Form No. 2792.

(6) The person who is authorised to verify the return of income of the specified entity under section 26593 shall verify Form No. 2792.

(7) Form No. 2792 shall be furnished on or before the due date referred to in section 263(1)(c)94 for the tax year in which the amount is chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91.

(8) For the purposes of this rule,—

(a)

the amount chargeable to tax under section 67(10)91 shall relate to revaluation of any capital asset or valuation of self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, of the specified entity, if the revaluation is based on a valuation report obtained from a registered valuer as defined in rule 56(f)95;

(b)

the specified entity shall not be entitled for the depreciation on—

(i)

the increase in value of an asset on account of its revaluation; or

(ii)

the recognition of the value of a self-generated asset or self-generated goodwill, due to its valuation; and

(c)

the expressions "self-generated asset" and "self-generated goodwill" shall have the meanings respectively assigned to them in section 67(11)(b)96.

(i)

one per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount up to one lakh rupees, subject to a minimum amount of two hundred and fifty rupees;

(ii)

one thousand rupees and half of a per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding one lakh rupees and up to ten lakh rupees; and

(iii)

five thousand and five hundred rupees and one tenth of a per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding ten lakh rupees, subject to a maximum amount of sixty thousand rupees.

the gross premium charged from a policy holder reduced by the amount allocated for investment, or savings on behalf of the policy holder, if such an amount is intimated to the policy holder at the time of supply of service;
