in case of single premium annuity policies other than (a), ten per cent. of single premium charged from the policy holder; or

in all other cases, twenty five per cent. of the premium charged from the policy holder in the first year and twelve and a half per cent. of the premium charged from the policy holder in subsequent years:

HEADNOTE: Section  5(8), read with section  3(12), of the Insolvency and Bankruptcy Code, 2016 -  Corporate insolvency resolution process -  Financial debt - Applicant - financial creditor claimed that it had disbursed a loan to corporate debtor - On corporate debtor’s failure to pay, an application under section 7 was filed against corporate debtor - It was noted that there was no credible evidence to establish that alleged disbursal was made against time value of money (an essential element for qualifying a claim as a ‘financial debt’ under Section 5(8)) - Transaction in question neither involved any stipulated interest component nor any contractual arrangement indicating accrual of financial gain, return, or profit to alleged Financial Creditor - Furthermore, there were no agreed terms of repayment, nor was there any contemporaneous communication or correspondence evidencing a request for a loan or acknowledgment of such a financial arrangement - Whether in absence of foundational elements, disbursal lacked commercial character necessary to constitute a financial debt under IBC - Held, yes - Whether application under Section 7 was barred by limitation as purported recall of an alleged loan was made nearly 17 years after its initial disbursal - Held, yes - Whether in absence of a categorical admission, a time-barred claim could not be revived - Held, yes - Whether financial creditor had failed to demonstrate, with cogent evidence, existence of a legally enforceable financial debt as defined under Section 5(8) and correspondingly, had not substantiated occurrence of a default as per Section 3(12), and, therefore, instant application was to be dismissed - Held, yes [Paras 14, 16, 22 and 24]

FACT: ■

The applicant- financial creditor claimed that it had extended a loan to the Corporate Debtor during the period from 13.06.2007 to 27.03.2009. The said loan was extended in his personal capacity and was repayable on demand.

■

Corporate Debtor had consistently acknowledged the said loan in its Audited Financial Statements over the years, classifying it as an “Unsecured Loan”.

■

A loan recall notice was issued by the financial creditor on 04.07.2022 demanding immediate repayment of the full outstanding loan. A reminder for payment was further issued via email on 01.08.2022. In response to the aforementioned notice, the Corporate Debtor, through its Financial Controller acknowledged the communication and expressed an intention to amicably settle the matter. Since no steps were taken by the Corporate Debtor to repay the debt a legal notice was issued by the financial creditor.

■

Thus, financial creditor filed instant petition under section 7 to initiate CIRP against corporate debtor for the alleged default on the part of the corporate debtor in repayment of financial debt.

■

The Corporate Debtor raised a dispute that the application under Section 7 was barred by limitation, as the alleged financial debt was stated to have arisen in the year 2005-06, and the demand was purportedly made for the first time in July 2022- after a lapse of nearly 17 years. The corporate debtor argued that such a stale claim could not be revived by unilateral recall or reliance upon self-serving accounting entries. Further, it was contended that the application failed to satisfy the statutory preconditions of Section 7.

■

The corporate debtor also claimed that financial creditor had failed to produce any loan agreement, repayment schedule, or even a basic acknowledgment of terms such as interest, tenure, or security. No board resolution or authorization was passed by corporate debtor to borrow funds from the financial creditor. The absence of any documentation, along with the lack of demand for repayment for nearly two decades, was said to indicate that the financial creditor never extended any loan capable of forming a financial debt.

HELD: ■

The Financial Creditor has pleaded that the loan advanced by him was a loan recallable on demand and qualifies as a financial debt under Section 5 (8). He has further pleaded that even though the loan was interest-free but qualified as disbursal against time value of money. (Para 11)

■

In order for an interest-free debt to qualify as financial debt, an financial creditor must show that the funds were disbursed with ‘consideration for time value of money’. The question of what constitutes ‘time value of money’ varies depending on the facts and circumstances; nonetheless, the financial creditor must demonstrate that it had an interest in the subject matter for which the loan was disbursed and was profiting from it. The pre-requisite is disbursal of money to the borrower for utilization by the borrower and that the disbursal must be against consideration for time value of money even if it is not interest bearing. (Para 13)

■

In terms of clause 5(8), if disbursement is made for consideration of time value of money, a person can claim to be a financial creditor with regard to amount paid. [Para 5]

Admittedly the appellant, has disbursed the amount for consideration of time value of money in favour of borrower, and not to the builder. Therefore, the Adjudicating Authority has rightly held that respondent is not the corporate debtor of the appellant and the application under section 7 is not maintainable. [Para 6]

Agreement' dated 21-11-2012 do not contemplated refund of the advance paid and resultantly, there was no understanding as to interest payable on refund thereof or any other form of 'time value of money' being consideration.

14. The Learned Counsel for the 'Appellant' refers to the Judgment of the Hon'ble Supreme Court in Anuj Jain v Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656 wherein at paragraph 46 it is observed as under: 46. "Applying the aforementioned fundamental principles to the definition occurring in Section 5(8) of the Code, we have not an iota of doubt that for a debt to become 'financial debt' for the purpose of part II of the Code, the basic elements are that, it ought to be a disbursal against the consideration for time value of money. It may include any of the methods for raising money or incurring liability by the modes prescribed in clauses (a) to (f) of Section 5(8); it may also include any derivative transaction or counter-indemnity obligation as per clauses (g) and (h) of Section 5(8); and it may also be the amount of any liability in respect of any of the guarantee or indemnity for any of the items referred to in clauses (a) to (h). The requirement of existence of a debt which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, in our view, remains an essential part even in respect of any of the transactions/dealings stated in clauses (a) to (i) of Section 5(8), even if it is not necessarily stated therein. In any case, the definition, by its very frame, cannot be read so expansive, rather infinitely wide, that the root requirements of disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money could be forsaken in the manner that any transaction could stand alone to become a financial debt. In other words, any of the transactions stated in the said clauses (a) to (i) of Section 5(8) would be falling within the ambit of 'financial debt' only if it carries the essential elements stated in the principal clause or at least has the features which could be trace to such essential elements in the principal clause. In yet other words, the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as 'financial debt' within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code. This debt may be of any nature but a part of it is always required to be carrying, or corresponding to, or at least having some traces of disbursal against consideration for the time value of money."

15. In effect, the submission of the Learned Counsel for the 'Appellant' is that an advance of Rs. 1,00,00,000/- which was paid by the 'Respondent' in terms of the 'Share Purchase Agreement' was not disbursed against the consideration for 'time value of money' and was merely an advance for purchase of Shares.

16. The Learned Counsel for the 'Appellant' points out the Judgment of this 'Tribunal' in the matter of Pushpa Shah (supra) wherein at paragraph 18 it is observed as under:

18. "On careful reading of the agreement such as 'SPA' and 'La-Fin LoU', we find that the 'IL & FS Financial Services Limited', (financial creditor) has disbursed the amount and the 'Corporate Debtor' has raised the amount with an object of having economic gain or commercial effect of borrowing. The clauses of 'SPA' if read along with the 'LoU', we find that the terms of transaction involved not only the purchase of shares but it shows the date by which the amount of transaction was to be repaid by the 'Corporate Debtor' which had fallen due on 19th August, 2012. There was an element of 'time value of money', particularly, when one of the conditions related to 'internal rate of return of 15%' on the transaction, therefore, the time value of money having already shown, we hold that the amount disbursed by 'IL & FS Financial Services Limited'- (financial creditor) and the 'Corporate Debtor' had agreed to reverse the transaction by purchasing the shares within a specified time along with the payment of 15% accrual on 20th August, 2009. We hold that the amount if disbursed by 'IL & FS Financial Services Limited' - (financial creditor) comes within the meaning of 'financial debt' therefore, the 'IL & FS Financial Services Limited'- (financial creditor) has been rightly claimed to be a 'financial creditor' and filed Form-1 under section 7 of the 'I&B Code'.

17. The Learned Counsel for the 'Appellant' emphatically points out that what is significant for the purpose of Section 5(8) of the Code, is the 'nature of debt' at the time of 'disbursal' and as such, placing reliance by the Respondent, upon the 'subsequent communications' between the parties whereby the 'Appellant' had purportedly agreed to refund the money with interest is a misplaced one.

5(8) of the Code referred to the Black's Law Dictionary 10th Edition which provides that "disbursement means money paid for the settlement of a debt or for a particular purpose". The Court had applied the same interpretation while dealing with the above-said case and concluded that the "disbursement against consideration for the time value of money" means that the money has been disbursed from the creditor, i.e., it is no longer with the loan giver, and is with the debtor. At the same time, the Court in the same case interpreted "Time Value of Money" and reference was made to Dictionary of Banking (2nd Edition) by Thomas P. Fitch which means the value of payment at present and payment due and payable in future which is discounted by the compounded interest. It also provides that the time value of money is the difference in the value to be received today as compared to a greater value to be received in future. Also, the Insolvency Law Committee Report2 has the time value of money which means the compensation for the duration for which the money has been disbursed by the creditor to the debtor which can be in form of either interest or factoring of discount in payment. Further, in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 78 taxmann.com 302/140 SCL 135 (NCLT - New Delhi), the Appellate Tribunal referred to the Black's Law Dictionary, 9th Edition to construe the meaning of time value of money and concluded that it is the compensation or the price paid for the time during which the money was disbursed, i.e., the time between lending and repayment.

Time Value of Money a Prerequisite of Financial Debt

Below-mentioned is the judgments of the Supreme Court, NCLAT and the NCLT highlighting the "consideration for the time value of money" as an essential part of the financial debt.

1.

Pioneer Urban Land & Infrastructure Ltd. (supra) (Pioneer's case): The Supreme Court stated that the disbursal and consideration for the time value of money are the essential constituents of financial debt without which the application under section 7 of the IBC remains incomplete.

2.

State Bank of India v. Rajendra Bhuta, IRP of Prabhat Technologies (India) Limited (IA No. 440 of 2020, dated 6-1-2021] in C.P. No. 1874/MB/2019): The NCLT Mumbai Bench while dealing with the question of terming a Forward Purchase Agreement (FPA) under the category of financial debt or not and observed that in order to categorise a debt as financial debt, it necessarily has to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Further, if an FPA is to be termed as financial debt it has to have two attributes, i.e., a) should be against consideration for the time value of money and, b) should have the commercial effect of borrowing. The AA held that the transaction entered into by the parties was a mere sale and purchase agreement and should not come within the definition of financial debt.

3.

K. N. Mahesh Prasad v. Medinnbelle Herbalcare (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT) (Insolvency) No. 512 of 2019, dated 22-1-2020]: The NCLAT upheld the decision of the AA which dismissed the application of the creditor stating that the transaction in the case in hand was a simple loan agreement which is denuded of any element of the time value of money and won't constitute a financial debt.

4.

Indiabulls Housing Finance Ltd. v. Rudra Buildwell Projects (P.) Ltd . [2019] 108 taxmann.com 57/155 SCL 32 (NCL-AT): An appeal was filed by the Appellant stating that it had given loans to the borrower vide loan agreement dated 6-4-2015. A subsequent agreement was entered into by the Respondent and the borrower wherein it was agreed that the interest for the former agreement shall be paid by the Respondent on behalf of the borrower. On default on repayment of the same, the FC filed an application under section 7 against the Respondent. The NCLAT dismissed the application highlighting the fact that though the disbursement of the loan was made against the consideration for the time value of money and the creditor was the FC still the application won't be accepted as the disbursement was made in favour of the borrower and not the Respondent.

Critical Analysis of the Supreme Court's Judgment in the Orator's case.

Considering the Orator's judgment by the Supreme Court in the light of various judgments and points discussed above, the authors vehemently states that the judgment has not removed the black cloud over the issue of interest not being an essential part of financial debt. Instead, it has brought forward various ambiguous points, upon which a necessary deliberation is required. Firstly , as observed from various judgments of the Supreme Court and the NCLAT, it can be concluded that the time value of money is the most important and quintessential part of the financial debt without which an application under section 7 will not get admitted. It is also evident from the various definitions as referred above that the time value of money includes the interest component, and is the difference between the present values of payment and the payment due and payable in future discounted by compound interest. Hence, for a debt to be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money, it needs to have an interest component in it. Further, as can be seen from the Insolvency Committee Report, 2018, the time value of money has two components, i.e., interest or factoring in discount of payment. Though, the Supreme Court has clarified that the word "interest" before the phrase "if any" under the definition of financial debt is not required to file a case under section 7 if there is no interest attached to the loan, however, a lot of clarity is required upon the component of interest which also exist in the phrase "time value of money". Thus, it can be said that the consideration for the time value of money under section 5(8) also includes interest as a major component. Hence, in the humble submission of the authors, the interest constituent is necessary for a debt to qualify as financial debt and the ratio in the case of Narendra Kumar Agarwal v. Monotrone Leasing Private Limited should be taken into consideration which provides that the interest component in a transaction is the time value of money.

Secondly , seeing the factual matrix of the present case in hand, the Appellant/FC in its application has mentioned Rs. 1.56 cr as the total default by the CD. Here, it is important to bring to the notice that the total loan amount sanctioned was Rs. 1.60 cr out of which the CD had only paid Rs. 4 lakhs, thereby making default on Rs. 1.56 cr. Although the loan disbursed was interest-free, the Supreme Court didn't take notice of the same and allowed the application to be admitted in which only the principal amount was given, the principal amount was partly paid, and application was also filed for the principal amount without any interest, thereby implying that the amount disbursed was not in consideration against the time value of money.

Thirdly , the Supreme Court has failed to deliberate upon the point basing which the NCLAT had given its judgment, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money is for the benefits of the FC and not the CD. The Supreme Court has unforeseen this aspect of the judgment by the NCLAT. In the present case, there was no consideration for the time value of money for the FC as the loan agreement was interest-free and the CD was only liable to repay the principal amount even after maturity of the contract, i.e., only Rs. 1.56 cr. Also, the Supreme Court in the case of Pioneer's case has held that the definition of financial debt under section 5(8) should be read as "means and includes" thereby providing an extensive meaning to the definition. This means that clauses (a) to (i) under section 5(8) is an extension of the definition of financial debt and is not an exhaustive list and thus, the substantial part of the definition cannot be ignored. In the present case, the Supreme Court is only putting its reliance on the clause (f) of Section 5 which provides for commercial effect of borrowing but is completing ignoring the principal/substantial part of the definition which provides for the component of time value of money in the financial debt. Hence, the Appellant should not be termed as FC by the Supreme Court and his application should have been rejected.

Conclusion

From the point of view of the authors, it is evident that the Supreme Court's decision in Orator's case can have negative implications as the Court has predominantly based its reasoning taking into consideration Section 5(8)(f) of the IBC only and have ignored the principal aspect of the definition of financial debt, i.e., the consideration for the time value of money. This obstinate view of the Court has created ambiguity and vagueness in the understanding of the substantial part of the definition of financial debt and hence, a much-needed clarification is required on interest being an essential constituent of "time value of money".

Section 5 (8)4 of the Code, defines "financial debt" as a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and include any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing. The bench observed that the allottees/ homebuyers were already included in the provision, thus the amendment was a merely an elucidation. In response to an argument from the petitioner that at the best, real estate developers were operational debtors and not financial debtors, the Court made many points of distinction; first one being that in case a real estate developer takes money in advance from allottees/ homebuyers for the construction of the building. Additionally, operational creditors do not concern themselves with the financial health of the Corporate Debtor. Whereas, a home allottees/ homebuyers is extremely concerned with the fact that whether the Corporate Debtor is financially sound or not, as it plays an imperative role in the final product of a real estate project, namely a house. The bench further remarked that payments that are made in advance for goods and services are not utilized in manufacture or production of such goods or services. Goods or Services provided to the Debtor contain no consideration for time value of money; the consideration being the goods or services themselves. In case of allottees/ homebuyers in a real estate project, the money raised from allottee/ homebuyer for the time value of money. The concept of Time value of money essentially says that "money available at the present time is worth more than the identical sum in the future due to its potential earning capacity. This core principle of finance holds that provided money can earn interest, any amount of money is worth more the sooner it is received."5 Allottees/ homebuyers invest in real estate primarily because of two reasons; either they see it as an investment that could benefit them in future; or for residential needs; or both of these reasons. Just because payment in case of a real estate project is made in instalments does not render it as operational debt. The Court made a reference to a previous NCLAT judgement Nikhil Mehta & Sons (HUF) v. AMR Infrastructures Ltd. [2018] 94 taxmann.com 131/148 SCL 221 (NCLT - New Delhi) wherein it was held that amounts raised by developers under assured return schemes had the "commercial effect of a borrowing". A major reason for concern of the Real Estate Developer was raised, that the Code be misused to blackmail and divert funds that are to be used for real estate development. This could result in winding up of a perfectly solvent company or worse dormancy of the project in case of non-approval of Resolution plan, at the instance of one allottees/ homebuyers. It was one of the contentions that the developer had obtained foreign funding and wasn't utilizing the funds paid by allottees/ homebuyers and so the money advance was not debt as there was no "borrowing". The Court also relied upon the Insolvency Committee Report to come to the conclusion that "amounts raised under the contracts of home buyers are in effect for the purposes of raising finance, and are a means of raising finance. Thus, the Committee deemed it prudent to clarify that such amounts raised under a real estate project from a home buyer fall within entry (f) of Section 5(8)."6 Further, it may be noted that the amount of money given by home buyers as advances for their purchase is usually very high, and frequent delays in delivery of possession may thus, have a huge impact. For instance, in Chitra Sharma v. Union of India [2017] 85 taxmann.com 209/144 SCL 1 (SC).the amount of debts owed to home buyers, which was paid by them as advances, was claimed to be Fifteen Thousand Crore, more than what was due to banks. It was noticed that the Assessing Officer had specifically proposed to treat the amount as the assessee company's income,as was seen from the assessment order itself. However, it could not have been treated as an unexplained cash credit or as an unexplained investment; since it was neither. The source was clear and there was proper explanation for the amount as seen from the books of account. Under the Act, the proposal is essentially to assess a particular amount, as income, which the assessee has not reckoned as such in its return. To propose under one head of income and in scrutiny or a reassessment to finalise under another head is perfectly permissible. [Para 9]

The further question is whether there was any possibility of it being recovered. If the recovery had been barred by limitation,necessarily, it has to be treated as an income from the business and the same had to be assessed under the Act. Even if the deviation from the proposal is found to be improper, the assessment has to be sustained, as an income from business; which was the original proposal. If the other company had occupied the premises the amounts would definitely be shown as income from business. [Para 10]

With respect to the contention of limitation having not expired in the relevant previous year, it is to be noticed that the assessment itself was finalised after three years, which was normal period of limitation for recovery of money, even calculated from the date on which the last refund was made. The assessee had also not produced any agreement and in all possibility there would have been a restrictive clause, insofar as forfeiture of the advance amounts, if the contract did not fructify. The assessment order itself was passed, after three years from the date of commencement of limitation and there was no claim made by the assessee, who participated in the assessment proceedings, as to any recovery proceedings having been commenced by the other company or a repayment having been effected.

In the said circumstances, though the treatment of the amounts as an unexplained investment or an unexplained cash credit cannot be approved, the assessment has to be upheld as an income from business. The questions stand answered accordingly and the appeal stands allowed, restoring the order of the Assessing Officer; but however making modification as herein, assessing the rent received in advance as income in the relevant previous year. In Madras Industrial Development Corpn. v. CIT [1997] 225 ITR 802 / 91 Taxman 340 the liability of the company with reference to the debentures existed for a span of 12 years. It was in the light of the subsistence of the corresponding liability for the 12 year period that the Supreme Court had held that the discount paid for selling those debentures had to be divided proportionately for the entire span of 12 years and the per year deduction should be on that pro rata basis. It was on the basis of the principle of ‘matching liability’ that the Supreme Court had held in that case that the assessee was entitled to claim a pro rata deduction of the discount element suffered by the company in issuing the debentures. The above ratio declared by the Supreme Court would not help the case of the assessee here. By exercising the option to receive the interest in lumpsum at a discounted rate, the assessee had foregone its right to receive the interest for the remaining two years. The assessee had no right at all for any interest for the remaining two years. When no such right to receive the interest existed for those two years, correspondingly there was no question of interest accruing or being received for those two years. Here, it was not a case of ‘interest received in advance’. It was a case of interest received at discounted rate. The right of the assessee to receive the interest for the future years was liquidated. Therefore, it was not possible for the assessee to divide the interest in three parts and offer only one part for assessment in the first year.

Hence, the Assessing Officer’s action was to be upheld, and the revenue’s appeal to be allowed.

However, by virtue of the amendment introduced by the Finance Act, 2016, specific time limits have been prescribed. In one contingency, the limitation is three months from the end of the month in which the order of the Tribunal is received, and in another, it is nine months. The assessee-company was in the business of selling timeshare units in its various resorts. During relevant assessment years, the assessee collected revenue from timeshare members but same was not recognised as revenue for the current year. The explanation of the assessee was that it had considered only 40 per cent of the membership fees collected as income and the balance 60 per cent was treated as deferred income. It was stated that the balance amount was to be spread over the next 33 years during which the assessee was expected to provide timeshare facilities to the members. It was also stated that in order to provide various facilities during the next 33 years, it had to incur many costs. Further explanation of the assessee was that the AMC was exclusively meant to cover the maintenance of various facilities which were an integral part of the timeshare property. These charges were for the maintenance of various electronic gadgets made available in the accommodation, furniture, kitchen equipments, central air-conditioning etc. On the other hand, the consideration for future obligations received in the initial stages was towards transfer facility from one resort to another, split, accumulation and advancing facility, domestic and international exchange, transmission, upgradation etc. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee was following mercantile system of accounting and, hence, income had to be accounted for on accrual basis. He was of the view that the receipt was undisputedly income as the assessee itself had shown it as deferred income. However, the Act does not recognise the concept of deferred income and, hence, the assessee’s explanation could not be accepted. Considering all these aspects, the Assessing Officer added certain amount being 60 per cent of the receipts shown by the assessee as advance subscription. On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the assessee had to construct holiday resorts and provide timeshare facilities over a period of time. Further, the annual subscription fee collected met only the maintenance of the resorts. The utility charges collected ‘were as per actual consumption of things like electricity, water etc. It did not cover major renovation and repairs. The Commissioner (Appeals) also took note of the fact that over a period of 24 years, the assessee had to incur about 171 per cent of the original investment for major renovation and replacement of assets. Accordingly, he upheld the contentions of the assessee and deleted the addition in all the years.

CHAPTER 3

ESSENTIAL ELEMENTS OF FINANCIAL DEBT 3.1 Disbursement of Money

The first essential element of financial debt is disbursement. Disbursement refers to the transfer of money from the creditor to the debtor. Financial debt must involve the actual disbursal of funds, which creates a liability on the borrower. Without such disbursement, the transaction cannot ordinarily qualify as financial debt.

3.2Consideration for Time Value of Money

The time value of money is the most important characteristic of financial debt. It reflects the principle that money today is worth more than the same amount in the future. The elements generally are:

Interest payments

Financial returns

Compensation for delayed repayment

In the absence of such consideration, the transaction may not qualify as financial debt.

In the matter of Shivam Agrioils (P.) Ltd. v. Shree Krishna Vanaspati Industries (P.) Ltd. [Company Appeal (AT)(Insolvency) No. 982 of 2022] NCLAT observed that Interest on loan is not the only binding criterion for determining the time value of money for Financial Debt under IBC.

Whether disbursement for the time value of money is an essential ingredient to prove a Financial Debt? – Kesoram Industries Ltd. v. Pratim Bayal [2024] 159 taxmann.com 27 (NCLAT - New Delhi)

Hon'ble NCLAT held that: Disbursement against the consideration for the time value of money has to be proved for a financial debt. There is no disbursement by the Appellant to the Corporate Debtor. When there is no disbursement for the time value of money, essential ingredients to prove a financial debt are missing.

3.3 Commercial Effect of Borrowing

Section 5(8) also includes transactions that have the commercial effect of borrowing. This provision ensures that sophisticated financial arrangements designed to function like loans are also covered under the definition.

Examples include:

Structured finance transactions

Forward sale agreements

Certain investment arrangements

CLARIFICATION REGARDING WHAT TYPE OF TRANSACTION/COMPONENTS CAN COME UNDER THE UMBRELLA OF "FINANCIAL DEBT"?

A liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a Financial Debt within Section 5(8) of IBC. Hon'ble Supreme Court concluded that a liability in respect of a claim arising out of a Recovery Certificate would be a "financial debt" within the meaning of clause (8) of Section 5 of the IBC. Consequently, the holder of the Recovery Certificate would be a financial creditor within the meaning of clause (7) of Section 5 of the IBC. As such, the holder of such a certificate would be entitled to initiate CIRP if initiated within a period of three years from the date of issuance of the Recovery Certificate.

Supreme Court's Decision Aggrieved by the decision of the NCLAT, the Appellant/FC (who is claiming to be the FC) appealed before the Supreme Court under section 62 of the IBC (Orator Marketing (P.) Ltd. (supra). The question which was posed before the Supreme Court was "whether a person who has given interest free loan to a Corporate Person becomes incompetent to file a petition under section 7 of the Code?"

The Appellant challenged the impugned order of the NCLAT & NCLT and argued that while interpreting the provision of the legislation, the focus should be on the legislative intent, object & purpose of the statute. It was argued that both the Adjudicatory Tribunal have overlooked the words in section 5(8) of the Code, i.e., "if any". The interpretation of the words provides that the financial debt will not necessarily have the component of interest and if there is no interest still the principal debt will qualify to be as financial debt. He further argued that the NCLAT & NCLT have failed to take notice of Section 5(8) (f) of the IBC which provides that financial debt will include any amount which is raised under other transactions having the commercial effect of borrowing. The Appellant argued that the word "includes" as per the interpretation given in the case of Dilworth v. Commissioner of Stamps [1899] AC 99, will have connotation "means and includes" which will give an extensive explanation to the meaning attached to the words or expressions and thus lending of money for the financial requirements of the CD will in no way be discerned as it does not have the commercial effect of borrowing and thus, cannot be excluded from the definition of financial debt.

The Court further referred to the judgment of Anuj Jain, IRP for Anuj Jain v. Axis Bank Ltd. [2020] 114 taxmann.com 656, wherein the Supreme Court held that the basic element for the debt to be financial debt is that it should be disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money. Time value of money remains an essential part of the financial debt. The Court further stated that "the essential element of disbursal, and that too against the consideration for the time value of money, needs to be found in the genesis of any debt before it may be treated as financial debt within the meaning of Section 5(8) of the Code". The Apex Court, in the present matter, applied the ratio of the Jaypee Infratech case and held that the facts of the present matter are distinguishable from the above-mentioned case in a sense that the debt in the former case was in a form of a third-party guarantee which was given by the CD for securing the advances to the borrower, but, in the present case, the interest-free loan was given to meet out the working expenditures and financial requirements of the CD and thus, the ratio of the former case cannot be applied to the present case.

Further, the court relied on the case of Prabhudas Damodar Kotecha v. Manhabala Jeram Damodar [2013] 15 SCC 358, wherein the court applied the golden rule of interpretation while interpreting Section 41(1) of the Presidency Small Cause Courts Act, 1882 and observed that the words or phrase of the statute must be given ordinary meaning when the language used by the legislature is precise and plain and thus concluded that the gratuitous licensee will be considered as a general licensee unless specifically excluded. Thus, relying on the reasoning of the above case the Court in the present matter concluded that the loan given without interest will qualify to be treated as a financial debt unless specifically excluded. Hence, the Supreme Court set aside the judgment of the NCLAT & NCLT and ordered the NCLT to revive the petition under section 7 of the FC.

Divided Opinions of the Court/Tribunals on Interest as Prerequisite for Financial Debt

Section 5(8) of the Code defines financial debt which provides that it's a debt alongwith interest, if any, disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes the debt and includes money borrowed against payment of interest. On the plain reading of the provision, it is evident that if there is any interest component in the debt then it will qualify as financial debt. However, if there is no interest component attached to the debt/loan amount then what treatment is to be provided to the loan is a question that seeks urgent attention. Although, the Supreme Court in the Orator's case has very clearly highlighted the fact that the debt having no interest constituent shall be termed as financial debt, but this judgment of the Hon'ble court cannot be read alone and should be read in the light of various judgments of various NCLTs and NCLAT wherein the position of law was divided.

On facts, the Court held that in real terms there was hardly any retrospectivity. The degree and extent of the unforeseen and unforeseeable financial burden was, in the circumstances, minimal and cannot be said to be unreasonable or unconstitutional. The Supreme Court also took cognizance of the fact that the revenue authorities could not reopen assessments which were already barred by limitation.

UOI AIR 1988 SC 191, Rules 9 and 49 of the Central Excise Rules, 1944 rules were made retrospective from the date the rules were framed that is, from 28-2-1944. The Supreme Court accepted that if one had to pay duty with retrospective effect from 1944 it would really cause great hardship. However it pointed out that the retrospective amendment was subject to section 11(a) of the Act under which the excise authorities could not recover duties not levied or not paid or short levied or short paid or erroneously refunded beyond the period of 6 months. In view of this, it held that the amended provisions of Rules 9 and 49 were not arbitrary, unreasonable or violative of the provisions of article 14 and article 19 (1)(g) of the Constitution of India.

Conclusion 10. There is a little doubt with regard to the fact that service tax is value addition tax. This tax is levied on the value added to the property. But in case of immovable property on rent, there is no value being added to the property by either tenant or the landlord. So, there should not be any service tax on renting of the immovable property. If renting of immovable property itself is made subject to the service tax, then the tax which is being collected by the Central Government would be tax on the property. And the tax on the property can be levied only by the State Government according to List II of 7th Schedule of the Constitution of India. So, levying service tax on renting of immovable property falls outside the legislative competence of the Parliament. Based on the above discussion, only one logical conclusion follows that the renting of immovable property per se should not be made taxable.

14.1 (a) In case of Braithwaite & Co. Ltd. (supra), the Hon’ble Supreme Court was to define the term ‘period of not less than seven years’ as appearing in the proviso to rule 1(v) of Schedule II to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 and was pleased to hold, after relying on the decision of Bombay High Court in case of CIT v. Ramsukh Motilal [1955] 27 ITR 54 that the only interpretation which can be given to the expression ‘during a period of not less than seven years’ in the proviso is that the period should go beyond seven years.

‘On a plain reading of the proviso to rule 1(v ) of Schedule II to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964, it is clear that in order to claim the benefit of rule 1(v ), the borrowed money has to be repaid during a period of more than seven years. The only interpretation which can be given to the expression ‘during a period of not less than seven years’ in the proviso is that the period should go beyond seven years. The period of seven years would not be complete till the last minute or even the last second is counted. In other words, till the last minute of the seven years period is completed, the period remains less than seven years (see p. 347A, B).

The respondent-company obtained a term loan of Rs. 50 lakhs from a bank. The agreement dated 1st August, 1961, provided for the repayment of the loan in five annual instalments. The last of the instalments of Rs. 16 lakhs was to be paid on 31st July, 1971. The question was whether the repayment under the agreement was ‘during a period of not less than seven years’ as contemplated by the proviso to rule 1(v) of Schedule II to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964, and the entire sum of Rs. 50 lakhs could be included in the capital base for the purpose of surtax. The Tribunal held that only the last instalment of Rs. 16 lakhs could be included in the capital base. On a reference at the instance of the respondent-company, the High Court held that the entire amount of Rs. 50 lakhs could be included in the capital base. On appeal to the Supreme Court :

Held, reversing the decision of the High Court, (i) that the whole of the term loan of Rs. 50 lakhs was repayable within a period of seven years and the term loan did not qualify for inclusion in the capital base under rule 1(v) (see p. 347H) :

(ii) that, however, since the Department had not challenged the order of the Tribunal granting relief to the respondent to the extent of Rs. 16 lakhs, only the balance of Rs. 34 lakhs could not be included in the capital base of the respondent-company (see p. 348B, C).

Decision of the Calcutta High Court in Braithwaite & Co. (India) Ltd. v. CIT [1978] 111 ITR 825 (Cal.) reversed on this point.

In respect of assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08, it may be noted that the limitation period, as such, would end by assessment year 2017-18. In other words, in respect of assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08, if the provision is literally interpreted, it may mean that the Credit would not be available, as from and after assessment year 2017-18, the credit of assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08 is not carried forward.

However, as per the other view, prima facie, it appears, it should not be so. It is settled that law in force as on the first day of assessment year applies. The question of claiming credit arises in the year in which it could be actually allowed. On that basis, in assessment year 2018-19, the limitation period of 15 years in respect of the said assessment years, it cannot be said, has come to an end.

In this connection, a reference may be made to the following decisions:

(i)

RELIANCE JUTE AND INDUSTRIES LTD. v. CIT [1979] 2 Taxman 417 (SC)

"It is a cardinal principle of the tax law that the law to be applied is that in force in the assessment year unless otherwise provided expressly or by necessary implication - CIT v. Isthmian Steamship Lines [1951] 20 ITR 572 and Karimtharuvi Tea Estate Ltd. v. State of Kerala [1966] 60 ITR 262. On that principle, it is abundantly clear that when an assessment for the assessment year 1960-61 is to be made and section 24(2) is invoked, it is section 24(2) as in force in that assessment year which has to be applied. That is the provision as amended by the Finance (No. 2) Act, 1957. There is no question of the assessee possessing any vested right under the law as it stood before the amendment. The assessment for one assessment year cannot, in the absence of a contrary provision, be affected by the law in force in another assessment year. A right claimed by an assessee under the law in force in a particular assessment year is ordinarily available only in relation to a proceeding pertaining to that year. Therefore, inasmuch as the provisions of section 24(2), as amended in 1957, govern the assessment for the assessment year 1960-61, the High Court is right in affirming that the unabsorbed loss of Rs. 15,50,189 of the assessment year 1950-51 cannot be carried forward for more than eight years, and consequently cannot be set off against the business income of the assessment year 1960-61." (Emphasis supplied)

(ii)

The Tribunal cited reference to the High Court judgment in the case of Indo-Nippon Chemicals Co. Ltd. v. Union of India 2005 (185) ELT 19 (Guj.)(HC). This was a case relating to refund of Modvat credit, and the refund was attributable to mistakes committed both by the assessee and the department. In such situations, the High Court held that the time-limit for making the claim was to be reckoned under section 17 of the Limitation Act and not under section 11B of the Central Excise Act. The general law laid down in section 17 of the Limitation Act is that the period of limitation should be reckoned from the date on which the mistake was discovered by the party claiming refund. The Tribunal remitted the matter back to the Commissioner (Appeals) for fresh disposal in the light of the aforesaid judgment of the High Court.

But the Income-tax Act does not provide for all expenditures which are allowable or not. So, if the Act does not provide for any expenses, then the accounting treatment plays a very important role. It is true that accounting practice does not override provisions of the Act, but it is also true that they have wide implication regarding allowability of expenses. Many court cases also provide that if accounting practice is recognized and it does not violate the provisions of the Act, then that will be valid for allowability. 3.2 Relevance of accounting for allowability of expenditure - The next question is, how far accounting is relevant for claiming expenditure under the Act? Income under the head ‘Business and profession’ is calculated as per method of accounting generally followed as per section 145. Also the assessee has to maintain accounts and records as per section 44AA. So, the assessee has to make the accounting entries in books maintained under section 44AA as per method of accounting followed under section 145. But the question is whether the accounting entries affect the allowability of expenditures? For example, if we do not make any entry in the accounts, whether the expenditure can be claimed under the Act? Generally, the accounting entries are relevant but not conclusive. Except where there is specific provision under the Act (for example in case of bad debts), the allowability is dependent on the provisions of law and accounting entries are not relevant. So, even if there are no accounting entries in the accounts then also the assessee can claim the expenditure if otherwise allowable under the Act.

3.3 In which year expenditure is allowable - If one comes to know that a particular expenditure is allowable, then the next thing is in which year it is allowable? Because if not claimed in right year, then that will not be allowable in the other year. Though generally the income is calculated as per method of accounting, yet there are special provisions which override this general proposition just as section 43B, etc. Then also there are certain circumstances in which it is very difficult to know the time of accrual as in the case of disputes or contingencies. So, it is very important to know the accrual of liability, so that it can be claimed in that year only. The next question is when the deduction can be claimed? It simply means, that whether the deduction can be claimed in the year different from the year of accrual? For example, as per agreement you have to pay rent for three years at the time of agreement, so the accrual is at that time. But the question is whether the total amount is allowable in one year or has to be allowed in three different years, though in other two years there will be not any accrual. Simply it means, whether the matching principle is applicable or not?

3.4 How to claim - The next point is how the deduction can be claimed? What is the method of making claim for deductions? It means whether the deduction can be claimed in the return of income only or it can be claimed during assessment or appeal, etc.? For example, if you come to know of a liability relating to the year at the time of its assessment or appeal, whether you can claim the same at that time even if you have not claimed it in the return? The answer is simply, yes. You can also claim it during assessment in certain cases. Due to ignorance of this fact, the assessee does not claim the same and in other years it is not allowed by the Assessing Officer. So, the assessee loses the claim for ever.

3.5 Allowable amount - Every other aspect that has found place in tax literature and standard books, may be a little or more, but one aspect which has hardly got attention is the amount of allowance. If you ask any Chief Finance Officer of any Company the time value of money, then you come to know that amount of allowance is a very important aspect, always ignored under the Income-tax Act. Though the total amount allowable in all these cases will be Rs. 50,000 only, yet the effective amount in all these three cases will be different. Let us see the present value of this amount in all the three cases :

Provided that where, in the opinion of the 47[Assessing] Officer, the computation of the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking or the business of the hotel or the operation of the ship 46[or the business of repairs to ocean-going vessels or other powered craft] in the manner hereinbefore specified presents exceptional difficulties, the 47[Assessing] Officer may compute such profits and gains on such reasonable basis as he may deem fit.

Explanation.-In this sub-section, “market value”, in relation to any goods, means the price that such goods would ordinarily fetch on sale in the open market.

(9) Where it appears to the 47[Assessing] Officer that, owing to the close connection between the assessee carrying on the business of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the opera­tion of the ship 46[or the business of repairs to ocean-going vessels or other powered craft] to which this section applies and any other person, or for any other reason, the course of business between them is so arranged that the business transacted between them produces to the assessee more than the ordinary profits which might be expected to arise in the business of the industri­al undertaking or the hotel or the operation of the ship 46[or the business of repairs to ocean-going vessels or other powered craft], the 47[Assessing] Officer shall, in computing the profits and gains of the industrial undertaking or the hotel or the ship 46[or the business of repairs to ocean-going vessels or other powered craft] for the purposes of the deduction under this sec­tion, take the amount of profits as may be reasonably deemed to have been derived therefrom.

|  |  | Section 102 deals with the extent, commencement and application of Chapter VII. |  |
|  |  |  | Section 103 is the definition provision. Sub-clause (5) of this section defines taxable commodities transaction to mean a transaction of purchase or sale of option in goods, or option in commodity derivative, or any other commodity derivative, traded on recognised associations. |

■

Over a period of 10 years, the assessee had collected and kept with it an amount of Rs. 1.83 crores and this amount had to be repaid in subsequent 5 equal installments. The Maharashtra State Government had come out with a 'Scheme of Incentive' as per which they scientifically calculated the Net Present Value of sales tax collected. In simple words, if the assessee prepays i.e., before five years, they would be paying lesser amount.

■

The assessee opted to repay its sales tax liability of Rs. 1.83 crores during the year under consideration at its NPV of Rs. 93.57 lakhs and this NPV was arrived at scientifically by State Government. Thus, the assessee had collected and kept sales tax of Rs. 1.83 crores for 10 years and repaid (prepaid) only Rs. 93.57 lakhs as final payment in this year i.e., no further payment was to be done by assessee. Thus, the assessee had got benefit of Rs. 90.22 lakhs.

■

The Assessing Officer considered it as 'income' in this year invoking section 2(24)(xviii).

■

On appeal, the Commissioner (Appeals) confirmed the order of the Assessing Officer.

only possible exclusion would be the parking area, which, in certain cases, was sold to the respective flat-buyers or leased out to the flat-buyers, and therefore, it had some value, which had to be included. The contention of the assessee that basement had no value was also rejected because car parking area was as much a saleable space as any other space. It could either be sold along with the flats or separately or might be retained for being leased to the flat-owners. The rates at which the flats were booked on various dates were to be considered for valuation of those flats. In case of any space earmarked for the appellant which had not been so agreed to be sold, but was intended to be retained by the appellant himself it had to be valued at the rate at which initial booking was started, because it was based on the initial understanding with the builder. However, upon the assessee deciding not to sell some flats at a later point of time, the rate that was prevalent then had to be adopted for those flats. The Tribunal being concerned with the market value of the flats and not their cost of construction, these need to be valued at the same rate at which it would be available to the public.

The adoption or estimate by the Commissioner (Appeals) of the rates at which some space could be made available to the buyers of the basements, upper ground floor, etc., was improper, because he did not consider the rates at which public was invited to buy the flat space. The rates were revised upwards more than once, which suggested that the public was slow in responding to the invitation but, all the same, it was those rates with which the flats were to be related and not any imaginery rate. If, as on 31- 3-1983, some flats in the ground floor, upper ground floor first, second and other floors were not booked, then the most proximate rate at which invitation was advertised should be adopted as the value for those flats. White adopting the rates, care must be exercised to ensure that the rates adopted were for those respective floors, i.e., the rates of second floor could not be adopted for valuing the third floor, unless both the floors had the same rate.

The rates at which the flat space was sold were similar to recoverable debt and since the flat price was payable in instalments spread over a few years, the instalments that became due after the valuation date needed to be discounted to arrive at the present worth of the space involved. Further, since the building in which the space was allotted to the several buyers required the sanction of the L & DO on payment of commercialisation charges, it was very much a charge on the present value of the flat space. Similarly, the settlement with the tenant, who had carried the matter to the High Court that was ultimately settled in 1986, was also a charge on the present value of the flats. Since the property was under construction as on the relevant valuation dates, and some more cost had to be incurred, as the construction got completed in 1987, i.e., almost four and three years from 31-3-1983 and 31-3-1984, respectively this element equated as interest also required to be allowed deduction of for arriving at the present value of the flat space.

The Assessing Officer was, accordingly, directed to recalculate the value of the space on the two valuation dates separately, as above.

The appeals were, accordingly, partly allowed.

Dr. O.K. Narayanan, Vice-President - This is a set of cross appeals filed by the assessee and the Revenue for the two assessment years 2006-07 and 2007-08. These appeals are directed against the orders passed by the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals), Large Taxpayer Unit at Chennai on August 25, 2011. The appeals arise out of the assessments completed under section 143(3) of the Income-tax Act, 1961.

2. We will first consider the cross appeals filed for the assessment year 2006-07.

3. The appeal filed by the assessee is in I.T.A. No. 1614(Mds)/2011.

4. The first ground raised by the assessee is that the Commissioner of Income-tax (Appeals) has erred in confirming the addition of Rs. 61,78,71,246 to the income of the assessee. It is the case of the assessee that the said sum was not chargeable to tax as income of the assessee for the assessment year under appeal.

5. The assessee is engaged in the business of running holiday homes on time share basis. Members are admitted as time shareholders and they are provided stay in the holiday homes maintained by the assessee for a specified number of days in a year. Whenever new members/customers subscribe to the membership of the assessee's holiday home plan, the assessee collects membership fees from them. The assessee provides holiday home facility for its members for a period of 25 years. A member is entitled to come and stay in the holiday home for a specified number of days in a particular year. While collecting membership fees from time shareholders, the assessee-company offers 60 per cent. of such membership collection as income of the year of collection. The balance 40 per cent. of the membership fees is treated as deferred income to be spread over the remaining period of holiday share owned by a member. In a 25 year plan, the 60 per cent. membership fees is treated as income of the assessee for the first year and the balance 40 per cent. is to be treated as income of the remaining 24 years on a pro rata basis.

6. This method of recognising the income was not accepted by the Assessing Officer. The Assessing Officer found that even if a time shareholder is entitled to enjoy the privilege of staying in the holiday homes of the assessee for a period of 25 years, the assessee-company is not incurring any expenditure in the subsequent years for providing such facilities to the members. In addition to the membership fees collected by the assessee-company, the assessee is also collected upkeep and maintenance charges from the members as annual charges. These annual charges will take care of the expenses, if any, required in connection with providing the facilities to the members for the subsequent years of the holiday plan. The Assessing Officer has further pointed out that the assessee claims the entire expenses incurred in a particular year as deduction in that year itself, but at the same time defers a portion of its income to be spread over the subsequent years, which is not in conformity with the matching principle of accountancy. The Assessing Officer also pointed out that the expenditure not incurred or loss not suffered in a particular assessment year cannot be deducted against the actual receipts of that particular year.

7. The Assessing Officer relied on the decision of the Income-tax Appellate Tribunal, Chennai Bench, rendered in the case of Sterling Holiday Resorts (India) Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2008] 111 ITD 116 (Chennai), wherein the Tribunal has held that the entire fee collected in a particular year in similar circumstances is the income liable for taxation in the year of receipt.

8. Accordingly, the Assessing Officer treated the entire hundred per cent. of the membership collection as income liable for taxation for the impugned assessment year 2006-07. It is how the addition of Rs. 61,78,71,246 has been made by the Assessing Officer.

is difficult to imagine that the time-limit within which action for reopening of the assessment was to be taken would have been set by the Legislature with reference to a future uncertain date. That is one more reason to hold that the words 'the order which was the subject-matter of the appeal, reference or revision, as the case may be, was made' refer to the assessment order passed by the Assessing Officer and not the appellate order passed by the Commissioner (Appeals). [Para 8] It was also contended by the assessee that the Tribunal's order dated 14-6-2000, which had attained finality, related only to the original compensation and not the enhanced compensation with regard to which there was no finding or direction by the Tribunal and, therefore, the inclusion of the enhanced compensation in the reassessment order was bad and without justification. It was further contended that even if the notice of re-assessment was taken to refer only to the enhanced compensation, the notice was invalid because the enhanced compensation was assessable only on receipt basis under section 45(5) in the assessment year 1986-87. It was true that the decision of the Tribunal dated 14-6-2000 had become final inasmuch as neither party had filed an appeal against the same, but it was equally true that the reference to section 45(5) in the order of the Tribunal was an inadvertence. The Tribunal had referred to section 45(5) as a supporting reason for holding that the capital gain could be said to have arisen only by virtue of the order of the LAO dated 25-3-1980. The reference to the section did not however whittle down the effectiveness of the direction of the Tribunal. One should understand the direction of the Tribunal de hors the provisions of section 45(5) which were not applicable to the relevant assessment year 1980-81 under appeal. It was not contended by the assessee that the finding of the Tribunal that the capital gain was assessable in the assessment year 1980-81 was a finding which was not necessary for the disposal of the appeal and, therefore, the same could not be given effect to by reopening the assessment for the assessment year 1980-81. Even if such a contention was to be taken, the same would not have been accepted having regard to the provisions of Explanation 2 to section 153. The fiction contained in the Explanation removes the bar of limitation irrespective of the question whether the appellate authority has, in fact, given or can, in law, give a finding or direction that the income should be taxed in a specified assessment year other than the year for which the appellate authority hears the appeal. If this principle was applied to the instant case, one should determine the assessability of the receipt having regard to the law as it stood in relation to the relevant assessment year 1980-81. The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the impugned order that the Tribunal did not refer to the assessability of the enhanced compensa-tion directed by the order of the District Judge dated 25-2-1985, which was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, therefore, the Assessing Officer could not bring the enhanced compensation to tax while making the reassessment for the assessment year 1980-81. He had further referred to section 45(5) to support the above conclusion. This part of the decision of the Commissioner(Appeals) had been challenged as incorrect on the footing that section 45(5) came into effect only from 1-4-1988 and having regard to the provisions of section 45(1) read with section 155(7A), even the enhanced compensation was assessable only in the assessment year 1980-81. Section 45(5) was inserted by the Finance Act, 1987, only with effect from 1-4-1988 and, therefore, became applicable only from the assessment year 1988-89 onwards. The enhanced compensation ordered by the District Judge was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that the same could be assessed only in the assessment year 1986-87. This conclusion was obviously wrong, since the enhanced compensation could not have been assessed on receipt basis under section 45(5) for the assessment year 1986-87 for the simple reason that the section did not come into effect for that assessment year. This decision of the Commissioner (Appeals) was, therefore unsupportable. The department referred to section 155(7A). Sub-section (7A) was inserted by the Finance Act, 1978, with retrospective effect from 1-4-1974 to empower the Assessing Officer to amend an order or award of additional compensa-tion in the case of compulsory acquisition of a capital asset. Sub-section (7A) was omitted by the Direct Tax Laws (Amendment) Act, 1987, with effect from 1-4-1992. Thus, it had effect for the assessment year 1980-81. [Para 8] It was also contended by the assessee that the Tribunal's order dated 14-6-2000, which had attained finality, related only to the original compensation and not the enhanced compensation with regard to which there was no finding or direction by the Tribunal and, therefore, the inclusion of the enhanced compensation in the reassessment order was bad and without justification. It was further contended that even if the notice of re-assessment was taken to refer only to the enhanced compensation, the notice was invalid because the enhanced compensation was assessable only on receipt basis under section 45(5) in the assessment year 1986-87. It was true that the decision of the Tribunal dated 14-6-2000 had become final inasmuch as neither party had filed an appeal against the same, but it was equally true that the reference to section 45(5) in the order of the Tribunal was an inadvertence. The Tribunal had referred to section 45(5) as a supporting reason for holding that the capital gain could be said to have arisen only by virtue of the order of the LAO dated 25-3-1980. The reference to the section did not however whittle down the effectiveness of the direction of the Tribunal. One should understand the direction of the Tribunal de hors the provisions of section 45(5) which were not applicable to the relevant assessment year 1980-81 under appeal. It was not contended by the assessee that the finding of the Tribunal that the capital gain was assessable in the assessment year 1980-81 was a finding which was not necessary for the disposal of the appeal and, therefore, the same could not be given effect to by reopening the assessment for the assessment year 1980-81. Even if such a contention was to be taken, the same would not have been accepted having regard to the provisions of Explanation 2 to section 153. The fiction contained in the Explanation removes the bar of limitation irrespective of the question whether the appellate authority has, in fact, given or can, in law, give a finding or direction that the income should be taxed in a specified assessment year other than the year for which the appellate authority hears the appeal. If this principle was applied to the instant case, one should determine the assessability of the receipt having regard to the law as it stood in relation to the relevant assessment year 1980-81. The Commissioner (Appeals) had observed in the impugned order that the Tribunal did not refer to the assessability of the enhanced compensa-tion directed by the order of the District Judge dated 25-2-1985, which was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, therefore, the Assessing Officer could not bring the enhanced compensation to tax while making the reassessment for the assessment year 1980-81. He had further referred to section 45(5) to support the above conclusion. This part of the decision of the Commissioner(Appeals) had been challenged as incorrect on the footing that section 45(5) came into effect only from 1-4-1988 and having regard to the provisions of section 45(1) read with section 155(7A), even the enhanced compensation was assessable only in the assessment year 1980-81. Section 45(5) was inserted by the Finance Act, 1987, only with effect from 1-4-1988 and, therefore, became applicable only from the assessment year 1988-89 onwards. The enhanced compensation ordered by the District Judge was received by the assessee in November, 1985 and, accordingly, the Commissioner (Appeals) had held that the same could be assessed only in the assessment year 1986-87. This conclusion was obviously wrong, since the enhanced compensation could not have been assessed on receipt basis under section 45(5) for the assessment year 1986-87 for the simple reason that the section did not come into effect for that assessment year. Further, since the building in which the space was allotted to the several buyers required the sanction of the L & DO on payment of commercialisation charges, it was very much a charge on the present value of the flat space. Similarly, the settlement with the tenant, who had carried the matter to the High Court that was ultimately settled in 1986, was also a charge on the present value of the flats. Since the property was under construction as on the relevant valuation dates, and some more cost had to be incurred, as the construction got completed in 1987, i.e., almost four and three years from 31-3-1983 and 31-3-1984, respectively this element equated as interest also required to be allowed deduction of for arriving at the present value of the flat space.

The Assessing Officer was, accordingly, directed to recalculate the value of the space on the two valuation dates separately, as above.

The appeals were, accordingly, partly allowed.

The assessee won the first prize of Tripura State lottery in the draw held on 14-6-1983. One ‘S’ filed suit claiming a share in the lottery amount as joint owner. The Munsif Court ordered stay of the disbursement of the prize amount to the assessee due to which a delay of three years was caused in the disbursement of the lottery prize to the assessee and the prize amount was disbursed to him in October 1987. For the assessment year 1984-85, the assessee filed return on 18-12-1987 declaring lottery income. The return was rejected as time-barred and the petition for condonation of delay was also rejected. However, while completing the assessment for the assessment year 1988-89, the Assessing Officer also included the income from lottery because the assessee had received the lottery amount during the previous year relevant to the assessment year 1988-89. The Assessing Officer observed that the assessee did not main- tain any books of account and, therefore, the income from the lottery winning would be assessed in the assessment year 1988-89 on receipt basis.

The Commissioner (Appeals) observed that the Assessing Officer himself had determined the tax to be deducted at source in respect of the lottery amount as early as in July 1983. From this fact, the Commissioner (Appeals) came to the conclusion that the Assessing Officer had recognized the assessee’s right to receive the amount during a period much earlier than the accounting period relevant for the assessment year 1988-89. The Commissioner (Appeals) considered that the assessee, in accordance with the method of accounting followed by him, accepted the right to receive the lottery amount as an accrual of income and accordingly filed a return of income for the assessment year 1984-85 and, hence, the same amount could not be assessed in a subsequent year.

of 250 days and if it failed to allot such plots after expiry of one year, corporate debtor had to pay back invested money along with interest. Corporate debtor failed to allot any plot to financial creditors. When financial creditors approached corporate debtor for payment of maturity value of investment, same was not paid. Corporate debtor submitted that there was delay in repayment as promised, since real estate market was in bad shape. However, debt was duly acknowledged by corporate debtor. Further, it did not raise any objection. In the receipt-cum-acceptance letter, it was stated on face of it, that these were for acquisitions and registrations of plots booked and maturity date of agreement was given as one year after date of registration and projected value was more than consideration value.

On these facts, the issue for the consideration of the NCLT was whether the buyers advancing the money came within the category of financial creditors entitled to invoke IBC for the recovery of the sums advanced. The Petitioner's case before the NCLT was that it was clear that under the garb of allotting land to the public, the respondent had been borrowing/accepting deposits/loans from the public by showing it as investment against property, i.e., by showing the depositors to register for plots of specific measurements and also showing the projected value of the said investment/deposit/borrowing on the maturity date. S.5(7) defines 'financial creditor' to mean a person to whom a financial debt is owed. Financial debt is defined in s.5(8) to mean a debt along with interest, if any, which is disbursed against the consideration for the time value of money and includes, inter alia, any amount raised under any other transaction, including any forward sale or purchase agreement, having the commercial effect of a borrowing [clause (f) of s.5(8).

According to the NCLT, receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot were for/time value of money and have the commercial effect of borrowing and, hence, sub-sections (7) & (8) of s.5 apply and, hence, the petitioner is to be taken as financial creditor. In coming to this view, the NCLT relied on the decision of the National Company Law Appellate Tribunal (NCLTA) in the case of Nikhil Mehta & Sons v. AMR Infrastructure Ltd. [2017] 84 taxmann.com 163/143 SCL 278 (NCL - AT) where the following decision was taken by the NCLTA:-

"….From the provisions of law and discussion as made and quoted above, we find following essential criterias, to be fulfilled for a creditor to come within the meaning of financial creditor:-

(i)

A person to whom a financial debt is owned and includes a person, whom such debt has been legally assigned transferred to;

(ii)

The debt along with interest, if any, is disbursed against the consideration for time value of money and include any one or more mode of disbursement as mentioned in clauses (a) to (i) of sub-section (8) of s.5".

The NCLT thus, pronounced its decision as under:-

"In the present case, the receipt-cum-acceptance letters (Annexure-A-1 to A-4 of the application) on the face of it state that they are for acquisition of plot and registration for plot booked. However, the maturity date of agreement is given as one year after the date of registration and the projected value is given, which is more than the consideration value given. Therefore, the time value of money has been built in and it has to be presumed that the receipt-cum-acceptance letters, even though stated to be for registration of plot, have the commercial effect of borrowing. In view of sub-ss.(7) & (8) of s.5 of the Code (supra), the petitioners are to be treated as financial creditors".

It may be stated in the context of this decision that in reply, the respondent did not raise any objection that the petitioners before NCLT are not financial creditors. Rather it specifically stated saying that "there is some delay on the corporate debtor's part in returning the amount of the financial creditor [emphasis is provided].

Hence, this decision may not be a binding authority to claim that a homebuyer comes in the category of 'financial creditor'.

The requirement in section 34(1)(a ) of 1922 Act is not merely the omission or failure of an assessee to file a return but also his omission or failure to disclose fully and truly the particulars of his income. Thus, even where an assessee might file a return, if he does not show in that return fully and truly his entire income, he exposes himself to action being taken against him under section 34(1)(a) of 1922 Act. The period of limitation for making an assessment under section 34(1)(a) of 1922 Act is eight years from the end of the assessment year in question. In this case the order under section 34(1)(a) of 1922 Act was made within this period. Therefore, the initiation of proceedings under section 34 of 1922 Act was valid in law.

As regards the point that the so-called interest was compensation or damages for wrongful detention of the money by the banks in which it was deposited. The banks had never wrongfully detained the money. All that the banks had done was that, having been restrained by the injunction order of the High Court, they did not make the payment in contravention of that injunction. The money was, therefore, not compensation or damages for wrongful detention but interest. Interest income on a bank deposit was undisputedly a revenue, and not a capital receipt and was assessable to tax.

As regards the Allowability of the sum of Rs. 1,03,000 as litigation expenses alleged to have been incurred by B in defending the Bombay suit.

In the suit in Bombay High Court a question of title to the sum of Rs. 18 lakhs was involved and that sum was in the nature of a capital asset. Expenditure incurred for establishment of title to a capital asset is not allowable expenditure under section 10(2)(xv). The Tribunal was, therefore, clearly wrong in treating the expenditure as an allowable expenditure. In this view even the sum of Rs. 10,000 which was allowed by it was wrongly allowed and no question of allowing the balance arose in this case.
