Modification of the provisions relating to deduction from profits derived from the business of providing long-term finance [Sec. 36(1)(viii)]

10.5 Under section 36(l)(viii), in case of a financial corporation, engaged in providing long-term finance for industrial or agricultural development or development of infrastructure facility in India or in case of a public company formed and registered in India, with the main object of carrying on the business of providing long-term finance for construction of purchase of house in India for residential purposes, an amount not exceeding 40% of the profits derived from such business and carried to a special reserve, is allowed as a deduction subject to certain conditions. An amendment carried out by the Finance Act, 1995, has resulted in allowing the deduction from total income computed before making any deduction under this 'section' and not before making deduction under this 'clause'. As this was not the intention this error has been rectified by providing with effect from assessment year 1996-97 that the deduction shall be allowed on total income before making deduction under section 36(1)(viii).

The expression long-term finance' was not earlier defined. Section 36 has now been amended with effect from assessment year 1996-97 to define the expression long-term finance' to mean any loan or advance, where the terms under which monies are loaned or advanced provide for repayment along with interest thereof during a period of not less than five years.

A loan would be reckoned as long-term finance even if, substantial amount of the loan is repayable before 5 years (say 90%) and only the balance is repayble in the 5th year. The proviso to rule 1(v) of the Second Schedule to the Companies (Profits) Surtax Act, 1964 reads as follows:

"Provided that such moneys are borrowed for the creation of a capital asset in India and the agreement under which such moneys are borrowed provides for the repayment thereof during a period of not less than seven years."

Courts have interpreted this proviso as follows:

If the moneys had been borrowed under an agreement whereby the moneys were to be repaid during a period of not less than seven years, then the fact that the assessee had been able to repay the amount before the expiry of seven years was not relevant. [CIT v. Zenith Steel Pipes Ltd. 181 ITR 291 (Bom.)]

If the agreement originally provides for repayment of the loan within 7 years and subsequently it is modified for repayment within 8 years and the loan is repaid within 8 years, the loan cannot be set to be repayable within the period of 7 years. [CIT v. New India Industries Ltd. 212 ITR 653 (SC)]

The aforesaid decisions would be relevant for interpreting the term long-term finance in section 36(1)(viii).

10.5-1 Amendment regarding computation of deduction - Section 36(1)(viii) has been amended still further. Under the second proviso to the said section as it stood prior to the amendment, the allowance in respect of special reserve was allowable only till such period upto which the aggregate of the amounts carried to such reserve from time to time did not exceed twice the amount of share capital. Further, in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves were to be excluded.

The said second proviso is now amended with effect from assessment year 1997-98 so as to provide that:

the allowance will be allowed till such period upto which the aggregate of special reserve does not exceed the aggregate of share capital and general reserves; and

in computing the share capital, the amounts capitalised from reserves are no longer required to be excluded.

Thus, in case of corporations making profits consistently and ploughing back the profits regularly by increasing the general reserves, the deduction in respect of special reserve could be allowed year after year almost perpetually.

Ladies and gentlemen,

I have been quoted repeatedly by some of the valuable speakers that judges are not expected to know everything. I had said this in a different context. Unfortunately, today the context is different. There is so much misconception and misinformation in this world. The context was that in India, appeals lie directly from regulatory authorities to the Supreme Court. Now, do you expect the Judges to know, when matters come before them, engineering terms, like port charges? Do you expect judges to know accountancy when they have to decide appeals in tariffs matters?. Unless people tell us what are electricity port charges, you don't expect judges to answer or deliver justice. But on the flip side of the matter, I can tell you, is that today at the Indian Supreme Court and today I am going to discuss only about the Indian Supreme Court and the Indian Tax Administration problems that we have. As far as the Supreme Court today is concerned, these types of appeals coming before the Supreme Court is the result of convergence after globalization- convergence of law, economics, science, accountancy and if a judge may not know all the details, we may rightly say – but he must understand some of the concepts and that concept need to be told to him otherwise it would not be possible for him to render justice.

Many of us today have discussed tax abuse and tax avoidance. All these are concepts. But what I have learnt in the past 22 years in the primary function of all constitutions in the world, which is the basic law of the country, is that the rule of interpretation is the most important doctrine and most important law which every judge must understand and must apply. Now let me give you an example: If you are reading the Constitution of India, the words used are double textual like "complete justice" and "common good". These are open textual words and we judges are required to interpret those words in the widest possible terms. But if I have to decide or interpret a charging section under the Income-tax Act, certainly I will go by literary interpretation, particularly if it is the deeming provision. And particularly today in the context of laws like Transfer Pricing provisions, and that of the GAAR I would request each and every lawyer, like each professor who is sitting in this hall today to focus on the language (a) and (b) on the concepts and principles behind those provision. Today the main problem of Transfer Pricing for example or in GAAR is interpretation. An officer in the tax department can interpret in a way which would suit his purpose because he is faced with the target of revenue collection. He may not go in the principle, because he may not go on the rationale behind the provision and this is what is happening today. Unless lawyers, tax professors and tax policy makers concentrate on the language which is used, concentrate on the principles which are to be applied, things will not become clear.

Let me give you an another example: In the past we had to go strictly by form and not substance. But today with the introduction of the provisions of the Income-tax Act we are required to go into value. We are required to go into methodology of arriving at Arm Length Price. Are these not subject to concepts? Economic substance is one of the subjects of transfer pricing. So there is a paradigm shift which goes from form into substance and consequently and this is what I am trying to emphasise. Consequently there is a wide discretion which is coming into the hands of the tax department and that wide discretion needs to be controlled As Lord Bingham has said "all Constitutions in the democratic world proceed under the rule of law" and Lord Bingham has said repeatedly that "law is not discretion". If you want to control discretion, that discretion must be based on manageable data otherwise you have a situation where under Transfer Pricing the demand today runs up to 14 Billion according to the newspapers in India.

Liability of chit funds liable to pay service tax after 1-6-2015

Question - We understand that after enactment of Finance Act, 2015, chit funds are liable to pay service tax. Kindly advise.

Answer - In Delhi Chit Funds Association v. Union of India [2013] 32 taxmann.com 332/39 STT 955 (Delhi), the levy of service tax on chit funds has been held as invalid. It was (in effect) held that it is mere transaction in money and hence outside the definition of 'service' itself.

Departmental SLP against this decision has been dismissed by Supreme Court - Union of India v. Delhi Chit Fund Association [2014] 43 GST 524/42 taxmann.com 52.

In Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2008] 17 STT 491 (AP), the Board circular dated 23-8-2007 extending service tax to business chit funds has been held as invalid and has been squashed. - SLP against the order dismissed by SC - Union of India v. Andhra Pradesh Federation of Chit Funds [2015] 49 GST 274/53 taxmann.com 237 (SC).

However, in All Kerala Association of Chit Funds v. Union of India [2013] 40 STT 500/35 taxmann.com 620 (Ker.), validity of service tax on chit funds has been upheld.

Some changes were proposed in Finance Act, 2015 to get over these decisions. However, these changes have not been made effective so far, as explained below.

Proposed changes in definitions - Following definitions are proposed vide section 107 of Finance Act, 2015. However, these definitions have not been notified when other provisions of the Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, the following definitions are not effective.

'Transaction in money' shall not include any activity carried out for consideration by foreman of chit fund Service tax will be payable by foreman of chit fund on services provided by way of conducting a chit. - proposed Explanation 2(ii)(b) to section 65B(44) of Finance Act, 1994 [which defines service] inserted by section 107(g) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this explanation is not effective.

Foreman of chit fund shall have the same meaning as is assigned to the term 'foreman' in section 2(j) of the Chit Funds Act - proposed section 65B(23A) of Finance Act, 1994 inserted by section 107(b) of Finance Act, 2015. - - However, this clause has not been notified when other provisions of Finance Act, 2015 were made effective from 1-6-2015. Thus, till notified, this definition is not effective.

It was clarified that these amendments have been made as intention of law has always been to levy service tax on these activities. However, in view of contrary decisions of various High Courts, specific amendments are made in statutory provisions - para 5.1(ii) of MF(DR) letter DOF No. 334/5/2015-TRU dated 28-2-2015.

Interestingly, these amendments, though passed, have not been made effective when other provisions were made effective from 1-6-2015. Reason for this is not clear.

Conclusion - Since these changes, proposed in Finance Act, 2015 have not been notified and not made effective, in my view, the decisions of Delhi High Court and Andhra Pradesh High Court are valid and no service tax should be payable on chit funds.

The Assessing Officer noted that assessee had earned tax free dividend income and he required the assessee to explain as to why disallowance under rule 8D should not be made. Assessee submitted that in order to pay 'upfront fee' of Rs. 150 crores to AAI, assessee had approached banks for such a payment and since funding by way of borrowing of such payment was taking time it was decided to bring equity and the surplus arising from the operation was kept in mutual funds. When the funding was received, then the same got substituted by the borrowed money of Rs. 150 crores from the banks which was utilised in incurring of cost of airport project. Thus, investment in funds was not made from borrowed funds but from share capital and internal accruals from time to time.

However, the Assessing Officer applied the provision of rule 8D for making the disallowance.

The Commissioner (Appeals) held that same could not be disallowed, because assessee had owned interest free funds sufficient to cover the investment made and therefore, no apportionment of any interest expenses could be made for the purpose of disallowance under section 14A. He further held that provision of rule 8D were not applicable in assessment year 2007-08 as the same had been made applicable for the assessment year 2008-09.

On appeal:

The appellant-revenue fairly submitted the substantial question of law that arose for consideration in this appeal has already been decided against the revenue and in favour of the assessee in the following judgments:

(i)

Harvey Heart Hospitals Ltd. v. Asstt. CIT [2021] 127 taxmann.com 805/431 ITR 83 (Mad.) wherein the Division Bench held that unabsorbed depreciation pertaining to assessment years 1997-98 to 2001-02 can be carried forward and adjusted after lapse of eight assessment years in view of section 32(2) as amended by Finance Act, 2001 and, therefore, is eligible for set off against any income of assessee for assessment year 2005-06.

(ii)

CIT v. Sanmar Speciality Chemicals Ltd. [2020] 122 taxmann.com 212/[2021] 278 Taxman 94/[2020] 428 ITR 237 (Mad.) wherein the Division Bench held that unabsorbed depreciation pertaining to assessment year 1997-98 could be allowed to be carried forward and set off after a period of eight years without any limit whatsoever in accordance with section 32(2) as amended by Finance Act, 2001.[Para 4]

(supra), the question of law i.e., whether on the facts and in the circumstances of the case, the Tribunal was right in holding that the assessee is entitled to carry forward the unabsorbed depreciation pertaining to assessment years 1997-98 and 1998-99 and set off against the income of assessment year 2007-08 which is beyond the period of eight assessment years, in the light of amendment with effect from assessment year 1997-98 putting a cap of eight years for carry forward of depreciation and the amendment with effect from 2002-03 removing the said cap of eight years for carry forward is decided against the revenue and in favour of the assessee. Accordingly, the Tax Case Appeal is dismissed. [Para 6]

■ Undisputedly, the issue is fully covered by the orders of coordinate bench in the assessee's own case for preceding years viz. assessment year 2014-15, assessment year 2015-16, assessment year 2018-19, assessment year 2020-21 and 2021-22, where the addition made in respect of transfer of electricity was deleted and the assessee's benchmarking approach of using the purchase price of electricity from SEB was upheld. It is also clear that the case of the assessee for assessment year 2014-15 travelled upto Delhi High Court and the Revenue's appeal on the issue of transfer of electricity was dismissed by the Court dealing with the issue fully on merits and by observing as follows: "Thus, the market for supply of electricity is regulated. To apply the CUP method, it is necessary to ascertain comparable transactions similar in material aspects and without differences that bear on price. IEX is a platform for short-term surplus power and not a source for uninterrupted supply. There is wide fluctuation in IEX rates, and rates quoted there are for power supplied and not the power consumed. These material differences between electricity supplied by SEBs or distribution companies and that secured by bidding on IEX have a significant bearing on price. The CUP method cannot be applied where there is significant dissimilarity between the comparable transactions. In Commissioner of Income Tax v. Jindal Steel and Power Limited [2023] 157 taxmann.com 207/297 Taxman 253/460 ITR 162 (SC), the Supreme Court held that 'market value' under Section 80IA(8) means the price determined in an open market in an environment of free competition and that, for captive power supplies, the rate at which the State Electricity Board supplied power to industrial consumers has to be taken as the market value for computing deduction under Section 80IA. As is apparent, the Supreme Court accepted the rates at which electricity was supplied by the SEBs to industrial consumers as being the market value for the purposes of Section 80IA(8)." [Para 16]

FACT: ■

The assessee, a cellular mobile telephony service provider, received about Rs. 133.79 crores from prepaid customers during the year, disclosed as advances since services had not been rendered; it recognised revenue on the basis of actual usage within the validity period.

■

The Assessing Officer held prepaid receipts were non-refundable and crystallised as income on receipt, and proposed to tax the entire amount of about Rs. 133.79 crores in the year of receipt.

■

The DRP accepted the assessee’s revenue recognition method, observing the obligation to provide services throughout the validity period, and directed deletion of the proposed addition.

■

The Assessing Officer passed the final order accordingly.

■

On appeal to the Tribunal:

HELD: ■

It is found that similar issue came up for consideration before the Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal in ACIT v. Shyam Telelinks Ltd. [2013] 31 taxmann.com 239 (Delhi - Trib.)/[2013] 141 ITD 416 (Delhi - Trib.), wherein the Co-ordinate Bench agreed with the similar mode of revenue recognition by the taxpayer. The Co-ordinate Bench of the Tribunal further directed the Assessing Officer to verify whether, in the subsequent year, the taxpayer has declared the revenue in respect of expired prepaid cards, and in case no discrepancy is found in this regard, the Co-ordinate Bench directed that no adjustment is called for with the assessee's mode of revenue recognition. The relevant findings are: "We restore the matter to the file of Assessing Officer for the limited purpose of verification whether in the subsequent year the assessee has declared the revenue in respect of expired prepaid cards or not. In case no discrepancy is found in this regard, no adjustment is called for with the assessee's mode of revenue recognition." [Para 63]

There is as such no dispute regarding the nature of expenditure, which is held to be capital in nature. DR further submitted that the assessee's submissions that the Tribunal in assessee's own case for the Assessment Year 2013-14 held that the receipt are also capital in nature was already discussed in the present assessment year by the Assessing Officer as well as by the DRP. ITO [2009] 181 Taxman 249/315 ITR 255/[2010] 230 CTR 199 judgment dated 26-2-2009. However, after the decision in this case the Hon'ble Delhi High Court had occasion to discussing the same issue in the case of CIT v. Indian Vaccine Corpn. Ltd. [2014] 44 taxmann.com 130/222 Taxman 207 (Mag)/363 ITR 295 (Delhi) and held that where there was no inextricably link between investment and project interest income on said investment could not be permitted to be adjusted against pre-operative expenses in respect of said project. In this case, the assessee was incorporated as a Company with object of manufacturing human vaccines and it received substantial financial grant. It invested said funds and promoter's capital with bank under portfolio management scheme under which assured return was granted by link. The assessee adjusted interest income on said bank deposited against pre-operative expenses relating to a project. Since investment had nothing to do with the project and there was no inextricable link between investment and project interest income could not be permitted to be an adjusted against pre-operative expenses. This decision of the Delhi High Court is dated 5-3-2014 which is later to the decision in case of India Oil Panipat Power Consortium Ltd. Case (supra). The Ld. DR submitted that in this case CIT v. Section  115JB of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Minimum alternate tax - Payment of tax (Computation of) - Assessment year  2017-18 - While computing book profit under section 115JB, Assessing Officer made additions of Rs. 29 lakhs and Rs. 2.17 crores respectively on account of disallowance under section 35D and difference in AIR reconciliation - Commissioner (Appeals) deleted additions - It was observed that there was no adverse comment by auditor regarding preparation of accounts in accordance with provisions of Schedule III to Companies Act, 2013 - Moreover, there was no such allegation by Assessing Officer and hence audited accounts comply with requirements of section 115JB(2) - Whether, therefore, order of Commissioner (Appeals) was to be upheld - Held, yes [Paras 49, 50 and 51] [In favour of assessee]

V. Section  37(1) of the Income-tax Act, 1961 - Business expenditure - Allowability of (Prior period expenditure) - Assessment year  2017-18 - In tax audit report for assessment year 2018-19, assessee had disclosed prior period expenses of Rs. 61.17 lakhs, out of which Rs. 11.98 lakhs pertained to assessment year 2017-18 - Assessee suo motu disallowed same in assessment year 2018-19 and claimed deduction in assessment year 2017-18 on ground that expenditure related to that year - Assessing Officer disallowed claim - It was observed that though payment of expenses were made during subsequent assessment year 2018-19, said expenses were incurred for period pertaining to impugned assessment year - Whether since assessee followed mercantile system of accounting and expenses were incurred for impugned year though paid later, same allowable in year in which they pertained - Held, yes [Para 56] [In favour of assessee]

Determination of value in respect of certain supplies

32. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the provisions of this Chapter, the value in respect of supplies specified below shall, at the option of the supplier, be determined in the manner provided hereinafter.

(2) The value of supply of services in relation to the purchase or sale of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be determined by the supplier of services in the following manner, namely:—

(a)

for a currency, when exchanged from, or to, Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to the difference in the buying rate or the selling rate, as the case may be, and the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for that currency at that time, multiplied by the total units of currency:

Provided that in case where the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for a currency is not available, the value shall be one per cent of the gross amount of Indian Rupees provided or received by the person changing the money:

Provided further that in case where neither of the currencies exchanged is Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to one per cent of the lesser of the two amounts the person changing the money would have received by converting any of the two currencies into Indian Rupee on that day at the reference rate provided by the Reserve Bank of India:

Provided also that a person supplying the services may exercise the option to ascertain the value in terms of clause (b) for a financial year and such option shall not be withdrawn during the remaining part of that financial year.

(b)

at the option of the supplier of services, the value in relation to the supply of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be deemed to be—

(i)

one per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount up to one lakh rupees, subject to a minimum amount of two hundred and fifty rupees;

(ii)

one thousand rupees and half of a per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding one lakh rupees and up to ten lakh rupees; and

(iii)

five thousand and five hundred rupees and one tenth of a per cent of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding ten lakh rupees, subject to a maximum amount of sixty thousand rupees.

(3) The value of the supply of services in relation to booking of tickets for travel by air provided by an air travel agent shall be deemed to be an amount calculated at the rate of five per cent of the basic fare in the case of domestic bookings, and at the rate of ten per cent of the basic fare in the case of international bookings of passage for travel by air.

Explanation.—For the purposes of this sub-rule, the expression "basic fare" means that part of the air fare on which commission is normally paid to the air travel agent by the airlines.

(4) The value of supply of services in relation to life insurance business shall be,—

(a)

the gross premium charged from a policy holder reduced by the amount allocated for investment, or savings on behalf of the policy holder, if such an amount is intimated to the policy holder at the time of supply of service;

(b)

in case of single premium annuity policies other than (a), ten per cent of single premium charged from the policy holder; or

(c)

in all other cases, twenty five per cent of the premium charged from the policy holder in the first year and twelve and a half per cent of the premium charged from the policy holder in subsequent years:

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-rule shall apply where the entire premium paid by the policy holder is only towards the risk cover in life insurance.

(5) Where a taxable supply is provided by a person dealing in buying and selling of second hand goods i.e., used goods as such or after such minor processing which does not change the nature of the goods and where no input tax credit has been availed on the purchase of such goods, the value of supply shall be the difference between the selling price and the purchase price and where the value of such supply is negative, it shall be ignored:

Provided that the purchase value of goods repossessed from a defaulting borrower, who is not registered, for the purpose of recovery of a loan or debt shall be deemed to be the purchase price of such goods by the defaulting borrower reduced by five percentage points for every quarter or part thereof, between the date of purchase and the date of disposal by the person making such repossession.

(6) The value of a token, or a voucher, or a coupon, or a stamp (other than postage stamp) which is redeemable against a supply of goods or services or both shall be equal to the money value of the goods or services or both redeemable against such token, voucher, coupon, or stamp.

The Finance (No. 2) Act, 2014 has inserted three new sub-sections (7A), (7B) and (7C) in section 35AD which provide as under:

New sub-section (7A) provides that any asset in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under this section shall be used only for the specified business, for a period of eight years beginning with the previous year in which such asset is acquired or constructed. New sub-section (7B) deals with a situation where any asset, in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under this section is used for a purpose other than the specified business during the period specified in sub-section (7A) otherwise than by way of a mode referred to in clause (vii) of section 28. In such a case, the total amount of deduction so claimed and allowed in one or more previous years, as reduced by the amount of depreciation allowable in accordance with the provisions of section 32 as if no deduction under said section 35AD was allowed, shall be deemed to be the income of the assessee chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" of the previous year in which the asset is so used.

New sub-section (7C) provides that nothing contained in sub-section (7B) shall apply to a company which has become a sick industrial company under sub-section (1) of section 17 of the Sick Industrial Companies (Special Provisions) Act, 1985, during the period specified in sub-section (7A).

These amendments will take effect from 1st April, 2015 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2015-16 and subsequent assessment years.

The Explanatory Memorandum explains these amendments as under :

II. The existing provisions of section 35AD do not provide for a specific time period for which capital assets on which the deduction has been claimed and allowed, are to be used for the specified business. With a view to ensure that the capital asset on which investment linked deduction has been claimed is used for the purposes of the specified business, it is proposed to insert sub-section (7A) in section 35AD to provide that any asset in respect of which a deduction is claimed and allowed under section 35AD, shall be used only for the specified business for a period of eight years beginning with the previous year in which such asset is acquired or constructed.

If any asset on which a deduction under section 35AD has been allowed, is demolished, destroyed, discarded or transferred, the sum received or receivable for the same is chargeable to tax under clause (vii) of section 28. This does not take into account a case where asset on which deduction under section 35AD has been claimed is used for any purpose other than the specified business by way of a mode other than that specified above. Accordingly, it is proposed to insert sub-section (7B) to provide that if such asset is used for any purpose other than the specified business, the total amount of deduction so claimed and allowed in any previous year in respect of such asset, as reduced by the amount of depreciation allowable in accordance with the provisions of section 32 as if no deduction had been allowed under section 35AD, shall be deemed to be income of the assessee chargeable under the head "Profits and gains of business or profession" of the previous year in which the asset is so used.

Option for claiming deduction

4.4-5 The section provides that the deduction shall be ‘allowed to the assessee.’ In CIT v. Mahendra Mills [2000] 243 ITR 56/ 109 Taxman 225, the Supreme Court has held that the word ‘allowed’ in section 32(1) suggests that the depreciation claim is optional and it cannot be thrust upon the assessee: a thing is allowed when it is claimed. Having regard to this and the same expression allowed being used in section 35AD, it could be argued that the deduction under section 35AD is optional and it cannot be thrust upon the assessee. In such a situation the special provisions of section 28(vii), section 50B and section 73A should not become applicable to the assessee.

Allowability of discount on ZCB

4.5 Explanation to section 36(1)(iiia) provides for the definition of the expression ‘discount’ as the difference between the amount received or receivable by an issuer upon issue of a ZCB and the amount payable by such issuer upon maturity or redemption of such bond.

The said Explanation has been amended with effect from assessment year 2009-10 to include scheduled banks in the category of issuers. The amendment is consequent upon change in the definition of ZCB.

Extension of special deduction under section 36(1)(viii)

4.6 Section 36(1)(viii) provides special deduction to financial corporations and banking companies of an amount not exceeding 20% of the profits subject to creation of a reserve.

Hitherto, the benefit of section 36(1)(viii) was available, inter alia, to entities engaged in long-term financing for construction or purchase of houses in India for residential purpose. The definition of eligible business has now been amended with effect from assessment year 2010-11 to provide that eligible business will include provision of long-term finance for development of housing in India. In other words, corporations engaged in providing long-term finance (including re-financing) for development of housing in India will now be eligible for the benefit under section 36(1)(viii).

The amendment, however, deletes the expression ‘construction or purchase of houses in India’. Now, purchase of existing house may not result in development of housing and hence, it appears that an entity engaged in long term financing for purchase of house may not qualify for the deduction.

32. (1) Notwithstanding anything contained in the provisions of this Chapter, the value in respect of supplies specified below shall, at the option of the supplier, be determined in the manner provided hereinafter.

(2) The value of supply of services in relation to the purchase or sale of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be determined by the supplier of services in the following manner, namely:- (a) for a currency, when exchanged from, or to, Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to the difference in the buying rate or the selling rate, as the case may be, and the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for that currency at that time, multiplied by the total units of currency:

Provided that in case where the Reserve Bank of India reference rate for a currency is not available, the value shall be one per cent. of the gross amount of Indian Rupees provided or received by the person changing the money:

Provided further that in case where neither of the currencies exchanged is Indian Rupees, the value shall be equal to one per cent. of the lesser of the two amounts the person changing the money would have received by converting any of the two currencies into Indian Rupee on that day at the reference rate provided by the Reserve Bank of India.

Provided also that a person supplying the services may exercise the option to ascertain the value in terms of clause (b) for a financial year and such option shall not be withdrawn during the remaining part of that financial year.

(b) at the option of the supplier of services, the value in relation to the supply of foreign currency, including money changing, shall be deemed to be-

(b.i) one per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount up to one lakh rupees, subject to a minimum amount of two hundred and fifty rupees;

(b.ii) one thousand rupees and half of a per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding one lakh rupees and up to ten lakh rupees; and

(b.iii) five thousand and five hundred rupees and one tenth of a per cent. of the gross amount of currency exchanged for an amount exceeding ten lakh rupees, subject to a maximum amount of sixty thousand rupees.

(3) The value of the supply of services in relation to booking of tickets for travel by air provided by an air travel agent shall be deemed to be an amount calculated at the rate of five per cent. of the basic fare in the case of domestic bookings, and at the rate of ten per cent. of the basic fare in the case of international bookings of passage for travel by air.

Explanation.- For the purposes of this sub-rule, the expression "basic fare" means that part of the air fare on which commission is normally paid to the air travel agent by the airlines.

(4) The value of supply of services in relation to life insurance business shall be,-

(a)

the gross premium charged from a policy holder reduced by the amount allocated for investment, or savings on behalf of the policy holder, if such an amount is intimated to the policy holder at the time of supply of service;

(b)

in case of single premium annuity policies other than (a), ten per cent. of single premium charged from the policy holder; or

(c)

in all other cases, twenty five per cent. of the premium charged from the policy holder in the first year and twelve and a half per cent. of the premium charged from the policy holder in subsequent years:

Provided that nothing contained in this sub-rule shall apply where the entire premium paid by the policy holder is only towards the risk cover in life insurance.

(5) Where a taxable supply is provided by a person dealing in buying and selling of second hand goods i.e., used goods as such or after such minor processing which does not change the nature of the goods and where no input tax credit has been availed on the purchase of such goods, the value of supply shall be the difference between the selling price and the purchase price and where the value of such supply is negative, it shall be ignored:

The sum of Rs.37 lakhs retained under section 132 exceed the amount required to meet the liability under section 132B(1)(i) and the department is, therefore, liable to make payment of interest at the rate applicable from the date of expiry of 120 days under section 132(4) to the date of regular assessment/re-assessment or last such assessment or re-assessment, as the case may be. [Para 14]

Although section 132B(5) has been deleted by the Finance Act No. 2 of 2002 with effect from 1-6-2002 and on the same date section 132B(4) has been introduced. The principal of law as laid down in the case of Chironjilal Sharma (HUF) v. Union of India [2014] 360 ITR 237/222 Taxman 352/41 taxmann.com 274 (SC) is not diluted in any manner because of the said amendment. Therefore, the assessee is entitled to interest at the rates applicable on the sum of Rs. 37 lakhs for the pre-assessment period in accordance with section 132B(4)(b) at the rates applicable from time to time after expiry of 120 days from the date of the seizure till the date of the assessment. [Para 14]

So far as the prayer for interest under section 243/244A is concerned, two division benches of this Court in the case of Vijay Prakash Agrawal v. CIT (Central) [2013] 355 ITR 114 and in the case of Prayag Udyog (P.) Ltd. v. Union of India [2012] 348 ITR 217/[2013] 33 taxmann.com 599 (All.) have laid down that the assessee would be entitled to interest at the rates which were applicable from time to time on the amount due from the date of block assessment till the date of actual payment which aspect of the matter has been ignored by the authorities while making payment of interest at the flat rate of .5 per cent per month to the assessee. In view of the above, the assessee is held entitled to interest at the rates applicable from time to time under section 243A on this sum of Rs. 37 lakhs from the date the money became refundable till the date of actual refund. [Paras 16, 17]

So far as issue of payment of compensation for the inordinate delay in the payment of interest under section 132(B)(4) and section 244A is concerned, it has to be examined as to whether there has been unexplained inordinate delay in the matter of payment of interest within the statutory period by the department or not. [Para 17]

From the facts it is apparent that the assessee became entitled to payment of interest at least for the pre-assessment period from the date his appeal by the Commissioner was allowed. This payment of interest has been denied to the assessee without any justifiable cause even after expiry of 9 years from the date interest was payable. Similarly, for the post-assessment period, the assessee should have been paid interest on the sum of Rs. 37 lakhs refunded to him on 2-2-2007 from the date of the appellate order till the date money was so returned. It has taken nearly 8 years from the department to make the payment of the interest and that too on wrong conclusion. [Para 19]

The assessee must be compensated for retention of money, i.e., interest due under section 132B(4) and section 244A by the department for long duration, namely, 9 and 8 years. Such payment of compensation has been recognized and accepted in the case of Sandvik Asia Ltd. (supra), as also in the subsequent judgment of the Apex Court in the case of CIT v. Gujarat Flouro Chemicals [2012] 348 ITR 319/210 Taxman 583/24 taxmann.com 338. [Para 20]

The department was legally not justified in retention of the amount of interest which was payable to the assessee both under section 134B(4) as well as under section 243A for the period of nearly 9 and 8 years respectively. The case of the assessee falls within the category of cases where there has been inordinate delay on the part of the department to pay the statutory interest and, therefore, the assessee is entitled to be compensated for such wrongful retention of the money by the department. In the facts of the case the assessee is entitled to be compensated at the same rates, i.e. 9 per cent as was provided for by the Apex Court in the case of Sandvik Asia Ltd. (supra). [Para 21]

Section 15(2)(b): Gurjinder Singh Sandhu, In re [2022] 145 taxmann.com 455/[2023] 96 GST 214/2023 (69) G.S.T.L. 321 (AAR – Uttarakhand) In this case, the recipient of goods has provided fuel to the applicant being a transporter, free of cost for transportation of goods. AAR held that the fuel provided free of cost shall form part of the value of supply in terms of Section 15(2)(b) of CGST Act as this cost of input incurred by recipient (as per the terms of agreement) has to be paid by the supplier.

Section 15(2)(c): Global Vectra Helicorp Ltd., In re [2021] 133 taxmann.com 382/[2022] 89 GST 588 (AAAR – Gujarat)

In this case appellant has arranged for ATF to fly the helicopter in order to supply rental service of helicopter to ONGC. Appellant collected the said amount in form of reimbursement from the recipient. Appellate Authority rejected the argument of appellant that the responsibility of arrangement of ATF is that of recipient since without ATF the appellant will not be a position to supply rental service. Also, whether there is any mark-up or otherwise on the reimbursement of ATF is not the sole factor for determination of value of supply. Appellate Authority has held that the arrangement of ATF for flying of helicopter is the activity done by appellant at time or before supply of renting service. Therefore, in terms of Section 15(2)(c) of CGST Act, the said amount is to be included in the value of supply of renting service.

Section 15(2)(d): Continental Engineering Corporation, In re [2021] 133 taxmann.com 75/2021 (55) G.S.T.L. 476/[2022] 89 GST 123 (AAR – Telangana)

In this case applicant has sought advance ruling with respect to taxability of compensation received pursuant to an arbitration filed for the work completed in pre-GST era. One of the item on which applicant has sought advance ruling includes taxability of interest on delayed payment of the compensation granted by arbitration tribunal. In this regard, AAR held that the said interest component is to be included in the value of taxable supply in terms of Section 15(2)(d) of CGST Act and therefore exigible to GST.

Section 15(2)(e): Hitze Boilers (P.) Ltd., In re [Order No. KAR. ADRG 32 of 2023, dated 15-9-2023]

Applicant in this case has sought advance ruling with respect to value to be considered for discharging GST liability since the recipient is of the view that value shall be considered after reducing the amount of subsidy received from Government. AAR held that since the subsidy received in the present case is neither directly linked to the price nor it affects the price of the supply and therefore the same is includable in the value of supply in terms of Section 15(2)(e) of CGST Act.

Sub-section (3) provides for deduction from value of supply towards discount component. The parameters under which discount can be reduced from value of supply are as below:

(a)

Discount given before or at the time of supply if the same is mentioned in the invoice

(b)

In case of post sales discount, if such discount is established in terms of agreement entered into at or before the time of supply and ITC corresponding to the same has been reversed

In one of the judicial pronouncement, the appellate authority has interpreted the above parameters in the following manner:

Santhosh Distributors, In re [2021] 132 taxmann.com 15/88 GST 566 (AAAR – Ker.)

Appellate authority held that the quantum of discount cannot be defined as open ended in the agreement be i.e. not based on any criteria. The parameter for determining the discount has to be clearly specified in the agreement i.e. bare use of the term discount without shall not fulfil the requirement of Section 15(3)(b)(i) of CGST Act. Further, the appellate authority held that in case where discount is reimbursed, the same shall partake the character of consideration.

Rule 27- This rule provides for valuation in case where consideration is not wholly in money. Section 43(1) of the Act defines actual cost. The definition does not specify the criteria as to what expenditures should be included in actual cost (i.e. components of actual cost). The definition merely specifies that portion of actual cost met by any other person or authority must be excluded from 'actual cost'. There are 15 existing Explanations in section 43(1) which specify how actual cost is to be worked out in various situations as per the Table below: 7.6A-1 New proviso inserted by Finance Act, 2017 to exclude from actual cost any expenditure involving cash payment above the threshold of Rs. 10,000

In order to discourage cash transactions even for capital expenditure, the Finance Act, 2017 has amended the provisions of section 43(1) of the Act by inserting a new proviso. The new proviso provides that where an assessee incurs any expenditure for acquisition of any asset in respect which a payment or aggregate of payments made to a person in a day, otherwise than by an account payee cheque drawn on a bank or account payee bank draft or use of electronic clearing system through a bank account, exceeds ten thousand rupees, such expenditure shall be ignored for the purposes of determination of actual cost of such asset.

These amendments will take effect from 1st April, 2018 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2018-19 and subsequent years.

7.6A-2 New proviso inserted in Explanation 13 to section 43(1) as regards situation where deduction allowed u/s 35AD is deemed income

Clause (1) of section 43 defines "actual cost" for the purposes of claiming depreciation under section 32 of the Act in certain situations. However, there is no clarity on determination of actual cost for the purposes of allowance of depreciation of such assets in respect of which the deduction which is already allowed in a pre-vious year under section 35AD of the Act, is withdrawn in terms of sub-section (7B) of the said section.

In light of the recommendations of Income-tax simplification committee and to bring clarity, provisions of the section 43 of the Act have been amended to provide that where any capital asset in respect of which deduction allowed under section 35AD is deemed to be the income of the assessee in accordance with the provisions of sub-section (7B) of the said section, the actual cost to the assessee shall be the actual cost to the assessee, as reduced by an amount equal to the amount of depreciation calculated at the rate in force that would have been allowable had the asset been used for the purposes of business since the date of its acquisition.

This amendment will take effect from 1st April, 2018 and will, accordingly, apply in relation to the assessment year 2018-19 and subsequent years.

7.6A-3 In case of conflict between ICDS-V (new) and section 43(1), section 43(1) shall prevail

ICDS-V (new) requires inclusion of all expenditure that meets the criteria in Para 5 of ICDS-V (new). This is irrespective of mode of payment of expenditure involved. However, the new proviso in section 43(1) (See Para 7.6A-1 above) provides for exclusion from actual cost of cash expenditure above threshold of Rs. 10000. The new proviso to section 43(1) shall prevail over Para 5 of ICDS-V (New) and the expenditure involving cash payment above Rs. 10000 shall be excluded from actual cost even if it meets the criteria of Para 5 of ICDS-V (New)

"Tangible fixed asset" is an asset being land, building, machinery, plant or furniture held with the intention of being used for the purpose of producing or providing goods or services and is not held for sale in the normal course of business. [Para 2(1)(a) of ICDS-V (New)]

7.7-2 "Fair value"

"Fair value" of an asset is the amount for which that asset could be exchanged between knowledgeable, willing parties in an arm's length transaction. [Para 2(1)(b) of ICDS-V (New)]

Words and expressions used and not defined in this Income Computation and Disclosure Standard but defined in the Act shall have the meanings assigned to them in that Act. [Para 2(2) of ICDS-V (New)]
